NGSA engine selection: RR, PW and CFM
pw_solo: conditional launch triggered by ngsa

public_statements.boeing:
We said we would turn this big ship, and I think we've turned it. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and MAX 10 are certified, and our balance sheet is back where it belongs. That is the work of a lot of people doing it the right way, and the financials followed our production performance.

It doesn't change how we run the place. The 737 line stays on the plan we've laid out, and the KPIs tell us when we're ready, not the calendar. We'll keep building 787 capacity in Charleston, because customers want more of that airplane and we intend to keep it the most efficient in its segment.

On a new airplane, our thinking hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. When we do, it will be planned around a stable supply of parts, starting with engines, and more than one engine source. I'm not going to give a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, we'll set the schedule with headroom in it, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s, and we plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. We are inviting all three narrowbody engine makers, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, to power it. A stable, diversified engine supply is a condition of a disciplined and controlled ramp-up and of serving our customers well. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: we will keep its lines running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We will take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we will keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we will recruit and train, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build this aircraft.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. Our customers fly LEAP and GEnx today, and our job is to deliver those engines and keep them on wing. LEAP durability upgrades are going into new engines and, through the shops, into the fleet. On the 787 we're upgrading the GEnx, because our airline customers make their money on time on wing, and so do we.

Here's what we don't know: when the next narrowbody will be launched, and by whom. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. CFM, with our partners at Safran, will be ready to support every airframer that moves, with a LEAP derivative or with a new engine. CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: I'll start with the bad news. For years the GTF fleet was not where our customers needed it to be. We own that, and we have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. So we control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch. It will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life, and time on wing, not just fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. It comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. For the fleet flying today, the GTF Hot Section kit is available at shop visit on standard terms, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. When we've seen the demand and we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. Our route into the narrowbody is a partnership, not a solo programme: Rolls-Royce stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. We take a narrowbody engine forward only for an airframe that has chosen it. Entry into service will be no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation, with in-service support through partner shops in place before entry into service. We don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
public_statements.embraer: Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We focused on delivering the results in our plan to 2030 with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. We keep doing that, with a very healthy cash generation to support a potential next move. On a new product, I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies because it is important that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. We need a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. Any large investment will be made with partners, and we talk to many partners and to all the engine makers. Today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. This does not depend only on us. It depends on the technology available in the market and on the partners, and the investment has to prove its return. On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions, and I can only speak for Embraer. On trade, Embraer is about engineering, and we focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic. We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost.

boeing.detail: Production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. Funded inside the debt lines. Not priced on the board.

boeing.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply
boeing.detail: Tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. No launch, no date and no engine selection this round. Serves Control's engine enabler without paying a premium (Board recommendation 9; inference).

airbus.move: Open NGSA engine selection: code 7 (CFM, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce)
airbus.detail: We announce that NGSA is open to all three narrowbody engine makers, with CFM as the floor. The invitation gives P&W and RR a live airframe that selects them this round, so their launch_if_selected engines can be ready by an EIS in the second half of the decade (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037). It is a request and costs nothing. No Airbus payment is offered to induce an engine launch: any such payment would be a separate Board item above EUR 300m, and none is proposed [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

Agreements with CFM and P&W cover the LEAP-1A and GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan through about 2045. Framework agreements with all three makers cover NGSA engines. Both are backed by long-range rate signals given early, as for the A320neo ramp [A-0159]. Announced in general terms only, with no volumes or internal plan targets [AX-0005].

airbus.move: Recruiting and training for the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training for NGSA engineering and the 2040s ramp, through schools and our European and global footprint [A-0485]. It does not target any rival's staff.

airbus.move: Industry-coalition trade advocacy: zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace
airbus.detail: We work with industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing included as an ally on trade, to keep a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
cfm.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme, with no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. We give no entry date and no flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice, and Safran is a full partner in RISE.
LEAP durability hardware keeps going into new engines and, at shop visits, into the fleet. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]. We report facts only, with no new promise dates [CX-0436].

pratt_whitney.detail: P&W will launch GTF2 in any round in which an airframer selects a code that includes P&W, sole or shared (codes 2, 6, 7). It is ready six years from launch, on standard terms, and does not enter service until durability is proven. No EIS date is stated, nothing is said about an airframer's dates, and no selection is claimed. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section durability kit for the in-service fleet
pratt_whitney.detail: Offered at shop visit on standard terms; upgrades are sold, not given [PX-0100]. No time-on-wing number is announced until it is proven in service (Mitchill's ground-4 advice). No grid effect [PX-0088][PX-0106].
No launch-style pricing, concessions or free upgrades to win a selection. We are not in the early entry phase [PX-0055]. No grid effect.

rolls_royce.move: Open the door to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney
rolls_royce.detail: The public statement says Rolls-Royce prefers a partner for the narrowbody and stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the UltraFan technology we bring. No dates. It is not a `jv_with_pw: commit` order; we commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record (the Board's rule, and the team rule of partner first).

rolls_royce.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
rolls_royce.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work goes on inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing. No programme launch, no new bill, no dates.

embraer.move: Deliver the plan to 2030 and build cash for a potential next move
embraer.detail: Keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan. Productivity comes before new capacity, and commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it. The cash this builds is there to support a potential next move [EX-0080, EX-0081, EX-0053, EX-0079]. The board does not price this move.

embraer.move: Keep technology readiness funded for a new product cycle
embraer.detail: Studies continue for a new cycle of products, naming no segment and no date. We keep talking to all the engine makers and select none, since engine selection comes before any business case [EX-0112, EX-0141, EX-0133, EX-0044]. We stay prepared to make that decision when the time comes.

embraer.move: Trade: argue for zero tariffs on aerospace, on data
embraer.detail: More than 40% of our aircraft is US content [EX-0124]. Tariffs mean fewer aircraft sold in the US, fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs [EX-0101]. We ask both governments to talk and take no side, and we discuss no politics [EX-0100, EX-0098, EX-0106].

boeing.move: CFM LEAP-1B capacity and durability support
boeing.detail: Joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our rate and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325], with embedded staff on durability. Our narrowbody is single-source today: CFM supplies about 2,592 narrowbody engines a year across both airframers (Pope's figure).

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
boeing.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Any future rate step needs demonstrated supplier output at the new rate first [B-2308].

Ask GE and Rolls-Royce for widebody engine proposals for a re-engined 787, durability first, so that a 2035 re-test has an engine on the record (Pope's launch condition). No commitment. No re-engined 787 built at rate before certification [BX-1263].

boeing.move: fps definition and production-system maturation (no launch, no date)
boeing.detail: Keep the fps team on requirements, the production system and Renton transition planning, so that a 2035 business case can be brought on the grid. Pope's condition applies: take down each Renton MAX line only after the fps is certified and has shown rate. No fixed-price development terms [BX-1262, BX-1304].

airbus.move: CFM capacity watch for the single-source floor case
airbus.detail: If P&W and RR hold, CFM carries all NGSA engines plus 60% of the A320neo tail: about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41 on Alt, against 51 today, while it also supplies Boeing [A-0731, A-0563]. We give CFM an early rate signal for that case and review its capacity at the 2035 round. This is Wagner's flag, not a fail. It protects our own supply and claims no capacity against anyone.

airbus.move: Secure our own raw materials and work packages
airbus.detail: Titanium forgings through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing (DED) to relieve titanium demand, continuity of rare-earth supply on the raw-materials watchlist, and integration of the Spirit work packages, all for our own ramp [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0455, A-0457, A-0458]. Supplier payment discipline for SMEs and continuous monitoring with alternative sources [A-0479, A-0360].

airbus.move: Run-at-rate wing demonstrator as the NGSA producibility gate
airbus.detail: The production system matures with the aircraft. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year. It never accelerates it and never cancels it [A-0443, A-0225, AX-0006].

airbus.move: Capital allocation through the NGSA development years (Board record)
airbus.detail: Toepfer's condition, which I accept: the dividend flexes within the 30-50% payout range, and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. The EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year. European launch aid is upside only, on market terms, and the plan never depends on it [AX-0102, AG-0058, AG-0059, AX-0004].

cfm.move: Engine talks with every airframer, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: CFM stays open to Airbus, Boeing and Embraer: a LEAP derivative, and a new CFM engine once an airframer commits. We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. No price, no launch-era terms and no concession. Any CFM narrowbody terms are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

Ali works the 9 suppliers behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613] to hold the LEAP climb to 2,553 engines in 2034 alongside the GE9X. He measures supplier output so that we know whether the stack can be carried before any 2035 launch [CX-0633, CX-0540]. There is no capital commitment and no board effect.

pratt_whitney.move: Exit plan written into the GTF2 package
pratt_whitney.detail: If the order triggers and the selecting airframe is cancelled, or goes publicly off P&W, before GTF2 is ready in 2036, a cancel is reviewed in 2035. The write-off is $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, which saves $0.33B against running on. The GTF2 stays protected while a live airframe whose code includes P&W can still be served. Eddy reports 2035 readiness against each live EIS.

pratt_whitney.move: Durability gate and design-freeze data (internal instruction to Eddy)
pratt_whitney.detail: If triggered: severe-environment endurance testing, and all life-limited parts at full life by the 2036 ready year. The test programme is not compressed to hold a 2037 EIS. Bring the 2030 GTF Advantage and Hot Section fleet removal data before the GTF2 hot-section design freezes. Any new feature not proven in time waits for a later block. Airbus engines and fleet lift keep first call on castings and forgings.

pratt_whitney.move: Forging capacity watch for an Embraer narrowbody on today's GTF (S8)
pratt_whitney.detail: Forging capacity takes 2 to 2.5 years to add [P-0079], so plan early for the ramp toward 8 a month and watch the 2034-40 window where GTF2 development, the Embraer ramp and the A320neo GTF could overlap. Internal planning only; no capital order and no grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce: no commitment, revisit on trigger
pratt_whitney.detail: Revisit in 2035 only if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7. At that point check the ready date: formation + 6, or 2036 with a 2030 GTF2 folded in. Terms share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233].

rolls_royce.detail: A no-capex study of partner-shop MRO on the Singapore Joint Venture model and of P&W's narrowbody network, plus narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers rather than on the Trent lines. If a Joint Venture is formed in 2035 the support plan is ready to name, so it is in place before any EIS.

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

embraer.move: Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
embraer.detail: The talks continue under the July 2026 civil MoU (research, unverified), and I follow them personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034]. On this brief's terms, a launch reaches zero only with our own share near 35%: partners near 65%, about $2.0B more than the $4.5B the brief shows. Nothing counts until a brief shows that money. No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control, and no military technology moves, so the state's consent should not be needed (golden share; inference).

embraer.move: Prepare the 2035 readiness package (CFO funding and ops window and supply)
embraer.detail: Santana brings the 2035 Launch row: the partner share that would close the gap, the net-debt path against the inherited 2x comfort and the ~$2B cash floor, and the risk column against the 5-point limit. Meijer counts the 2035 window (entry into service 2039) from this round's bulletin. He also maps supplier headroom for a second line beside the E2 ramp: about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039, 1.8 times the 2030 target, with bottlenecks that move between suppliers [EX-0088, EX-0159]. He sets certification of a clean sheet in four years against the E2's roughly five.

boeing.public_statement:
We said we would turn this big ship, and I think we've turned it. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and MAX 10 are certified, and our balance sheet is back where it belongs. That is the work of a lot of people doing it the right way, and the financials followed our production performance.

It doesn't change how we run the place. The 737 line stays on the plan we've laid out, and the KPIs tell us when we're ready, not the calendar. We'll keep building 787 capacity in Charleston, because customers want more of that airplane and we intend to keep it the most efficient in its segment.

On a new airplane, our thinking hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. When we do, it will be planned around a stable supply of parts, starting with engines, and more than one engine source. I'm not going to give a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, we'll set the schedule with headroom in it, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field. fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no order goes to the Board as an item.

H1 AND H3 RULING (Board recommendation 2). I lift H1 (no fps in Round 1) and the first half of H3 (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) for 2030. Their 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and debt not yet repaired [B-2326, BX-1305]. By 2030:
- the 777X has delivered since 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
- the MAX 7/10 is certified [BX-1873];
- on the tracker, net debt is $0.0B at end-2029 ($3.3B in the stress case, then $0.0B in 2030) (brief §2);
- Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' gate passes;
- the 'about two more years' I gave in July 2026 [BG-0068] has run.
Lifting the rules opens the question; it does not answer it. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 stand. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

MY FOUR TESTS
(1) KPIs [BX-1271]. Pope confirms that no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live and the board has no injects, so the gate is open. She notes the brief gives only the absence of a problem, not measured KPIs.
(2) Market, technology and balance sheet [BX-1296]:
- balance sheet: ready;
- technology: not binding;
- market: fails for the fps. Every fps row is at least $4.41B below Do Nothing in every column. The best is the 10-year at Renton: -4.41 (S1, S4) to -6.03 (S8).
(3) Certification slip [BX-1319], Malave's buffer test on S6 against Do Nothing's -0.07 (limit -2.07). Every fps row fails:
- 10-year at Renton -5.45 (gap -5.38); at new sites -5.84 (-5.77);
- the best fps row, 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, -3.23 (-3.16);
- 7-year -6.52 to -10.32;
- via Embraer -21.53 to -24.60.
His veto binds on every fps row and I accept it. I would have reached the same answer anyway: the S2-to-S6 gap is only $0.00-0.09B, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. The Re-engine (+3.23) and the Rate Increase (-0.91) pass the buffer.
(4) Doing less, better [BX-1239]. Only the Re-engine beats Do Nothing by more than ε, and only outside S4 and S5. No fps clears it.

LEVER BY LEVER
fps: hold. It fails the business case, Malave's binding veto and the Board's tests. The engine enabler would need an objective premium of at least $4.41B ($5.38B in S2), more than twice the $2B cap, so I do not pay it.
- Via Embraer is rejected. It runs $17.48-17.49B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S6 and $13.57-14.08B behind in S7-S8 (Pope's correction, accepted). Its undiscounted debt penalty is $52.5B, and on its own it breaks the stress case (peak $1.8-3.1B).
- Engine code stays null while the fps is held.
- fps_site stays new_site. Renton (+0.36 to +1.32, about $3.0B of capex avoided) will be weighed at launch, subject to Pope's wind-down condition.

Rate Increase: hold. Pope's gate is open and Airbus is not the reason (H6), but the grid prices the step below zero in every column: -0.45 (S1, S4), -0.84 (S2, S5, S6), -1.05 (S3), -0.86 (S7), -1.15 (S8).
- Capacity does not bind until 2039 (Pope: 20-189 idle slots a year in 2030-38).
- The step would add about 200 LEAP-1B engines a year to a single source.
- It is offered only in 2030, so holding gives it up for good, but at no grid cost: hold is $0.84B better in S2. It is not a premium.

787 Re-engine: hold, under the Board's risk limit. This is the one place my orders leave the grid's best plan in my expected column, so I set out the case in full.
For it:
- +3.30 against Do Nothing in S1-S3 and S6-S8;
- the best plan in S2 (+3.23 against -0.07);
- it passes Malave's buffer and keeps every debt line, stress peak $0.0B;
- undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B;
- Pope finds operations ready (strain $0, one development);
- company doctrine (§6) allows a 2030 Re-engine when no fps is in development.
Against it:
- it shows -2.48 in S4 and S5, where Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round. That breaks the Board's $1B-per-item limit in two plausible columns, and the Board has said it would veto. I have no override, and I will not bring the Board a case that fails its own stated test.
- Pope's launch condition is not met: no widebody engine is on the record, and an UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036, a year after a 2035 EIS. I do not launch an airplane on an engine that is not there yet [BX-1298].
- On Malave's breakevens, the Re-engine clears ε only if the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below 39.8% (57.1% for any gain at all). Doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt (profile §7, inference), and my confidence on Airbus is Low.
- My independent check [BX-1316] would not carry it as a plan we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0548].
Logged: the $3.30B it gives up in S2 is the Board's binding risk limit, not a management premium.
The option stays open. Malave and Pope both confirm that a Re-engine deferred to 2035 overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by only 2 years, which is legal under H4 ($1.2B of undiscounted strain). If an A350 Re-engine reaches the record, H3 bars ours for good and we stand aside; in S4 that saves $2.48B against having launched. I re-test it on the 2035 brief.

GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1-S8)
- Submitted row, Do Nothing: -0.12 / -0.07 / -0.29 / -2.74 / -2.69 / -0.07 / -2.80 / -2.83.
- Re-engine row, for reference: +3.18 / +3.23 / +3.01 / -5.22 / -5.17 / +3.23 / +0.50 / +0.47.
- Rate Increase row: -0.57 / -0.91 / -1.34 / -3.19 / -3.53 / -0.91 / -3.66 / -3.98.
- Best fps row, 10-year at Renton: -4.53 / -5.45 / -6.02 / -7.15 / -8.07 / -5.45 / -8.32 / -8.86.
Expected column S2; risk case S6.

OBJECTIVE METRICS (Do Nothing)
- Repair the balance sheet: net debt at the historical level in 2029. Met.
- Keep it repaired: held at $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050. Met.
- Stress case: back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B. Met.
- Incumbency: worst year 40.0%. Met.
- 50/50 split: worst year 40.0% (42.7% in 2040). Not met.

[BX-1271] (2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305] (3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave's risk-case column. The grid, as item value against Do Nothing in each column. The grid's ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted debt penalty; I do not subtract it again.

- fps via Embraer: -19.21 to -23.61. S6 is -23.32 / -22.94. On its own it breaks the stress case (peak $1.8-3.1B). It runs about $17-18B behind the best Solo launch in every column.

Answers to my four questions as I read the brief.

(2) Readiness: the balance sheet is ready on the tracker, and technology is not binding (earliest fps EIS 2037). The market leg fails: every fps row is at least $4.41B below Do Nothing in every column. That is not all three.
(3) Certification slip: S6 is the risk case. Every fps fails Malave's $2B buffer by $5.38B or more; the Re-engine passes.
(4) Doing less, better: only the Re-engine beats Do Nothing by more than ε, and only outside S4/S5.

My own red line: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263].

frame.initial_lean:
On the fps and the 737, my lean is Do Nothing. Hold the fps, hold the Rate Increase, keep fps_site at new_site and leave the engine code null.

The fps has to wait for a business case. I have lifted H1, but the market leg fails: every launch is at least $4.41B below Do Nothing in every column, and every launch fails Malave's buffer by $3.16B or more. Meeting the engine enabler this round would need a premium of at least $4.41B, more than twice the $2B cap. When the fps does come, I expect the 10-year ramp, no date before launch, a conservative EIS, and a code chosen with the enabler in mind.

The Rate Increase loses value in every column, so holding it costs nothing on the grid and is no premium.

The 787 Re-engine is the one open question, and the data points toward it.
- It is a derivative, not a clean sheet [BX-1247].
- It is the grid's best plan in six of eight columns, including my expected column, S2 (Airbus launches NGSA): +3.23 against -0.07.
- It passes the buffer test, keeps every debt line, and sequences ahead of a 2035 fps with no overlap.
- Company doctrine already allows a 2030 Re-engine when no fps is in development.
- Under H8 I cannot drop $3.30B in my expected column for a soft doctrine reason.

So if Malave's test and Pope's readiness results come back clean, I lean to bring the Re-engine to the Board as our one tested case. I would show the full eight-column row against the same row with re787 at hold.

I say plainly that the downside is real. If Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round (S4, S5) it is -2.48 against Do Nothing, beyond the Board's $1B limit, and the Board has said it would veto. If it does, I revise to its alternative, hold. I would log the $3.30B given up in S2 as the Board's risk limit, not as a management premium, and re-test the Re-engine next round, never after an A350 Re-engine (H3).

If Pope flags engineering, engine or supplier readiness, I hold it myself, because readiness outranks the grid. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early.

tests.name: Buffer test, slip leg (my veto): the fps-hold rows
tests.threshold: In S6 (Risk case: NGSA plus Airbus Delay Tactics), the plan may be no more than $2B below Do Nothing's -0.07, so at or above -2.07. I run it as the baseline, not as a sensitivity.

tests.numbers: Ask (1), one correction. S6, gap to Do Nothing in brackets. 10-year: new sites -5.84 (-5.77); Renton -5.45 (-5.38); with the Re-engine -3.62 (-3.55); Renton with the Re-engine -3.23 (-3.16). That last is the best fps row and is still $1.16B outside the limit. With the Rate Increase: -7.11 (-7.04), Renton -6.59 (-6.52), plus the Re-engine -4.89 (-4.82), Renton -4.37 (-4.30). 7-year: alone -8.86 (-8.79); Renton -7.82 (-7.75); range from -6.52 (-6.45, Renton with the Re-engine) to -10.32 (-10.25, with the Rate Increase). tests.name: Meet and beat
tests.threshold: Expected column S2 (named by the CEO). Among plans within ε ($1B) of the best, prefer the one with the higher worst column (inference). Each plan's worst column is also reported against Do Nothing, as advice.
tests.numbers: Ask (5). The best in S2 is 'fps: hold + 787 Re-engine' at +3.23. 'fps: hold + 737 rate up + 787 Re-engine' at +2.39 is within ε (gap 0.84). Their worst columns are -5.22 (S4) and -6.01 (S5), so the Re-engine alone wins and the Rate Increase drops out. Advice: Do Nothing is $3.30B behind in S2, outside ε, but its worst column is -2.83 (S8) against the Re-engine's -5.22. In the same column the Re-engine is -5.22 vs -2.74 (S4) and -5.17 vs -2.69 (S5): -2.48 each time, a larger downside than my $2B buffer allows on the slip leg. Breakeven chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine: 3.30/5.78 = 57.1% for expected value, and 2.30/5.78 = 39.8% to clear ε. The CEO's arithmetic is confirmed. My view: the +3.30 holds barring a same-round A350 Re-engine. That condition is outside our control, and company doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt (profile §7). So I would not carry the Re-engine this round as a plan we can meet and potentially beat.

tests.name: Balance sheet first
tests.threshold: The grid's ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted debt penalty (α 0.30, debt × α × (debt ÷ EV)², debt $45B, EV $130B), so it is never subtracted again. Undiscounted figures are for scale only and are not additive. Within ε on the expected column, prefer the smaller added penalty (inference).
tests.numbers: Ask (2), confirmed. The rules net the debt penalty in airframer payoffs, and I do not count it twice. tests.threshold: When each bill lands on the board (at EIS) and on the tracker (as spent, on the standard curve), whether two land together, and whether all three debt lines hold, stress case included, with the peak from 2030.
tests.numbers:
Ask (3). Board booking for a 2030 launch: Re-engine $5B in 2035; Rate Increase $2.94B in 2032; 10-year fps $60.32B in 2040; 7-year $65.00B in 2037; via Embraer $100B in 2040. No two land in the same year. Tracker spend, where programme cash enters free cash flow at 79%:

- 10-year fps: about $6.0B a year over 2030-39, roughly $3.0B in year 1 (5%) and $8.4B at the year-7 peak (2036). That is $6.7B after the 79%, below stress FCF, so $0.0B in every column.

- Rate Increase: about $1.0B a year over 2030-32.
Other rows that break the stress case:
- 7-year with the Re-engine: at new sites in every column ($2.4-2.7B); at Renton in S4, S5, S7 and S8 ($1.6-1.9B).
- 7-year with the Rate Increase at new sites: S7 and S8 ($0.7B).
- 7-year with the Rate Increase and the Re-engine: at new sites in every column ($2.6-2.8B); at Renton in S4, S5, S7 and S8 ($1.8-2.0B).
- Via Embraer at Renton, alone: every column ($1.8-2.3B).

Chosen row (Do Nothing): net debt reaches $0 in 2029; held at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050; stress case back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B; one engine source (CFM) on our narrowbody in 2050, and two makers in the market.

tests.name: H4 strain overlap and sequencing
tests.threshold: A Solo fps (EIS-7 to EIS) and the 787 Re-engine (EIS-5 to EIS) may overlap at most 2 years. Strain costs $3B × overlap years ÷ 5 before discounting, and I count it as cost while debt is high (inference).

A 7-year fps with the Re-engine overlaps 2030-35, 5 years, $3.0B; barred by H4. cfo.memo:
Kelly, my test on the grid's own numbers, with the risk case as the baseline.

The buffer test, the slip leg: S6 no more than $2B below Do Nothing's -0.07. Every fps fails it. The best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -3.23, $3.16B below; the 10-year at Renton alone $5.38B; the 7-year $6.45-10.25B; via Embraer $21.46-24.53B. The fps fails on its base case, not the slip: Delay Tactics move it $0.09B at most. That veto binds under the team rule.

The fps-hold rows pass, but S6 equals S2 for each, so the risk case does not test the Re-engine. Its risk column is S4/S5: -2.48 against Do Nothing, more than my buffer and beyond the Board's $1B limit. Your breakevens, 57% and 40%, are right. The +3.30 holds barring a same-round A350 Re-engine, a condition we do not control. I would not carry it as a plan we can meet and potentially beat. Hold it, log the $3.30B in S2 as the Board's risk limit, and re-test it in 2035.

The Rate Increase passes the buffer but loses $0.45-1.15B in every column: hold.

Do Nothing keeps every debt line: zero net debt in 2029, 2030 in the stress case, peak $0.0B. The 777X is cash-positive from 2029, so the fps is fundable; what it lacks is a business case.

It's maintaining the focus on fully restoring the health of our balance sheet, and we're bullish on our outlook.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record: BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S6 (NGSA plus Delay Tactics) against S2 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. Where S6 does not test a plan's own date, read its worst column.
tests.numbers: S6 minus S2, by plan: Do Nothing 0.00; 787 Re-engine 0.00 (+3.23 in both); Rate Increase 0.00; fps 10-year -0.03 (Renton 0.00); fps 7-year -0.09 (Renton -0.06); via Embraer -0.02. Under Delay Tactics, under 1% of any row depends on the fps date. Every fps row fails on its bill, not on its date. S6 does not test the Re-engine's own date. Its worst columns are S4 and S5 (-5.22 and -5.17, item -2.48), which is a rival-timing risk, not a delivery risk. The grid does not price a Re-engine slip. The doctrine prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). My sensitivity: about $0.31B of item value per year of slip (+3.30 x (1 - 1/1.105)), or $0.60B for 2 years, within epsilon (inference). 737 MAX at 57 a month from 2030: 47 cleared at the FAA capstone in May 2026 [BG-0069]. Then 52 and 57 in steps of 5, at least 6 months apart [B-2351], is reachable by mid-2027 at the earliest. The plan dates 57 to 2030, which leaves headroom. Basis: doctrine for the rate; my record for the delivery-first rule.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase: my binding veto (doctrine; CEO asks 1 and 2)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Never a reply to Airbus (H6).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. The gate is open, so my veto has no ground this round. Airbus has launched nothing (bulletin), so H6's Airbus half is not engaged. Tempo: +100 aircraft a year from 2032 is +8.3 a month on 57, about 65. That is two steps of 5 (62, 67) inside 2030-32, feasible on tempo. On the brief, the line is stable at the public plan of 57 (Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line). The brief carries no KPI data beyond the absence of a problem: I confirm only that, not a measured six-KPI result [B-2283, B-2274].

tests.name: Supplier readiness, a hard gate (doctrine)
tests.threshold: No move without demonstrated supplier output at the new rate [B-2308]; above 47, the supply chain binds [B-2340].
tests.numbers: Recommended package (737 at the public 57, 787 as planned): pass, with no live supply problem in the brief. Rate Increase: not demonstrated, so it gets advice, not a veto. A step to about 65 adds 200 LEAP-1B engines a year to a single source. That is +7.7% on CFM's 2,592 narrowbody engines a year (our 684 aircraft plus 60% of Airbus's 1,020), on top of the aftermarket and durability work [BX-1264, BX-1325]. The 2018 step to 52 broke Spirit and CFM supply [B-1449]. 787 Re-engine: see the readiness test. The engine is the one input not on the record.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity (doctrine; H4; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years. Strain is $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS. One major development at a time [B-0341].
tests.numbers: Recommended package (fps held, Re-engine 2030-35): overlap 0, strain $0. Same-round 10-year fps and Re-engine: 2033-40 against 2030-35 is 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, legal. Same-round 7-year fps and Re-engine: 2030-37 against 2030-35 is 5 years, $3.0B, which breaches H4. Sequencing (CEO's arithmetic confirmed): a Re-engine launched now leaves a 2035 fps free, with a 10-year window of 2038-45 and a 7-year window of 2035-42, so 0 overlap either way. That is the 'feather in' pattern [B-1393]. A Re-engine deferred to 2035 would overlap a 2035 7-year fps by 5 years (barred) and a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years. If the Re-engine slips the doctrine's 2 years, a 2035 7-year fps would overlap it in practice by 2 years (2035-37), still within H4. The 10-year fps would not overlap it at all. Engineering: the 777X has delivered since 2027 and the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026, so the Re-engine is the one major development. The Charleston expansion is production capacity, not development [BX-1317, B-2336].

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2030 launch and a 2035 EIS (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Engineering capacity free; no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; supplier and engine readiness by EIS, with durability addressed [BX-1298].
tests.numbers: This is a conditional pass: not a stop, but a launch condition. Engineering: pass, one development and strain $0. Concurrency: pass only if no re-engined 787 is built at rate before certification [BX-1263, B-2228]. Suppliers: no live problem. Engine: none is launched on the record, and the board ties no engine to the Re-engine's EIS. On the rules' timings, UltraFan widebody launched in 2030 is ready in 2036, one year after our 2035 EIS. A GEnx or Trent 1000 upgrade launched by 2032 is ready by 2035 (3 years). Durability is the airlines' open question [BX-1298]. A one-year slip paced by the engine costs about $0.31B, within epsilon (inference). H5 means we re-baseline once and never cancel. Capacity: +1 pp a year of a 170-aircraft market is about 1.7 more 787s a year from 2035, which the Charleston expansion for rates in the teens covers (inference). The fps can start in 2035 as the Re-engine rolls off.

tests.name: Ramp choice: 10-year over 7-year (inference, BX-1331)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State each ramp's strain and EIS.
tests.numbers: 10-year: EIS at launch + 10 (2040 now, 2045 from 2035). Strain $0 alone, $1.2B with a same-round Re-engine. Worst column -9.51 (new sites) or -8.86 (Renton). Every debt line held. 7-year: EIS 2037 now, 2042 from 2035. Strain $3.0B with a same-round Re-engine (H4 breach). Worst column -13.01 or -12.20. At new sites it breaks the stress-case debt line (peak $0.5-0.7B). Clean-sheet slip prior +3 years (range +2 to +5). Engine margin with code 7 from a 2035 launch: GTF2 ready in 2041 and UltraFan NB in 2042, which is 4 and 3 years before a 2045 EIS but 1 and 0 years before a 2042 EIS. Operations can deliver the 10-year ramp predictably; the 7-year leaves no margin. The fps is held this round on value, so this test is for when it launches.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (record: BX-1330, BX-1333, applied by inference; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: Boeing's bill on the board is $100B against $60.32B for the 10-year Solo (+$39.7B), with the same EIS (launch + 10) and no capacity or strain relief. Against the 10-year Solo: -17.48 to -17.49 in S1-S6, and -13.57 (S7) and -13.79 (S8) at new sites, -13.69 and -14.08 at Renton. This corrects 'about $17-18B in every column'. The $3.7-3.9B narrower gap in S7 and S8 is the one thing the partner brings: it blocks Embraer's own narrowbody. It is far short of the gap. On its own it breaks the stress case (peak $1.8-3.1B). Not priced: Korean industry (KAI and others) builds structures for Boeing today, so an Embraer-Korea narrowbody would compete for the same suppliers (watch item, inference). The Solo airframe and the 787 Re-engine build on Boeing's own IP: invest.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase (one remark, BX-1329; inference)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column, and only where demand is visible.
tests.numbers: Item value against the same plan without it: -0.45 (S1, S4), -0.84 (S2, S5, S6), -1.05 (S3), -0.86 (S7), -1.15 (S8); with the 10-year fps, -1.20 to -1.44. In the expected column S2 it is -0.84. Demand is not visible: with Do Nothing, Boeing delivers below its 684 capacity every year 2030-38. The idle slots are 130 (2030), 66 (2032), 42 (2033), 20 (2034), 56 (2035), 58 (2036), 63 (2037) and 189 (2038). Capacity first binds in 2039, after the 2032-36 window of the step.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record: BX-1327, BX-1332, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. Every debt line met, the stress case included.
tests.numbers: Do Nothing: no bill. Net debt $0 from 2029 (stress case 2030). Free cash flow $13.79B a year from 2030 ($9.19B in the stress case). 787 Re-engine: $5B over 2030-35, about $1.0B a year, which is 7% of base and 11% of stress free cash flow. Net debt stays at $0 in every column, stress peak $0.0B. Undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B. Rate Increase: $2.94B spent to 2032; debt lines held, but item value negative. fps 10-year: $60.32B over 10 years (governments carry 2%), about $3.0B in year 1, peaking near $8.4B (14%) in year 7. The peak is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow. Debt lines held; penalty $19.1B. fps 7-year: $65.00B over 7 years, about $9.3B a year, above the $9.19B stress free cash flow. At new sites it breaks the stress case ($0.5-0.7B); penalty $22.0B. Via Embraer: $100B, about $10B a year with a peak near $14B, above base free cash flow. It breaks the stress case on its own ($1.8-3.1B); penalty $52.5B. Recommended package: pass.

tests.name: Renton MAX wind-down strain, for the next round (doctrine; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: No production-certification concurrency. Predictable delivery through the transition.
tests.numbers: The fps is held, so Renton has no effect this round; keep new_site. At launch: Renton's three lines carry 47 of our 57 a month (564 aircraft a year, 82% of MAX capacity). They wind down as the fps ramps, and only the Everett North Line carries on (up to 15 a month). The Rate Increase rides on Renton and would wind down too. Value +0.36 to +0.65 on the 10-year ramp and +0.81 to +1.32 on the 7-year, plus $3.0B of capex avoided in full if Renton is chosen at least 3 years before EIS. Condition: take down each Renton MAX line only after the fps is certified and has shown rate on its replacement line, so that a clean-sheet slip (+3 years central) does not leave a delivery gap.

tests.name: Engine makers ready by a 2045 EIS under code 7 (doctrine and rules; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Each named maker has a new narrowbody engine ready by EIS, with durability margin [BX-1298]. CFM capacity across our rates and Airbus's [BX-1264, BX-1325].
tests.numbers: The fps is held, so code null this round. For a 2035 10-year launch (EIS 2045) with code 7: P&W GTF2 is ready in 2041 (6 years) and RR UltraFan NB in 2042 (7 years), both 3-4 years ahead. A P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041. CFM is always available, with ducted ready 6 years after launch and Open Fan not before 2045. Code 7 avoids the barred (3,3) pair. Today CFM carries all 684 of our aircraft a year and 60% of Airbus's 1,020: 2,592 narrowbody engines a year, a single-source exposure for us. Three fitted makers would split the fps share three ways. A 7-year ramp from 2035 (EIS 2042) leaves P&W 1 year and RR 0 years of margin, too tight for durability maturation (inference).

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI doctrine veto NOT invoked. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem and the board has no injects, so my veto has no ground this round. H6's Airbus half is not engaged either, since Airbus has launched nothing. Advice only, not binding: hold it. It fails capacity-follows-demand (-0.45 to -1.15 in every column, -0.84 in S2; 20-189 idle slots a year 2030-38). Supplier readiness at about 65 a month is not demonstrated (+200 LEAP-1B a year on a single source).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr together with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto: 5 years of overlap (fps 2030-37 against Re-engine 2030-35) and $3.0B of undiscounted strain, beyond the 2-year cap. The rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice: fails invest-or-partner on IP. $100B against $60.32B, with the same EIS and no capacity relief. It runs $17.5B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S6 and $13.6-14.1B in S7-S8, and breaks the stress-case debt line on its own ($1.8-3.1B).

vetoes.plan: re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice: launch conditions, not a veto. (1) An engine path ready by the 2035 EIS: none is launched on the record, and UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036. (2) No re-engined 787 built at rate before certification. (3) A conservative public EIS that states the slip range, with about $0.31B of value per year of slip. Under H5, a slip means one re-baseline, never a cancel. The Board's $1B downside limit (-2.48 in S4 and S5) is the Board's test, not an operations test.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my orders. (1) A brief that reports a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem: then my KPI veto binds against any Rate Increase, and I would also hold the Re-engine until it clears. (2) The bulletin showing no widebody engine path to 2035-36, or a durability problem on the candidate engine: I would ask for the Re-engine to be re-baselined, or held if not yet launched. (3) An A350 Re-engine on the record: no 787 Re-engine, ever (H3). (4) Supplier data showing demonstrated output at about 65 a month, together with a grid where the step adds more than epsilon in the expected column: I would back the Rate Increase. Here it is offered only in 2030 and loses value everywhere. (5) An fps row that beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon and passes Malave's buffer: the 10-year Solo with code 7, and Renton only if each MAX line comes down after fps certification. (6) A partner that brings capital, capacity or IP Boeing lacks, so that via Embraer beats Solo by more than epsilon in every column.
ops.memo:
My record is thin. Nothing from my BCA years is in the evidence, so my KPI, supplier and strain results are Boeing's operations doctrine. Delivery, IP and cash are my BGS rules, applied by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and 57 a month in 2030 fits the doctrine tempo: two steps of 5 above 47, at least 6 months apart. My KPI veto does not bind this round.

Second, the Rate Increase does not follow demand. Our line runs 20 to 189 aircraft a year below its 684 capacity from 2030 to 2038, and the grid prices the step at -$0.45B to -$1.15B in every column. It would also add 200 LEAP-1B engines a year to one source. Hold.

Third, the 787 Re-engine is operations-ready, with one condition. Engineering is free and strain is $0. It builds on our own 787 IP. The $5B lands in 2030-35, and every debt line holds, the stress case included. The condition is the engine: none is launched on the record. UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036, one year after EIS, and each year of slip costs about $0.3B. Commit an engine, set a conservative date and build nothing at rate before certification. A 2035 fps then follows with no overlap.

And finally, the fps. Hold it. When it comes: the 10-year ramp, Solo, code 7. Via Embraer adds $39.7B of bill and no time.

other_moves.move: Continue the Charleston 787 capacity expansion
other_moves.detail: Production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. Funded inside the debt lines. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply
other_moves.detail: Tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. No launch, no date and no engine selection this round. Serves Control's engine enabler without paying a premium (Board recommendation 9; inference).

other_moves.move: CFM LEAP-1B capacity and durability support
other_moves.detail: Joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our rate and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325], with embedded staff on durability. Our narrowbody is single-source today: CFM supplies about 2,592 narrowbody engines a year across both airframers (Pope's figure).

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Any future rate step needs demonstrated supplier output at the new rate first [B-2308].

other_moves.move: 787 Re-engine engine-path work (no launch)
other_moves.detail: Ask GE and Rolls-Royce for widebody engine proposals for a re-engined 787, durability first, so that a 2035 re-test has an engine on the record (Pope's launch condition). No commitment. No re-engined 787 built at rate before certification [BX-1263].

other_moves.move: fps definition and production-system maturation (no launch, no date)
other_moves.detail: Keep the fps team on requirements, the production system and Renton transition planning, so that a 2035 business case can be brought on the grid. Pope's condition applies: take down each Renton MAX line only after the fps is certified and has shown rate. No fixed-price development terms [BX-1262, BX-1304].

decision.public_statement:
We said we would turn this big ship, and I think we've turned it. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and MAX 10 are certified, and our balance sheet is back where it belongs. That is the work of a lot of people doing it the right way, and the financials followed our production performance.

It doesn't change how we run the place. The 737 line stays on the plan we've laid out, and the KPIs tell us when we're ready, not the calendar. We'll keep building 787 capacity in Charleston, because customers want more of that airplane and we intend to keep it the most efficient in its segment.

On a new airplane, our thinking hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. When we do, it will be planned around a stable supply of parts, starting with engines, and more than one engine source. I'm not going to give a date before we're ready to launch. When we launch, we'll set the schedule with headroom in it, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field. fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no order goes to the Board as an item.

H1 AND H3 RULING (Board recommendation 2). I lift H1 (no fps in Round 1) and the first half of H3 (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) for 2030. Their 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and debt not yet repaired [B-2326, BX-1305]. By 2030:
- the 777X has delivered since 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
- the MAX 7/10 is certified [BX-1873];
- on the tracker, net debt is $0.0B at end-2029 ($3.3B in the stress case, then $0.0B in 2030) (brief §2);
- Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' gate passes;
- the 'about two more years' I gave in July 2026 [BG-0068] has run.
Lifting the rules opens the question; it does not answer it. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 stand. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

MY FOUR TESTS
(1) KPIs [BX-1271]. Pope confirms that no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live and the board has no injects, so the gate is open. She notes the brief gives only the absence of a problem, not measured KPIs.
(2) Market, technology and balance sheet [BX-1296]:
- balance sheet: ready;
- technology: not binding;
- market: fails for the fps. Every fps row is at least $4.41B below Do Nothing in every column. The best is the 10-year at Renton: -4.41 (S1, S4) to -6.03 (S8).
(3) Certification slip [BX-1319], Malave's buffer test on S6 against Do Nothing's -0.07 (limit -2.07). Every fps row fails:
- 10-year at Renton -5.45 (gap -5.38); at new sites -5.84 (-5.77);
- the best fps row, 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, -3.23 (-3.16);
- 7-year -6.52 to -10.32;
- via Embraer -21.53 to -24.60.
His veto binds on every fps row and I accept it. I would have reached the same answer anyway: the S2-to-S6 gap is only $0.00-0.09B, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. The Re-engine (+3.23) and the Rate Increase (-0.91) pass the buffer.
(4) Doing less, better [BX-1239]. Only the Re-engine beats Do Nothing by more than ε, and only outside S4 and S5. No fps clears it.

LEVER BY LEVER
fps: hold. It fails the business case, Malave's binding veto and the Board's tests. The engine enabler would need an objective premium of at least $4.41B ($5.38B in S2), more than twice the $2B cap, so I do not pay it.
- Via Embraer is rejected. It runs $17.48-17.49B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S6 and $13.57-14.08B behind in S7-S8 (Pope's correction, accepted). Its undiscounted debt penalty is $52.5B, and on its own it breaks the stress case (peak $1.8-3.1B).
- Engine code stays null while the fps is held.
- fps_site stays new_site. Renton (+0.36 to +1.32, about $3.0B of capex avoided) will be weighed at launch, subject to Pope's wind-down condition.

Rate Increase: hold. Pope's gate is open and Airbus is not the reason (H6), but the grid prices the step below zero in every column: -0.45 (S1, S4), -0.84 (S2, S5, S6), -1.05 (S3), -0.86 (S7), -1.15 (S8).
- Capacity does not bind until 2039 (Pope: 20-189 idle slots a year in 2030-38).
- The step would add about 200 LEAP-1B engines a year to a single source.
- It is offered only in 2030, so holding gives it up for good, but at no grid cost: hold is $0.84B better in S2. It is not a premium.

787 Re-engine: hold, under the Board's risk limit. This is the one place my orders leave the grid's best plan in my expected column, so I set out the case in full.
For it:
- +3.30 against Do Nothing in S1-S3 and S6-S8;
- the best plan in S2 (+3.23 against -0.07);
- it passes Malave's buffer and keeps every debt line, stress peak $0.0B;
- undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B;
- Pope finds operations ready (strain $0, one development);
- company doctrine (§6) allows a 2030 Re-engine when no fps is in development.
Against it:
- it shows -2.48 in S4 and S5, where Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round. That breaks the Board's $1B-per-item limit in two plausible columns, and the Board has said it would veto. I have no override, and I will not bring the Board a case that fails its own stated test.
- Pope's launch condition is not met: no widebody engine is on the record, and an UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036, a year after a 2035 EIS. I do not launch an airplane on an engine that is not there yet [BX-1298].
- On Malave's breakevens, the Re-engine clears ε only if the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below 39.8% (57.1% for any gain at all). Doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt (profile §7, inference), and my confidence on Airbus is Low.
- My independent check [BX-1316] would not carry it as a plan we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0548].
Logged: the $3.30B it gives up in S2 is the Board's binding risk limit, not a management premium.
The option stays open. Malave and Pope both confirm that a Re-engine deferred to 2035 overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by only 2 years, which is legal under H4 ($1.2B of undiscounted strain). If an A350 Re-engine reaches the record, H3 bars ours for good and we stand aside; in S4 that saves $2.48B against having launched. I re-test it on the 2035 brief.

GRID ROWS FOR THE BOARD (S1-S8)
- Submitted row, Do Nothing: -0.12 / -0.07 / -0.29 / -2.74 / -2.69 / -0.07 / -2.80 / -2.83.
- Re-engine row, for reference: +3.18 / +3.23 / +3.01 / -5.22 / -5.17 / +3.23 / +0.50 / +0.47.
- Rate Increase row: -0.57 / -0.91 / -1.34 / -3.19 / -3.53 / -0.91 / -3.66 / -3.98.
- Best fps row, 10-year at Renton: -4.53 / -5.45 / -6.02 / -7.15 / -8.07 / -5.45 / -8.32 / -8.86.
Expected column S2; risk case S6.

OBJECTIVE METRICS (Do Nothing)
- Repair the balance sheet: net debt at the historical level in 2029. Met.
- Keep it repaired: held at $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050. Met.
- Stress case: back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B. Met.
- Incumbency: worst year 40.0%. Met.
- 50/50 split: worst year 40.0% (42.7% in 2040). Not met.
- Engine enabler: the 737 MAX has CFM only (1 source) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the market has two makers (CFM, P&W) in 2045 and 2050. Not met.

DOCTRINE VERSUS MY RECORD
- The engine code stays null and, at launch, code 7 is the Board's request and company doctrine, since my record on engine selection is Low. Code 7 still names CFM, so my CFM lean is kept.
- The chicken-game reading of the widebody is company doctrine (§7), not my record.
- Everything else rests on my record: data-gated sequencing, doing less better, debt first, the slip leg and no date before launch.

EXCO DELIBERATION
- Malave recommended hold on every field. His fps veto binds.
- Pope recommended hold on the fps and the rate, and launch on the Re-engine with conditions. Her KPI veto was not invoked.
- I decided Do Nothing on every field. Nothing is overridden, and no red line is touched.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's seat is thin (one call, Low), so I weigh his views as advice except his buffer test, which binds under the team rule.
- His veto on every fps row stands, and I accept it. I also accept his correction: the fps rows with the Re-engine fail by $3.16-4.82B, not $5.38B or more.
- I take his finding that the fps fails on its base case, not the slip, since Delay Tactics move it by $0.09B at most.
- I take his cash path: only the fps-hold rows, the 10-year rows and the 7-year at Renton peak at $0.0B. His debt-penalty figures (not additive) and his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' pass, which supports lifting H1 on its cash ground, also stand.
- His Re-engine advice (hold, re-test in 2035, log $3.30B as the Board's risk limit) is advice, not a veto. As a soft CFO view alone it could not carry $3.30B past H8, and he says so. It carries weight because it matches the Board's binding limit and because his breakevens (39.8% and 57.1%) sit near doctrine's expectation of an early A350 attempt.
- His addition on sequencing (a 2035 Re-engine against a 2035 10-year fps overlaps only 2 years, which H4 allows) keeps the option open, and I use it.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat is played by operations doctrine and is very thin on airplane evidence. Her KPI veto binds only under a live problem, and none is reported.
- I take her gate result (open), her capacity-follows-demand finding against the Rate Increase (20-189 idle slots a year in 2030-38) and the single-source LEAP exposure as the reasons the Rate Increase is a clean hold.
- I take her invest-or-partner result against via Embraer, with her corrected gaps ($17.48-17.49B in S1-S6, $13.57-14.08B in S7-S8) and the Korean-supplier watch item.
- I take her ramp view: the 10-year ramp, and with code 7 from a 2035 launch a 3-4 year margin for the engines.
- I take her Renton condition: take down each MAX line only after fps certification and demonstrated rate.
- I depart from her Re-engine recommendation (launch). She makes it conditional on an engine path by 2035, and none is on the record: an UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036. That is a technology-readiness gap where my risk appetite is Low [BX-1298]. It reinforces the Board's limit rather than standing alone. Her own memo leaves the $1B downside test to the Board.

decision.expected_scenario: S2: Airbus launches NGSA, with no same-round A350 Re-engine. I named this column in my frame. My confidence on Airbus is Low. Company doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt, so S4 and S5 carry real weight, and that weight is why the Board's downside limit matters.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, +3.23 in S2 (+3.30 against Do Nothing's -0.07). I do not take it. It fails the Board's $1B-per-item downside limit (-2.48 in S4 and S5), which binds, and its engine path is not on the record. Chosen plan: Do Nothing, -0.07 in S2.
decision.premium_reason:
Management doctrine plus objective premium: $0.
- The $3.30B gap in S2 between the grid's best plan (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +3.23) and Do Nothing (-0.07) is logged as the Board's binding risk limit, not as a management premium. The Re-engine shows -2.48 against the Board's $1B per-item limit in S4 and S5, and the Board would veto it; I have no override. The Board asked for it to be recorded this way.
- Holding the Rate Increase costs $0, since hold is $0.84B better in S2.
- Holding the fps costs $0, since every fps row is below Do Nothing.
- The engine enabler is not paid for. It would need at least $4.41B ($5.38B in S2), above the $2B cap in H8.
- What would break the number: a same-round A350 Re-engine turns the Re-engine's +3.30 into -2.48, and a certification slip of our own would deepen every fps row.
decision.objective_note:
Control's objectives on Do Nothing:
- Repair the balance sheet: met. Net debt reaches the historical level ($0) in 2029.
- Keep it repaired: met. Net debt is $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: met. Back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B.
- Defend incumbency: met (worst year 40.0%).
- Hold the 50/50 split: not met (worst year 40.0%, 42.7% in 2040).
- Engine enabler: not met. The 737 MAX has one source (CFM) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the market has two makers (CFM, P&W).
Reaching the enabler or the split this round would need an fps at a premium of at least $4.41B, above the $2B cap, so I pay neither. The public statement and the engine-requirement move point the engine makers toward a multi-source next narrowbody at no cost on the grid. At launch I will weigh code 7, which names CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce and is the only way to three sources if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch when selected.
decision.predictions:
Airbus:
- NGSA more likely than not in 2030 or 2035 (doctrine: Turn 1 or 2). S2 is my single most likely column.
- A same-round A350 Re-engine is a real possibility (doctrine expects an early attempt). I put it at roughly a third to two-fifths, with Low confidence.
- Delay Tactics, if ordered, cannot bite while our fps is unlaunched. S6 equals S2 on every fps-hold row.

Embraer: may launch its narrowbody (S7, S8). On Do Nothing that costs us about $2.7B through price pressure (-2.80 against -0.12).

Engine makers: P&W and Rolls-Royce are likely to sit on conditional launches. With no fps selection from us, nothing triggers on our airframe this round. CFM keeps LEAP-1B on the 737 MAX.

Our score: -0.07 in S2, range -0.07 to -2.83 across S1-S8. Every debt line is met in every column.

Next bulletin: observed Boeing narrowbody delivered share stays at about 39.4% and widebody at 58.8%. We publish no launches.

2035 round: re-test the fps (10-year, Solo, likely Renton, code 7) against Malave's buffer and the Board's limits. Re-test the 787 Re-engine only if no A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3), with an engine path in hand.

board_response.response: Taken up. Do Nothing meets all three lines: $0 in 2029, held at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the stress case back to $0 in 2030 with a $0.0B peak. Any return of cash to owners stays with the Board and is not in this package.

cfo.red_line: None. The orders hold every field at its default: no fps order (H1 met anyway), no 787 Re-engine (H3 met anyway), no overlap (H4), nothing launched so nothing can be cancelled (H5), no Rate Increase (H6), no crisis inject (H7), and $0 management premium (H8).
