cfo.note:
Veto check, round 1 (2030). I concur.

I re-ran the buffer test (the slip leg) on the exact plan ordered: fps hold, fps_engine_code null, rate_737 hold, re787 hold, fps_site new_site. That is the 'fps: hold + 787: hold' row, which is Do Nothing. In S6 (Risk case: NGSA plus Airbus Delay Tactics) it scores -0.07. Do Nothing in the same column is also -0.07, so the gap is $0.00B. The limit is -2.07, so it passes with the full $2.00B of buffer to spare. I ran it as the baseline, not as a sensitivity [BX-0553].

My binding vetoes are respected. All of them were on fps launches: the 10-year at -3.23 to -7.11 in S6, the 7-year at -6.52 to -10.32, and via Embraer at -21.53 to -24.60. No fps is ordered, so the CEO has nothing to revise.

Advice only, not a veto ground:
- Worst column. The ordered row's worst is S8 at -2.83, against -5.22 for the Re-engine row (S4) and -3.98 for the Rate Increase row (S8). Holding gives us the strongest floor on the grid, which is what I mean by a plan we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0548].
- Debt lines. All three hold on this row in every column: net debt reaches the historical level in 2029, stays at $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the stress case is back to $0 in 2030 with a $0.0B peak [BX-0556].
- Premium. The management premium is $0. I agree with logging the $3.30B the Re-engine gives up in S2 as the Board's risk limit, since it shows -2.48 in S4 and S5. The number holds barring a same-round A350 Re-engine [BX-0552].
- Red lines. No hard rule is broken.

My test memo and this check go to the Board with the decision. Every field is at its default, so there are no Board items.

In my voice: this baseline puts us in a position to not only meet it but potentially beat it. It's maintaining the focus on fully restoring the health of our balance sheet, and we keep the fps and the 787 Re-engine open for a re-test on the 2035 brief, on the grid's numbers then.

ops.red_line: None. The orders break no company hard rule. H4 is not engaged: no fps and no Re-engine, so overlap is 0 and strain is $0. H5 is not engaged because nothing is launched, so nothing can be cancelled. H6 is not engaged: there is no Rate Increase, and Airbus is not the reason for any order. H3: the 787 Re-engine is held, and no A350 Re-engine is on the record. H1 and H3's first half: the CEO lifted both for 2030, but neither the fps nor the Re-engine is launched, so neither is breached under either reading.
ops.note:
I concur. This is my veto check for the Board. My record is thin, so the KPI, supplier and strain results below come from Boeing's operations doctrine. The delivery and cash points come from my 2022 BGS record, applied to airplanes by inference.

First and foremost, the KPI gate (doctrine) [B-2221, B-2351, B-2308]. The CEO orders rate_737: hold. My veto applies only to a Rate Increase ordered while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. No Rate Increase is ordered. I re-read the brief and it reports no such problem; the board has no injects. So my veto has no ground and I do not invoke it. The CEO's reasons for the hold match my advice: the step costs -0.84 in S2, our line has 20 to 189 idle slots a year in 2030-38, and the step would add about 200 LEAP-1B engines a year to a single source.

Second, strain and hard rules. The overlap is 0 and the strain is $0. H3, H4, H5 and H6 are untouched. The CEO's lifting of H1 and H3's first half is his call; it is moot this round because nothing launches.

Third, the 787 Re-engine. The CEO departs from my recommendation to launch, which was advice and not binding. I accept that. He holds it because of the Board's $1B downside limit (-2.48 in S4 and S5), which binds on him, and because my engine-path condition is not met: no engine is on the record, and an UltraFan widebody launched now is ready in 2036, one year after a 2035 EIS. His request to GE and Rolls-Royce for widebody engine proposals answers that condition for the 2035 re-test. A Re-engine deferred to 2035 overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years, which H4 allows ($1.2B of strain).

And finally, cash (my record) [BX-1327, BX-1332]. Do Nothing carries no bill. Net debt is $0 from 2029, the stress case is $0 from 2030, and the stress peak is $0.0B. Keeping fragile suppliers funded and the CFM capacity work are sound readiness moves. Any future rate step still needs demonstrated supplier output at the new rate first [B-2308].

board_review.note: No Board items: every order is the default.

other_moves.move: Open NGSA engine selection: code 7 (CFM, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce)
other_moves.detail: We announce that NGSA is open to all three narrowbody engine makers, with CFM as the floor. The invitation gives P&W and RR a live airframe that selects them this round, so their launch_if_selected engines can be ready by an EIS in the second half of the decade (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037). It is a request and costs nothing. No Airbus payment is offered to induce an engine launch: any such payment would be a separate Board item above EUR 300m, and none is proposed [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

other_moves.move: Long-term, rate-gated engine supply agreements
other_moves.detail: Agreements with CFM and P&W cover the LEAP-1A and GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan through about 2045. Framework agreements with all three makers cover NGSA engines. Both are backed by long-range rate signals given early, as for the A320neo ramp [A-0159]. Announced in general terms only, with no volumes or internal plan targets [AX-0005].

other_moves.move: CFM capacity watch for the single-source floor case
other_moves.detail: If P&W and RR hold, CFM carries all NGSA engines plus 60% of the A320neo tail: about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41 on Alt, against 51 today, while it also supplies Boeing [A-0731, A-0563]. We give CFM an early rate signal for that case and review its capacity at the 2035 round. This is Wagner's flag, not a fail. It protects our own supply and claims no capacity against anyone.

other_moves.move: Secure our own raw materials and work packages
other_moves.detail: Titanium forgings through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing (DED) to relieve titanium demand, continuity of rare-earth supply on the raw-materials watchlist, and integration of the Spirit work packages, all for our own ramp [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0455, A-0457, A-0458]. Supplier payment discipline for SMEs and continuous monitoring with alternative sources [A-0479, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Run-at-rate wing demonstrator as the NGSA producibility gate
other_moves.detail: The production system matures with the aircraft. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year. It never accelerates it and never cancels it [A-0443, A-0225, AX-0006].

other_moves.move: Recruiting and training for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training for NGSA engineering and the 2040s ramp, through schools and our European and global footprint [A-0485]. It does not target any rival's staff.

other_moves.move: Industry-coalition trade advocacy: zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace
other_moves.detail: We work with industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing included as an ally on trade, to keep a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation through the NGSA development years (Board record)
other_moves.detail: Toepfer's condition, which I accept: the dividend flexes within the 30-50% payout range, and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. The EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year. European launch aid is upside only, on market terms, and the plan never depends on it [AX-0102, AG-0058, AG-0059, AX-0004].

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s, and we plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. We are inviting all three narrowbody engine makers, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, to power it. A stable, diversified engine supply is a condition of a disciplined and controlled ramp-up and of serving our customers well. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: we will keep its lines running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We will take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we will keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we will recruit and train, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build this aircraft.
airbus.rationale:
ExCo decision, round 1 (2030). I decide by the team rule. The ExCo is unanimous: both memos recommend the orders below and none of them needs an override.

STEP 1. DELETE WHAT BREAKS A RED LINE OR THE FIVE PILLARS.
- Row D, NGSA (Alt or base) + A350 Re-engine (+2.32 in S2, the best grid row in seven columns), is deleted on three grounds:
  - Rule 6: two new launches in one round, with five years of overlap (2030-35). The one-launch clause has no $1B exception.
  - Toepfer's peak-cash line: $6.67B a year in 2030-34 against $5.2B.
  - The Board's would-veto list: the item loses $2.15B in S6 and S7.
  The red line costs $1.74B in S2. It is a deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted on two grounds:
  - Rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws a $48.32B fine. One move on row A loses $0.11-15.75B and gains in no column.
  - The five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].

STEP 2. SURVIVORS THAT PASS BOTH TESTS.
- Row A, NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold.
- Row B, NGSA + A350: hold (base plan), the company default.
- Row C, hold / hold.
- Row E (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails Wagner's A350F and Spirit absorption test and Toepfer's robustness test (-0.64 against Do Nothing in S6 and S7). It trails A in every column, by +0.34 to +11.49, so no override margin exists.

STEP 3. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND CHOICE.
- I name S2, Boeing launches fps 10-yr in 2030 (EIS 2040). Boeing has said its new aircraft comes not before 2035, wants a repaired balance sheet first, and will not match our timeline (profile §7). But under sealed moves and the EIS-lead rule, every year it waits gives us a permanent edge. A 10-year programme fits its caution.
- In S2, A is at +0.58 and the default B at -0.87. The gap of $1.45B is outside the $1B default band, so A is chosen.
- The choice does not hinge on S2:
  - A beats B in all nine columns, by +0.69 (S6) to +1.45, with a mean of +1.13 at equal weights and +1.16 on my weights.
  - A lifts the worst column (S9) from -7.37 to -5.98.
  - Only in S1, S3, S6 and S8 would the lead fall inside the band and the default win the tie-break.
- Against holding, launching NGSA gains in every column: +3.59 (S4, the tightest) to +10.86.

STEP 4. TIE-BREAKS AND ROBUSTNESS.
- No early EIS: 2037 is after the 2035 technology-ready year [AX-0020, A-0409].
- One programme, so concurrency is zero.
- Capex timing: 2030 is the last year of the window, so no later start exists.
- I record one honest exposure. A one-year NGSA slip would put EIS in 2038, outside 2035-2037. No earlier option exists, so the answer is gate discipline (the run-at-rate wing), re-timed on maturity, never accelerated or cancelled.
- No plan keeps every raw column positive. A is the most robust passing plan: it is best of the survivors in every column, and it beats Do Nothing in every column.

STEP 5. ENGINE CODE 7.
- Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's ask.
- It is the only code that can trigger both P&W's and RR's conditional launches, with GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both by EIS. This round is the last in which either can be ready by 2037.
- CFM is the floor, so there is no EIS risk, and code 7 is in no forbidden pair.
- It does not change our payoff.

STEP 6. FORWARD FLAGS.
- An A350 Re-engine in 2035 overlaps NGSA in 2035-36 at $6.67B a year. That fails peak cash, and the Board vetoes such a Re-engine. It is closed on these bills unless the facts change, and rule 3 closes it if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine.
- Poaching comes back to the Board only once an fps is public, and only with every Board condition met.

BOARD-GATE LINES.
(1) ngsa: launch 2030 (EIS 2037), with engine code 7 riding on it. Qualified Majority, $35.52B at EIS [AG-0049].
- Five pillars: pass. No covert move, windows rather than dates, an open engine competition.
- Toepfer: pass. $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year over 2030-36 against the $5.2B line, with $0.13B of headroom. Liquidity passes with the payout flexing and no new buyback in 2030-36 without a re-test.
- Wagner: pass on engineering capacity (no overlap, one launch), production readiness, the ramp shield and supply. Code 7 is his recommendation.
- Grid ΔPV against hold: +3.59 to +10.86 on Alt (+2.15 to +10.16 on base), +5.64 in S2. The item loses in no column. Row A leads every passing option in the worst column (S9: -5.98 against -7.37 and -11.10) and in S4.
(2) a320_plan: alt, about $0.75B.
- Five pillars: pass. A mature product on running lines below today's rate, with no design change.
- Toepfer: pass. The $0.75B is recorded as post-EIS line cost in 2037-44 (about $0.09B a year), so the peak stays $5.07B. Spread over seven development years it would be $5.18B, still passing. No development year carries more than $0.13B of it.
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and supply crunch. The lines never ask for more than 82 engine sets a month, against the 85 supplied today. The CFM watch item is in other_moves.
- Grid ΔPV against base: +0.69 to +1.45, and +1.45 in S2. It loses in no column.
rea350: hold and delay_tactics: none are defaults and not Board items. No overrides; the override budget is unused.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's memo is role-derived (Low confidence), and I take his numbers as the cash record.
- Passed: peak cash for NGSA alone ($5.07B against $5.2B); peak cash for NGSA + Alt, conditional on the $0.75B timing; robustness of rows A and B against Do Nothing; the Board downside and worst-column tests on the ngsa and a320_plan items; liquidity and shareholder returns; Board items; the engine code (no cash).
- Failed: row D (peak cash $6.67B and a rule 6 red line), row E (robustness, -0.64 in S6 and S7), and any Delay Tactics (rule 4, naked fine).
- His vetoes on D and E and on Delay Tactics are binding, and I accept them. D and Delay Tactics coincide with company red lines, which no grid margin can restore. E trails the best passing option in every column, so no override is possible.
- I accept his conditions in full. The $0.75B Alt cost is recorded as post-EIS line cost; no development year carries more than $0.13B of it. The payout flexes within 30-50%, with no new buyback in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. A 2035 A350 Re-engine is closed on these bills.
- Nothing he raised needed revision.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's memo is role-derived (Very low confidence), and I defer to him on production, quality and engines.
- Passed: engineering capacity for NGSA alone; production readiness (EIS 2037, two years after technology-ready, behind the run-at-rate wing gate); the A320 ramp shield; supply crunch and safety and quality on the Alt plan; engine code 7; the own-supply other moves; the pillars check on orders and public line.
- Failed: row D (rule 6 red line, engineering overlap, A350F absorption), row E (A350F and Spirit absorption, a soft veto), and any Delay Tactics (rule 4 and the pillars).
- All three vetoes are binding and accepted. D and Delay Tactics are red lines. E trails row A in every column, by 2.38 in S2, so the $1B override condition cannot be met.
- I take his watch items into other moves:
  - CFM capacity if P&W and RR hold (about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41);
  - hiring and training for the 2040s ramp.
- His 2035 view (the Re-engine passes his capacity test at a 2-year overlap) is noted, but it stays closed on Toepfer's cash line.
- Nothing he raised needed revision. Because the Board accepts no override of his safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch results, his explicit pass on Alt is what lets the Alt item go forward.

airbus.expected_scenario: S2: Boeing launches fps 10-yr in 2030 (EIS 2040); Embraer and Boeing's widebody hold. Worst plausible column for the plan: S9 (-5.98). Tightest column for the NGSA item: S4, fps 7-yr (+3.59 against hold).
airbus.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine at +2.32 in S2. It is deleted by company rule 6 (two launches in one round, five years of overlap), by the $5.2B peak-cash line ($6.67B a year) and by the Board's veto, so the red line costs $1.74B. Best surviving plan, and the one chosen: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold at +0.58 in S2. The company default, NGSA + A350: hold on the base plan, scores -0.87.
airbus.premium_reason: No doctrine premium is paid. The chosen plan is the highest-grid survivor in S2, and in every other column too. The company default (base plan) trails it by $1.45B in S2, outside the $1B band, so the rule picks the Alt plan on PV. The $1.74B gap to the best grid row (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) is the cost of a company red line (rule 6) and the cash line. It is a deletion, not a premium, and it was never traded.
airbus.objective_note:
This note covers the briefing goal and the enabler. The GM scores them; neither changes the payoff, and I trade no PV for them.
- Defend 60/40 and protect the A320 family: not met in the status quo (worst 57.3% in 2040). An NGSA EIS in 2037 helps until an fps arrives. But in S2 (fps 2040, a 3-year lead) shares move toward a long-run 47/53, so 60/40 is unlikely to hold in 2045 and 2050. I accept that rather than pay for it. - rea350: hold, one programme at a time, re-tested in 2035 against peak cash and any 787 Re-engine [AX-0022, AX-0082, AX-0019].
- delay_tactics: none.

WHY ALT OVER BASE. My provisional expected scenario is S2, Boeing fps 10-yr. That is the prior from profile §7: Boeing has said not before 2035, wants a repaired balance sheet, and will not match our timing. The bulletin rules nothing out, so all nine columns count. In S2 the best passing plan is A at +0.58, against the default B at -0.87. That gap of 1.45 clears the $1B bar. A also dominates B in all nine columns and lifts the worst column (S9) from -7.37 to -5.98.

COST OF THE RED LINES. The best grid row in S2 is NGSA (Alt) + A350 Re-engine at +2.32. It is deleted by rule 6 and the cash line, not traded, so the red line costs $1.74B.

OVERRIDES. None planned. The override budget stays unused.

BOARD ITEMS: ngsa launch, with the code riding with it, and a320_plan alt. Each line will cover the five pillars, Thomas's test, Lars's test and grid delta PV.

OBJECTIVE NOTE. The 60/40 goal is unlikely to hold once an fps follows, and I will not trade PV for it. The engine enabler hinges on code 7 and on P&W's and RR's own choices.

PUBLIC LINE.
- Safety and quality first, and a "disciplined and controlled" ramp [AX-0081, AX-0010].
- The next single-aisle in service in the second half of the 2030s, preparing "the Airbus of the 30s" [AX-0073].
- An open invitation to all three engine makers.
- Zero-for-zero trade advocacy [AX-0088].
- No dates beyond windows, and no mention of Delay Tactics.

WHAT WOULD MOVE ME. A concrete production or supply constraint from Lars, a breach of the cash line from Thomas, or a Board challenge on risk. A Boeing announcement alone would not.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA launched 2030 alone (row B, base plan)
tests.threshold: Peak annual programme cash no higher than about one year's FCF: EUR 4,753m x assumed $1.10 = about $5.2B. Bill spread evenly over its development years (cash view, inference)
tests.numbers: NGSA $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in each of 2030, 2031, 2032, 2033, 2034, 2035, 2036; 2037 (EIS) $0. Peak $5.07B, about 97% of the line, headroom $0.13B a year. No strain, no Delay Tactics. This confirms the Board's 2030-36 reading. The launch alone would fail only if the bill rose above about $36.4B (7 x $5.2B). Spend treated as fully incremental to FY2025 FCF (prudent).

tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA + A320 Alt plan (row A)
tests.threshold: No development year above about $5.2B
tests.numbers: The brief does not say when the $0.75B falls. Reading 1, line cost while the A320 lines run longer (about 8 years from EIS, 2037-44): $0.09B a year, no development year touched. Table: 2030-36 $5.07B each year; 2037-44 about $0.09B each year. Peak $5.07B. Reading 2, spread over 2030-36: $5.07B + $0.11B = $5.18B a year, passing by $0.02B. Spread over six years it is $5.20B, on the line; over five years $5.22B and lumped in one year $5.82B, both fails. Condition: the Board item records the $0.75B as post-EIS line cost or spread over at least six development years, and no single development year carries more than $0.13B of it.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA + A350 Re-engine launched 2030 (row D, either A320 plan)
tests.threshold: No year above about $5.2B
tests.numbers: Re-engine development 2030-34 (EIS 2035), NGSA 2030-36. Strain $3B x 5/5 = $3.0B over five overlap years = $0.60B a year. 2030-34: $5.07B + $5B/5 = $1.00B + $0.60B = $6.67B a year, or $6.78B with the Alt plan spread, which is $1.47B above the line in each of five years. 2035-36: $5.07B. Strike confirmed for the record.

tests.name: Peak annual cash, forward flag for round 2: A350 Re-engine launched in 2035 (not an order this round)
tests.threshold: No year above about $5.2B; overlap of 2 years or less
tests.numbers: Re-engine development 2035-39 (EIS 2040). Overlap with NGSA is 2035-37, 2 years, so rule 6's overlap limit is met. Strain $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B, or $0.60B a year. 2035 and 2036: $5.07B + $1.00B + $0.60B = $6.67B, failing by $1.47B. 2037-39: $1.00B a year, which passes. On these bills 2035 is closed. It reopens only if the grid shows at least $1B over the best passing option and an override is recorded (at most one a game), and the Board vetoes a Re-engine that breaks peak cash. The first year with no overlap is 2037, when there is no round; the next round is 2045. Rule 3 also bars it if a 787 Re-engine is launched first.

tests.name: Robustness: row A, NGSA (Alt) + A350 hold, against Do Nothing in the worst plausible column

tests.numbers: A minus Do Nothing, S1-S9: +10.86 / +5.64 / +6.16 / +3.59 / +5.64 / +10.85 / +5.64 / +9.64 / +5.12. Tightest is S4 at +3.59. The raw grid's worst is S9 at -5.98 (holding gives -11.10). tests.threshold: Same as above

tests.name: Board downside test and Qualified Majority worst-column test: ngsa launch item

tests.numbers: Against hold, the item gains in every column: Alt +3.59 (S4) to +10.86 (S1); base +2.15 (S4) to +10.16. It loses in no column. Among the passing rows (A, B, holding), A is best in every column, including S9 (-5.98 against -7.37 and -11.10) and S4 (-2.62 against -4.06 and -6.21).

tests.numbers: D (Alt) minus A: +1.74 in S1, S2, S3 and S5, +1.75 in S4 and S8, +1.74 in S9, and -2.15 in S6 and S7 (the 787 Re-engine columns). That is a loss beyond the Board's $2B limit. D (base) minus B gives the same pattern (+1.74/1.75, -2.15). The plan itself stays above Do Nothing (D Alt minus holding, at its tightest in S7: +3.49), but the item fails the downside test.

tests.name: Robustness: row E, NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine
tests.threshold: Plan minus Do Nothing positive in the worst plausible column
tests.numbers: E minus Do Nothing: +3.26 / +3.26 / +3.25 / +3.25 / +3.26 / -0.64 / -0.64 / +3.26 / +3.25. It is negative in S6 and S7. Cash is $1.0B a year over 2030-34, which passes peak cash. E trails A in every column by +0.34 (S4) to +11.49 (S6), and it gives up the last year of the NGSA window.

tests.name: Overlap: rows A and B
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less, unless the grid shows at least $1B more; at most one new launch per round (rule 6)
tests.numbers: One launch (NGSA). No A350 Re-engine in development, so the overlap is 0 years and the strain is $0.

tests.name: Overlap and one launch per round: row D
tests.threshold: Same as above. A second new launch in one round has no exception (red line, rule 6)

tests.numbers: NGSA: 2030 is the last year of the window, so no later start exists, and launching beats holding by at least $2.15B in every column. A against B: the gap in S2 is $1.45B, outside the tie-break. In S1, S3, S6 and S8 (gaps $0.69-0.86B) the tie-break would favour the base plan.

tests.name: Board items
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Row A has 2 items: ngsa launch, with the code riding on it (Qualified Majority above EUR 800m, $35.52B), and a320_plan alt (about $0.75B). Row B has 1. They are not within $1B in S2 (+1.45), so A stands. In S1 (+0.70) this tie-break would favour B. No Delay Tactics items, no cancellations.

tests.name: Engine code 7, riding with the NGSA item (cash view)
tests.threshold: No added programme cash in any year; the code is not a cash veto ground
tests.numbers: The code changes neither Airbus's payoff nor its annual cash on the board ($0 in every year), so the 2030-36 peak stays $5.07B. I defer to Wagner on supply; I expect him to request code 7, the only code that can give 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050 (1 and 1 if P&W and RR hold). Any Airbus payment to induce an engine launch would be a separate item above EUR 300m. None is proposed.

tests.name: Liquidity and shareholder returns (Board ask 3)
tests.threshold: Net cash stays positive; the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback stay fundable without an equity raise; the A+/A1 rating is protected
tests.numbers: The board prices only a debt penalty (about $1.2B before discounting for NGSA, already in the grid). It does not model FCF or net cash, so this is inference. The EUR 5bn buyback runs over 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year; on the FY2025 base, FCF of $5.2B covers dividend plus buyback (about $2.8B + $1.8B = $4.6B a year). Static FY2025 base: NGSA takes 97% of FCF. At a 48% payout the dividend (about $2.8B, analyst context EUR 2,527m) draws $2.6B a year, so $13.4B of net cash lasts about 5 years. At the 30% floor it draws $1.6B a year, or $11.1B over 7 years, and net cash stays positive through 2036. Growth path: the board's operating profit rises 78% from 2026 ($3.6B) to 2030 ($6.4B). On the analyst context (2030E FCF EUR 10.7-11.6bn, about $11.8-12.7B; net cash EUR 31.8-33.1bn) NGSA is 40-43% of a year's FCF. No equity raise is needed on either path, provided the payout flexes within its 30-50% range and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without a re-test. The record holds no rating-agency thresholds. Net cash stays positive on both paths, which is the anchor for A+/A1 (inference).

tests.name: CFO read of the expected scenario (ask 5)
tests.threshold: No own threshold: the record is silent on how I read Boeing, so I take the CEO's view and test all nine columns
tests.numbers: I plan on the CEO's S2 (fps 10-yr). My cash tests do not depend on the column. Alt's lead over base is $1B or more in S2, S4, S5, S7 and S9. In S1 it is +0.70, under $1B, so there the default (base) would win on tie-breaks. Alt never loses in any column, so the S1 risk is a forgone tie-break, not a loss.

tests.numbers: Nothing has been launched, so there is no cancel option and no write-off. Reported and adjusted EBIT are unaffected this round.

The Re-engine item also loses $2.15B in S6 and S7, beyond the Board's $2B limit. Grid margin over the best passing option (row A): +1.74 in S2, +1.74/1.75 in seven columns, -2.15 in S6 and S7. On the soft veto alone the S2 margin would clear $1B, but the red line deletes the option whatever its PV.

A bottleneck move beyond a first claim on capacity is an integrity flag I could not defend to the Audit Committee (five pillars). Grid margin against row A: -0.11 to -15.75; the move gains in no column.

vetoes.plan: Row E: NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine
vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test (soft veto): -0.64 against Do Nothing in S6 and S7. Grid margin against the best passing option (row A): E trails A in every column, by +0.34 (S4) to +11.49 (S6), so no override margin exists. Peak cash ($1.0B a year) passes.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my position. (1) The A320 Alt plan's $0.75B is booked inside 2030-36 at more than $0.13B in any single year, for example as up-front tooling: Alt then fails peak cash and I move to the base plan. I also move to base if Wagner fails Alt on safety, quality, ramp or supply. (2) The NGSA bill rises above about $36.4B (7 x $5.2B): the launch itself would then fail peak cash and need a recorded override. (3) A passing plan shows at least $1B over row A on the grid in the expected scenario. (4) The Board decides otherwise. (5) FCF does not grow from the FY2025 base: I would then ask the Board to move the payout toward the 30% floor and commit no new buyback during 2030-36, though the launch stands. For row D or any Delay Tactics move, no grid margin changes my position, because those are red lines. Only a change in the facts would (a public fps launch, for Delay Tactics in a later round).
cfo.memo:
CFO test memo, round 1 (2030).

Fundability. NGSA at $35.52B over 2030-36 is $5.07B a year against a peak-cash line of one year's FCF, about $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at an assumed $1.10). Headroom: $0.13B a year. The A320 Alt plan's $0.75B passes if it falls as line cost in 2037-44 (peak stays $5.07B) or is spread over at least six development years ($5.18B over seven). Lumped, it breaches. The Board item must record its timing.

Downside. Against holding, the launch gains in every column: Alt +3.59 (S4) to +10.86, base +2.15 to +10.16. S9 is the plan's worst: -5.98 on Alt, against -11.10 for holding. Alt over base: +0.69 to +1.45, never negative.

Strikes. NGSA with a 2030 A350 Re-engine: $6.67B a year in 2030-34, five years of overlap, two launches in one round. A red line; its +1.74 cannot restore it, and the item loses $2.15B in S6 and S7. Any Delay Tactics move is naked: a $48.32B fine, losing $0.11-15.75B. Struck.

Financial flexibility. The EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year. On a static FY2025 base NGSA takes 97% of FCF, and $13.4B of net cash carries the dividend through 2036 only near the 30% floor. On the analyst context NGSA is 40-43% of 2030E FCF. No equity raise is needed.

2035. A Re-engine then costs $6.67B a year in 2035-36: closed on these bills.

Orders: launch NGSA, code 7 per Wagner, Alt if he passes it, A350 hold, no Delay Tactics.

tests.name: Ask 1: engineering capacity, NGSA 2030 alone (rows A and B)
tests.threshold: NGSA and A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more; at most one new launch per round (rule 6)
tests.numbers: NGSA development runs 2030-2037 (EIS 2037). With the A350 on hold the overlap is 0 years and the strain is $0. There is one launch in the round. The A320 sits at 85 a month (capacity 1,020 a year) and deliveries are demand-led (852 in 2030, 1,020 by 2034), so NGSA engineering runs beside a steady line, not an open ramp. The A350F competes with NGSA for teams only if a Re-engine is added. Talent binds both the ramp and new programmes [A-0366, A-0485, A-0423], and holding to one programme keeps that inside the limit.

tests.name: Engineering capacity, NGSA + A350 Re-engine in 2030 (row D, either A320 plan)
tests.threshold: Overlap of 2 years or less unless at least $1B more on the grid; never a second new launch in one round (rule 6, red line)
tests.numbers: A350 development 2030-35 falls inside NGSA 2030-37: 5 years of overlap and $3B of strain ($0.6B a year). That is two new launches in one round. The Re-engine increment over row A is +1.74 in S1-S5, S8 and S9 and -2.15 in S6 and S7 (row D Alt: +12.60 / +2.32 / +3.41 / -0.87 / +2.32 / +7.84 / -2.43 / +3.95 / -4.24). The one-launch clause has no $1B exception, so this is a red line.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit absorption (rows D and E)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Game proxy: not in round 1 (2030). The company window is 2033-35, so round 2 at the earliest
tests.numbers: Any rea350: launch in 2030 fails. Row E (NGSA hold + Re-engine) trails row A in every column, by 0.34 (S4) to 11.49 (S6), and by 2.38 in S2. Row D is also struck by rule 6.

tests.name: Ask 1: production readiness, NGSA launch in 2030
tests.threshold: Launch inside the 2028-2030 window once the rate-capable wing and the production system are on track; never an EIS before the 2035 technology-ready year (rule 1, red line)
tests.numbers: A 2030 launch gives EIS 2037, two years after technology-ready, in the last year of the window. Wing of Tomorrow began final load tests in 2025 [A-0442]; the run-at-rate wing demonstrator stress-tests the production system [A-0443], and the production system matures with the aircraft [A-0225]. The brief reports no inject and no quality event. The NGSA ramp reaches rate 50 around 2041, 80 around 2043 and 100 around 2045. Against holding, the NGSA item gains in every column: +3.59 (S4) to +10.86 on Alt, +2.15 to +10.16 on base.

tests.name: Ask 2: A320 ramp shield (NGSA launch and Alt plan)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open A320 ramp commitment
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment to rate 70-75 [AX-0054] falls before the 2030 round. On both plans the A320 stays at 85 a month until NGSA EIS in 2037, and NGSA spend does not cut A320 capacity on the board. After EIS, Alt winds down at 82/62/52/42/14 a month over about 8 years; base winds down at 72/52/42/14 over about 5.

tests.name: Ask 2: supply crunch (A320 Alt alongside the NGSA ramp)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply crunch, no new concurrency. The Alt tail must ask no supplier for a step-up
tests.numbers: The brief reports no crunch. Alt never asks for more than 82 A320neo engine sets a month (164 engines), against the 85 (170 engines) supplied through 2037, so neither LEAP-1A nor GTF has to step up. The brief gives about 1,500 more A320s (my straight-line estimate is 1,368), roughly 2,700-3,000 more engines at CFM 60 / P&W 40, all on existing lines. Watch item: if P&W and RR hold, CFM's Airbus sets rise from 51 a month in 2037 to about 62-75 a month in 2038-41 on Alt (56-63 on base), and to about 100-108 by 2045 on either plan. That rise comes from single-sourcing NGSA, not from Alt. CFM also supplies Boeing's rates [A-0731]. The record is silent on CFM's capacity, so this is a flag, not a fail.

tests.name: Ask 2: safety and quality (A320 Alt alongside the NGSA ramp)
tests.threshold: No order whose execution or public explanation contradicts safety and quality (five pillars, binding)
tests.numbers: Alt keeps a mature product on running lines, below today's rate, with no new A320 line and no design change. My straight-line reading of total output: Alt 79-94 a month in 2038-43 (104-114 in 2044-45, mostly NGSA at 90-100); base 64-80 a month in 2039-43; status-quo board capacity 85-88 a month. The base plan's trough in 2041-42 (64-65 a month) leaves trained staff idle and forces a re-ramp later, so Alt is the smoother load. Watch item: on Alt the NGSA ramp can draw less on staff moving across from the A320, so hiring and training for the 2040s carries more of it [A-0485]. The brief reports no safety or quality event.

tests.name: Ask 3: engine supply, NGSA engine code
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7); code 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS. A recommendation, not a veto ground
tests.numbers: Code 7. The bulletin shows no new NB engine launched. Readiness by EIS 2037 for a launch this round: P&W GTF2 2036 (1 year of margin), RR UltraFan NB 2037 (no margin), Joint Venture formed now 2036 (1 year). Any of them launched in 2035 is ready in 2041-42, after EIS, so this round is the last chance. CFM is always available (LEAP derivative, or ducted if launched by 2031); Open Fan comes no earlier than 2045. Row A in 2050: 1 source and 1 maker if P&W and RR hold (1 and 2 in S8 and S9, because Embraer flies P&W); 3 and 3 if both launch when selected. Code 7 is in no forbidden (fps, NGSA) pair. An unready maker is dropped and CFM is the floor, so there is no EIS risk (rule 8 cannot bind). Codes 5 and 6 cap NGSA at 2 sources, code 3 at 1, and code 4 gives the Joint Venture alone (1). A single source on our next family is not acceptable as a choice, only as the floor of a request. In 2025 an engine maker's failure to commit slipped our ramp [AX-0054], and the A320neo precedent is two makers [A-0243].

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year; do not cancel
tests.numbers: The brief reports no inject.

tests.name: Ask 4: supply moves for other_moves (own supply only)
tests.threshold: Moves must protect Airbus's own supply and never act against a rival's (five pillars)
tests.numbers: Recommended moves: (1) a public NGSA engine selection open to CFM, P&W and RR; (2) long-term, rate-gated supply agreements with CFM and P&W for the LEAP-1A and GTF tail through about 2045 on Alt, and for NGSA engines with all three makers, backed by long-range rate signals as before [A-0159]; (3) titanium forgings through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing (DED) to relieve titanium, and the raw-materials watchlist, with continuity on rare earths [A-0457, A-0455, A-0458, AX-0062, AX-0063]; (4) integration of the Spirit work packages [AX-0060, AX-0061]; (5) the run-at-rate wing demonstrator as the NGSA producibility gate [A-0443]; (6) supplier payment discipline for SMEs [A-0479] and continuous monitoring with alternative sources [A-0360]; (7) our own recruiting and training for the Airbus of the 30s [A-0485]. None of them claims or denies a rival's capacity.

tests.name: Ask 5: forward flag, A350 Re-engine in 2035
tests.threshold: Overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B); A350F absorption proxy satisfied from the 2033-35 window; no new concurrency under a supply crunch
tests.numbers: Not ordered this round. A 2035 launch develops over 2035-40 against NGSA's 2030-37: 2 years of overlap (2035-37) and $1.2B of strain ($0.6B a year). That is at the rule 6 limit and passes my capacity test, and 2035 is inside the company window, so it also passes the A350F proxy. It stays open on my tests if Boeing has no 787 Re-engine (rule 3), the brief reports no supply crunch and NGSA is on schedule. The cash line (about $6.67B a year in the overlap years on the Board's figures) is Toepfer's test.

tests.name: Delay Tactics (rules 4-5, five pillars): any move this round
tests.threshold: No Delay Tactics before an fps is launched, never a second move (both counts as two), bottleneck only as a first claim on capacity for our own ramp, poaching only while a programme is in development
tests.numbers: No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws a $48.32B fine. With NGSA on Alt, one move against none scores -15.75 / -0.18 / -0.53 / -0.11 / -0.18 / -15.74 / -0.18 / -15.74 / -0.14 and loses in every column. On the Board's reading, bottleneck and both also breach the pillars.

tests.name: Ask 6: quality and pillars check, recommended orders and public line
tests.threshold: No order or public statement that contradicts safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security
tests.numbers: No covert move. The public line gives windows ('second half of the 2030s') and promises no EIS date and no NGSA rate number. Engine makers are counted only once their launch is public. The Alt plan is public and is described as keeping the A320 family in production through the transition. Delay Tactics are not mentioned.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the record.

vetoes.plan: Row D: NGSA (Alt or base) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2030
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 6: a second new launch in one round, with 5 years of overlap (2030-35) and $3B of strain. It also fails my A350F and Spirit absorption test and my engineering-capacity test. The Re-engine increment is +1.74 in S1-S5, S8 and S9 but -2.15 in S6 and S7. The one-launch clause has no $1B exception, so no override can answer it. Acceptable alternative: rea350 hold, re-tested in 2035.

vetoes.plan: Row E: NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine
vetoes.ground: Failed A350F and Spirit absorption test (soft veto). Against the best passing option (row A) it trails in every column, by 0.34 (S4) to 11.49 (S6), and by 2.38 in S2, so the $1B override condition cannot be met. It also gives up the last year of the NGSA window.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both, on any plan)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws a $48.32B fine. Both counts as two moves, and bottleneck and both also breach the five pillars. Against row A, one move loses in every column (-0.11 to -15.75). Not overridable.

ops.would_change_mind_if: (1) The brief reports a supply crunch on LEAP-1A, GTF, titanium or rare earths, or a quality escape on the A320 lines. Then I move from Alt to base, because the Alt tail is where short engine supply bites first, and I accept no new concurrency. (2) Evidence that CFM cannot carry the LEAP-1A tail and a CFM-only NGSA ramp together (about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41 on Alt, against 51 today). Then base. (3) A failed run-at-rate wing or production-system gate, or an engine maturity slip. Then NGSA is re-timed so EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year, never cancelled. (4) On the engine code, nothing on this board moves me off 7. It costs nothing, carries no EIS risk, and is the only code that can bring a second and third maker by 2037. (5) For a 2035 A350 Re-engine, a 787 Re-engine, a reported supply crunch or an NGSA slip would close it on my tests. A larger grid gain does not move a red line.
ops.memo:
Operating test, 2030. My tests are role-derived; nothing on record is mine (Very low confidence).

NGSA launch, EIS 2037: pass. Last window year, two years after technology-ready, one programme, no A350 overlap, no strain. The A320 holds 85 a month to EIS; the end-2027 ramp date is behind us.

Alt plan: pass on safety, quality, ramp shield and supply crunch. It never asks LEAP-1A or GTF for more than 82 a month, below the 85 they supply to 2037, on lines we already run. On my straight-line reading the base plan drops total output to about 64-65 a month in 2041-42, against roughly 87 of capacity; Alt holds 79-92 and keeps both A320neo engines in production longer. Watch: if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, CFM carries all NGSA and 60% of the tail, and supplies Boeing too.

Engine code 7, for supply alone. Ready by 2037 only if launched this round: GTF2 and a Joint Venture 2036, UltraFan NB 2037 with no margin. CFM is the floor. An engine maker's shortfall slipped our ramp in 2025; I would not choose a single source for the next family; only code 7 can avoid one.

A350 Re-engine 2030: no. A350F and Spirit packages still absorbing; a second launch with 5 years of overlap ($3B) is a red line. 2035 overlaps 2 years ($1.2B): at my limit, open on my test; cash is Thomas's.

Delay Tactics: none. No fps on record; any move is naked. Red line.

I concur with Guillaume's lean.

other_moves.move: Open NGSA engine selection: code 7 (CFM, Pratt & Whitney, Rolls-Royce)
other_moves.detail: We announce that NGSA is open to all three narrowbody engine makers, with CFM as the floor. The invitation gives P&W and RR a live airframe that selects them this round, so their launch_if_selected engines can be ready by an EIS in the second half of the decade (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037). It is a request and costs nothing. No Airbus payment is offered to induce an engine launch: any such payment would be a separate Board item above EUR 300m, and none is proposed [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

other_moves.move: Long-term, rate-gated engine supply agreements
other_moves.detail: Agreements with CFM and P&W cover the LEAP-1A and GTF tail on the A320 Alt plan through about 2045. Framework agreements with all three makers cover NGSA engines. Both are backed by long-range rate signals given early, as for the A320neo ramp [A-0159]. Announced in general terms only, with no volumes or internal plan targets [AX-0005].

other_moves.move: CFM capacity watch for the single-source floor case
other_moves.detail: If P&W and RR hold, CFM carries all NGSA engines plus 60% of the A320neo tail: about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41 on Alt, against 51 today, while it also supplies Boeing [A-0731, A-0563]. We give CFM an early rate signal for that case and review its capacity at the 2035 round. This is Wagner's flag, not a fail. It protects our own supply and claims no capacity against anyone.

other_moves.move: Secure our own raw materials and work packages
other_moves.detail: Titanium forgings through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing (DED) to relieve titanium demand, continuity of rare-earth supply on the raw-materials watchlist, and integration of the Spirit work packages, all for our own ramp [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063, A-0455, A-0457, A-0458]. Supplier payment discipline for SMEs and continuous monitoring with alternative sources [A-0479, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Run-at-rate wing demonstrator as the NGSA producibility gate
other_moves.detail: The production system matures with the aircraft. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year. It never accelerates it and never cancels it [A-0443, A-0225, AX-0006].

other_moves.move: Recruiting and training for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training for NGSA engineering and the 2040s ramp, through schools and our European and global footprint [A-0485]. It does not target any rival's staff.

other_moves.move: Industry-coalition trade advocacy: zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace
other_moves.detail: We work with industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing included as an ally on trade, to keep a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Capital allocation through the NGSA development years (Board record)
other_moves.detail: Toepfer's condition, which I accept: the dividend flexes within the 30-50% payout range, and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. The EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year. European launch aid is upside only, on market terms, and the plan never depends on it [AX-0102, AG-0058, AG-0059, AX-0004].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. It is the centre of our work to prepare the Airbus of the 2030s, and we plan for it to enter service in the second half of this decade, once its technologies, its production system and its engines are mature. We are inviting all three narrowbody engine makers, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, to power it. A stable, diversified engine supply is a condition of a disciplined and controlled ramp-up and of serving our customers well. The A320neo family, with its two engine options, stays in production through the transition: we will keep its lines running longer while the new aircraft ramps up, so customers are served without a break. We will take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we will keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we will recruit and train, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build this aircraft.
decision.rationale:
ExCo decision, round 1 (2030). I decide by the team rule. The ExCo is unanimous: both memos recommend the orders below and none of them needs an override.

STEP 1. DELETE WHAT BREAKS A RED LINE OR THE FIVE PILLARS.
- Row D, NGSA (Alt or base) + A350 Re-engine (+2.32 in S2, the best grid row in seven columns), is deleted on three grounds:
  - Rule 6: two new launches in one round, with five years of overlap (2030-35). The one-launch clause has no $1B exception.
  - Toepfer's peak-cash line: $6.67B a year in 2030-34 against $5.2B.
  - The Board's would-veto list: the item loses $2.15B in S6 and S7.
  The red line costs $1.74B in S2. It is a deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted on two grounds:
  - Rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws a $48.32B fine. One move on row A loses $0.11-15.75B and gains in no column.
  - The five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].

STEP 2. SURVIVORS THAT PASS BOTH TESTS.
- Row A, NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold.
- Row B, NGSA + A350: hold (base plan), the company default.
- Row C, hold / hold.
- Row E (NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine) fails Wagner's A350F and Spirit absorption test and Toepfer's robustness test (-0.64 against Do Nothing in S6 and S7). It trails A in every column, by +0.34 to +11.49, so no override margin exists.

STEP 3. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND CHOICE.
- I name S2, Boeing launches fps 10-yr in 2030 (EIS 2040). Boeing has said its new aircraft comes not before 2035, wants a repaired balance sheet first, and will not match our timeline (profile §7). But under sealed moves and the EIS-lead rule, every year it waits gives us a permanent edge. A 10-year programme fits its caution.
- In S2, A is at +0.58 and the default B at -0.87. The gap of $1.45B is outside the $1B default band, so A is chosen.
- The choice does not hinge on S2:
  - A beats B in all nine columns, by +0.69 (S6) to +1.45, with a mean of +1.13 at equal weights and +1.16 on my weights.
  - A lifts the worst column (S9) from -7.37 to -5.98.
  - Only in S1, S3, S6 and S8 would the lead fall inside the band and the default win the tie-break.
- Against holding, launching NGSA gains in every column: +3.59 (S4, the tightest) to +10.86.

STEP 4. TIE-BREAKS AND ROBUSTNESS.
- No early EIS: 2037 is after the 2035 technology-ready year [AX-0020, A-0409].
- One programme, so concurrency is zero.
- Capex timing: 2030 is the last year of the window, so no later start exists.
- I record one honest exposure. A one-year NGSA slip would put EIS in 2038, outside 2035-2037. No earlier option exists, so the answer is gate discipline (the run-at-rate wing), re-timed on maturity, never accelerated or cancelled.
- No plan keeps every raw column positive. A is the most robust passing plan: it is best of the survivors in every column, and it beats Do Nothing in every column.

STEP 5. ENGINE CODE 7.
- Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's ask.
- It is the only code that can trigger both P&W's and RR's conditional launches, with GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both by EIS. This round is the last in which either can be ready by 2037.
- CFM is the floor, so there is no EIS risk, and code 7 is in no forbidden pair.
- It does not change our payoff.

STEP 6. FORWARD FLAGS.
- An A350 Re-engine in 2035 overlaps NGSA in 2035-36 at $6.67B a year. That fails peak cash, and the Board vetoes such a Re-engine. It is closed on these bills unless the facts change, and rule 3 closes it if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine.
- Poaching comes back to the Board only once an fps is public, and only with every Board condition met.

BOARD-GATE LINES.
(1) ngsa: launch 2030 (EIS 2037), with engine code 7 riding on it. Qualified Majority, $35.52B at EIS [AG-0049].
- Five pillars: pass. No covert move, windows rather than dates, an open engine competition.
- Toepfer: pass. $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year over 2030-36 against the $5.2B line, with $0.13B of headroom. Liquidity passes with the payout flexing and no new buyback in 2030-36 without a re-test.
- Wagner: pass on engineering capacity (no overlap, one launch), production readiness, the ramp shield and supply. Code 7 is his recommendation.
- Grid ΔPV against hold: +3.59 to +10.86 on Alt (+2.15 to +10.16 on base), +5.64 in S2. The item loses in no column. Row A leads every passing option in the worst column (S9: -5.98 against -7.37 and -11.10) and in S4.
(2) a320_plan: alt, about $0.75B.
- Five pillars: pass. A mature product on running lines below today's rate, with no design change.
- Toepfer: pass. The $0.75B is recorded as post-EIS line cost in 2037-44 (about $0.09B a year), so the peak stays $5.07B. Spread over seven development years it would be $5.18B, still passing. No development year carries more than $0.13B of it.
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and supply crunch. The lines never ask for more than 82 engine sets a month, against the 85 supplied today. The CFM watch item is in other_moves.
- Grid ΔPV against base: +0.69 to +1.45, and +1.45 in S2. It loses in no column.
rea350: hold and delay_tactics: none are defaults and not Board items. No overrides; the override budget is unused.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's memo is role-derived (Low confidence), and I take his numbers as the cash record.
- Passed: peak cash for NGSA alone ($5.07B against $5.2B); peak cash for NGSA + Alt, conditional on the $0.75B timing; robustness of rows A and B against Do Nothing; the Board downside and worst-column tests on the ngsa and a320_plan items; liquidity and shareholder returns; Board items; the engine code (no cash).
- Failed: row D (peak cash $6.67B and a rule 6 red line), row E (robustness, -0.64 in S6 and S7), and any Delay Tactics (rule 4, naked fine).
- His vetoes on D and E and on Delay Tactics are binding, and I accept them. D and Delay Tactics coincide with company red lines, which no grid margin can restore. E trails the best passing option in every column, so no override is possible.
- I accept his conditions in full. The $0.75B Alt cost is recorded as post-EIS line cost; no development year carries more than $0.13B of it. The payout flexes within 30-50%, with no new buyback in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. A 2035 A350 Re-engine is closed on these bills.
- Nothing he raised needed revision.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's memo is role-derived (Very low confidence), and I defer to him on production, quality and engines.
- Passed: engineering capacity for NGSA alone; production readiness (EIS 2037, two years after technology-ready, behind the run-at-rate wing gate); the A320 ramp shield; supply crunch and safety and quality on the Alt plan; engine code 7; the own-supply other moves; the pillars check on orders and public line.
- Failed: row D (rule 6 red line, engineering overlap, A350F absorption), row E (A350F and Spirit absorption, a soft veto), and any Delay Tactics (rule 4 and the pillars).
- All three vetoes are binding and accepted. D and Delay Tactics are red lines. E trails row A in every column, by 2.38 in S2, so the $1B override condition cannot be met.
- I take his watch items into other moves:
  - CFM capacity if P&W and RR hold (about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41);
  - hiring and training for the 2040s ramp.
- His 2035 view (the Re-engine passes his capacity test at a 2-year overlap) is noted, but it stays closed on Toepfer's cash line.
- Nothing he raised needed revision. Because the Board accepts no override of his safety, quality, ramp-shield or supply-crunch results, his explicit pass on Alt is what lets the Alt item go forward.

decision.expected_scenario: S2: Boeing launches fps 10-yr in 2030 (EIS 2040); Embraer and Boeing's widebody hold. Worst plausible column for the plan: S9 (-5.98). Tightest column for the NGSA item: S4, fps 7-yr (+3.59 against hold).
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine at +2.32 in S2. It is deleted by company rule 6 (two launches in one round, five years of overlap), by the $5.2B peak-cash line ($6.67B a year) and by the Board's veto, so the red line costs $1.74B. Best surviving plan, and the one chosen: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold at +0.58 in S2. The company default, NGSA + A350: hold on the base plan, scores -0.87.
decision.premium_reason: No doctrine premium is paid. The chosen plan is the highest-grid survivor in S2, and in every other column too. The company default (base plan) trails it by $1.45B in S2, outside the $1B band, so the rule picks the Alt plan on PV. The $1.74B gap to the best grid row (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) is the cost of a company red line (rule 6) and the cash line. It is a deletion, not a premium, and it was never traded.
decision.objective_note:
This note covers the briefing goal and the enabler. The GM scores them; neither changes the payoff, and I trade no PV for them.
- Defend 60/40 and protect the A320 family: not met in the status quo (worst 57.3% in 2040). An NGSA EIS in 2037 helps until an fps arrives. But in S2 (fps 2040, a 3-year lead) shares move toward a long-run 47/53, so 60/40 is unlikely to hold in 2045 and 2050. I accept that rather than pay for it. The Alt plan keeps the A320 family in production through the transition.
- Enabler, engine sources: code 7 is the only code that can give 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050, if P&W and RR launch when selected. If they hold, NGSA flies CFM alone: 1 and 1, or 1 and 2 in S8 and S9 through Embraer's P&W. That is worse than the status quo's 2 and 2, a cost of launching that no other code avoids. The open public selection and the supply agreements aim to make the makers' launches likely. The Alt plan keeps the dual-sourced A320neo in production to about 2045 (inference), which supports the 2040 and 2045 readings.
decision.predictions:
Boeing:
- Most likely: an fps 10-yr in 2030 (my S2, about 30%) rather than a hold (about 15%).
- An fps 7-yr (S4) and a Renton variant (S3) are each about 10%.
- A 787 Re-engine this round is unlikely (about 5% alone, about 5% combined with fps). Its widebody focus is the 777X and 787 rate.
- An early 737 Rate Increase is possible; it is not in the grid's columns.
Embraer: a new-narrowbody launch is a real chance (S8 and S9 together about 20%).
Engine makers:
- With our code 7 selection on the record, I expect P&W and RR to use launch_if_selected (GTF2 ready 2036, UltraFan NB 2037).
- CFM likely commits to a derivative or ducted engine.
- A P&W-RR Joint Venture is possible.
Weighted grid value of the chosen plan: about +1.8B. Equal weights give +1.9B; S2 alone gives +0.58B.
Round 2 (2035):
- NGSA stays on its clock.
- The engine code stays 7.
- The A350 Re-engine stays closed on peak cash ($6.67B in 2035-36), and under rule 3 if a 787 Re-engine is launched.
- Delay Tactics are re-tested only if an fps is public.

board_response.recommendation: Launch NGSA this round (2030, EIS 2037); it beats holding in all nine columns.
board_response.response: Taken up. ngsa: launch in 2030, the last year of the 2028-2030 window, giving EIS 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. It is decided on our own technology clock, not on Boeing's calendar. Against hold, the item gains +3.59 (S4) to +10.86 on the Alt plan and loses in no column. Both Toepfer and Wagner pass it. It comes to you as a Qualified Majority item.

board_response.recommendation: One programme at a time; keep the A350 Re-engine on hold until NGSA spend rolls off; CFO to bring the 2035 arithmetic; rule 3 if a 787 Re-engine is launched.
board_response.response: Taken up. rea350: hold. Toepfer has already brought the 2035 arithmetic: a 2035 Re-engine overlaps NGSA in 2035-36 at $6.67B a year against the $5.2B line, so it is closed on these bills unless the facts change. In S6 and S7, company rule 3 keeps it out. We will re-test it in 2035, but we do not plan on it.

board_response.recommendation: Select NGSA engine code 7 and name the selection openly.
board_response.response: Taken up. Code 7 (RR, P&W, CFM) rides with the NGSA item, and the selection is public as an open invitation to all three makers. Wagner recommends it for supply alone. CFM is the floor, so it carries no EIS risk, and it is in no forbidden pair. No payment to induce an engine launch is proposed.

board_response.recommendation: A320 Alt plan, if Wagner confirms no strain and the CFO shows the years in which the $0.75B falls.
board_response.response: Taken up. Wagner passes Alt on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and supply crunch. The lines never ask LEAP-1A or GTF for more than 82 sets a month, against the 85 supplied today. Toepfer records the $0.75B as post-EIS line cost in 2037-44 (about $0.09B a year), so the peak stays at $5.07B. Spread over seven development years it would be $5.18B, still passing, and no development year carries more than $0.13B of it. Against base it gains +0.69 to +1.45 and loses in no column. It also keeps the A320neo's two engine sources in production longer.

board_response.recommendation: Keep Delay Tactics off; poaching returns to the Board only once an fps is public and every condition holds.
board_response.response: Taken up. delay_tactics: none. No fps is on the record, so any move would be naked. If an fps becomes public, any poaching re-test would come to you only with all your conditions met, including a gain of at least $1B in the expected scenario and my recorded decision on the team's stricter condition. That is not a commitment to bring one.

board_response.recommendation: Bring a scenario-led case: expected scenario, worst plausible column, peak-cash table, payout and buyback fundable without an equity raise.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
- Expected scenario: S2, fps 10-yr. The plan's worst column is S9 (-5.98, against -11.10 for holding). The NGSA item's tightest column is S4 (+3.59).
- Peak cash: $5.07B a year over 2030-36, with $0.13B of headroom.
- Shareholder returns: the EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before the first NGSA cash year. The dividend flexes within the 30-50% payout range, and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without your re-test. Net cash stays positive and no equity raise is needed (Toepfer).

board_response.recommendation: In public: windows not dates, safety and a disciplined ramp first, no Delay Tactics, state support as upside only; lobbying and dual-sourcing agreements welcome in other_moves.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
- The statement leads with the five pillars and gives 'the second half of this decade' for EIS. It gives no rate number, no cost figure and no internal targets.
- It says nothing about Delay Tactics.
- Funding is from our own cash flow; launch aid is upside only, on market terms.
- Zero-for-zero trade advocacy and the engine supply agreements are in other_moves.

Peak cash: pass. NGSA $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year over 2030-36, against one year's FCF of about $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at an assumed $1.10), with $0.13B of headroom [AX-0104]. ops.note:
Veto check, round 1 (2030). Lars Wagner, CEO Commercial Aircraft. My tests come from my role. Nothing on record is in my own words, so confidence is Very low.

I concur. The orders match my recommendation field by field: ngsa launch, ngsa_engine_code 7, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. I have no veto ground.

Tests against the orders:
- Engineering capacity: pass. One launch this round. NGSA develops over 2030-37 with the A350 on hold, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0.
- Production readiness: pass. A 2030 launch gives EIS 2037, the last year of the window and two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. The run-at-rate wing gate is in other_moves. A failed gate re-times NGSA; it is never accelerated or cancelled.
- A350F and Spirit absorption: pass. No Re-engine is ordered in 2030.
- A320 ramp shield: pass. The end-2027 commitment is behind us, and the A320 holds 85 a month to EIS.
- Supply crunch: pass. The brief reports no crunch, and the Alt plan never asks LEAP-1A or GTF for more than 82 sets a month, against the 85 supplied today.
- Engine maturity slip: not applicable. There is no inject.
- Quality and the five pillars: pass. No Delay Tactics. The public line gives a window ("second half of this decade"), with no EIS date and no rate number. The engine invitation is open, and no inducement payment is offered. Recruiting does not target any rival's staff. Every supply move secures our own inputs and claims no capacity against anyone.

Company red lines: none broken.
- Rule 1: EIS 2037 is not before 2035.
- Rule 4: no Delay Tactics move, and no fps is public.
- Rule 5: no poaching.
- Rule 6: one launch, no overlap.
- Rule 8 cannot bind, because CFM is the floor.

Override check: no override is used, so the budget is still unused this game. My binding vetoes on row D, row E and every Delay Tactics row are honoured as deletions.

Engine code: 7, the same as mine. It is the only code that can trigger both conditional launches, GTF2 by 2036 and UltraFan NB by 2037. This round is the last chance for either to be ready by EIS.

Noted, not veto grounds:
1. Guillaume closes a 2035 A350 Re-engine on Thomas's cash line. On my capacity test it overlaps NGSA for 2 years ($1.2B of strain) and stays open. Cash is Thomas's test.
2. Watch items carried forward:
   - CFM load if P&W and RR hold: about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41, against 51 today, while CFM also supplies Boeing. Review at 2035.

recommendations.text: Shareholder returns stay reserved to the Board. The Board takes note of the ExCo's private record: the payout flexes within 30-50%, and no new buyback is committed in 2030-36 without a Board re-test. The Board, not management, will set each year's dividend proposal and any buyback. On the CFO's static FY2025 base, a 48% payout would draw net cash down for about five years against a seven-year NGSA bill. So unless FCF grows as the brief's profit path implies, the payout should move toward the 30% floor. The Board asks the CFO to report net cash, peak-cash headroom (only $0.13B a year) and the rating to the Audit Committee each year through 2036.

On engine supply, keep code 7 and the open public invitation. Any take-or-pay, advance or payment to induce an engine launch above EUR 300m in the supply agreements is a separate Board item. If P&W and RR hold this round, NGSA flies CFM alone: 1 source and 1 maker in 2050, against 2 and 2 today, and no later selection can bring a second maker by a 2037 EIS. In that case the Board wants Wagner to re-run his supply-crunch test at the 2035 round. CFM's load would be about 62-75 Airbus sets a month in 2038-41 while it also supplies Boeing. He should also report what contingency protects the NGSA ramp.

Report the NGSA gates (the run-at-rate wing and the production system) to the full Board at its twice-yearly product-safety review. A failed gate or an engine maturity slip re-times NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year. It never accelerates the programme and never cancels it for a Boeing move. The Board notes the honest exposure the CEO recorded: a one-year slip would put EIS in 2038.

The Board concurs that an A350 Re-engine is closed in 2035 on these bills: about $6.67B a year in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line. Under its plan-level rule the Board would veto such a Re-engine, never NGSA. Wagner's view that 2035 is open on his capacity test is noted, but cash governs. In S6 or S7, company rule 3 also keeps it out.
Keep Delay Tactics off. Bottleneck and both are vetoed in every round. Poaching may come back only once an fps is on the public record and every one of the Board's conditions holds.

Other moves and the public line. The statement is acceptable: it leads with the five pillars, gives a window rather than a date, and does not mention Delay Tactics. 'One major development at a time ... from our own cash flow' is a capital-markets commitment. The Board endorses it, but it binds future rounds and holds only with the payout flexing. Zero-for-zero trade advocacy with Boeing in an industry coalition is welcome. It should stay strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information (an integrity point for the ECSC, inference). Recruiting stays our own and untargeted. State support remains upside only.
For round 2, bring the same scenario-led case on the 2035 bulletin. Show which columns the bulletin has ruled out, the worst plausible column, the peak-cash table and the engine makers' actual moves.

board_review.note: The Board approves both items. The NGSA launch, with engine code 7, carries a Qualified Majority; the A320 Alt plan needs a Simple Majority. cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. Our customers fly LEAP and GEnx today, and our job is to deliver those engines and keep them on wing. LEAP durability upgrades are going into new engines and, through the shops, into the fleet. On the 787 we're upgrading the GEnx, because our airline customers make their money on time on wing, and so do we.

Here's what we don't know: when the next narrowbody will be launched, and by whom. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. CFM, with our partners at Safran, will be ready to support every airframer that moves, with a LEAP derivative or with a new engine. CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
Nothing is launched and no rival engine is on the record. The game is the installed base: keep each new narrowbody (NGSA, fps, Embraer's jet) on a CFM engine, keep the 787 on GEnx, and get paid for any risk we take [CX-0422, CX-0630]. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- GEnx: upgrade_genx9.
- Hold the Ducted, the Open Fan, Partner Embraer and Lobby.
- RISE stays all in as technology.
- Premium $0. No RISE allowance used.

THE BOARD ITEM: GEnx, against its default (hold everything), S1-S7
- Submitted row: +0.78 / -10.99 / -37.39 / -19.59 / -29.89 / -52.15 / -3.27.
- Default row: 0.00 / -11.77 / -38.16 / -20.37 / -30.67 / -52.93 / -4.05.
- Item value: +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78.
- It is one project: no strain and no R&D on the board. It is GE alone, so no Safran gate.
- It is the best plan in S1, S3, S4 and S6.
- It is the best weighted plan at my weights (-11.25), at Ghai's (-12.23) and at equal weights (-21.79).
- Every other field is at its default, so nothing else goes to the Board.

THE TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Before any new narrowbody is on the record, a launch buys nothing in S1 and costs its whole bill:
  - Ducted: $4.00B against hold, $4.78B against GEnx alone.
  - Package (Ducted + Embraer + GEnx): $6.00B against GEnx alone.
  - Open Fan: $8.78B against GEnx alone.
  - At my weights the package trails GEnx alone by $2.05B and the Ducted alone trails it by $2.62B. At equal weights the gaps are $0.99B and $1.90B. None clears the Board's $1B margin in any record-based weighting.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column S1, from the record, not from hoped-for selections.
- No birthright [CX-0564]. I read the columns where we are not selected as hard as the ones where we are.
  - In S3 (-37.39) and S6 (-52.15) nothing on this grid buys the slot back. The Ducted is -1.07 and -4.00 there against hold.
  - So the hard-rule-3 trigger is met on the grid, but it permits a launch; it does not pay for one. I do not invoke it.
- H2. Any Open Fan launched now is ready in 2045, 8 years after a 2037 NGSA and 5 years after a 2040 fps. It carries the wait penalty: -28.53 (S2), -14.55 (S4), -30.26 (S5). Hold.
- H3. A Ducted is defence only. Not launched.
- H5. RISE is not cancelled and stays funded as technology.
- H7. No CFM narrowbody order this round, so the gate is not engaged. The joint RISE technology work continues inside joint practice.
- H8. The statement names no one and blames no one.
- H9. Premium $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.
- My 20% and durability lines.
  - No Ducted is launched, and the statement does not call anything 'the next generation'. RISE stays the next engine, at 'more than 20%' as a design goal that has not yet been flight-proven [CX-0001, CX-0217].
  - Any future Ducted would be a defensive derivative with less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183]. Its durability would be gated by test and never traded for its date [CX-0208].
- Tie-break. Not needed: GEnx alone leads every alternative by more than ε at every record-based weighting.

COLLEAGUES' TESTS
- Ghai. His binding vetoes fall on the Ducted, Embraer, the Open Fan, Lobby without an Open Fan, and Ducted + GEnx. All are held, so I make no override. His GEnx tests all pass.
- Ali. No binding veto. No safety or durability flag. The statement carries no date. His supply advice against the stack in S1 agrees with the decision.

THE COST OF HOLDING, said plainly
My deference to airframers can make us late [CX-0452].
- In S5, holding gives up $3.02B against a Ducted alone and $4.07B against the package. In S2 it gives up $1.08B and $1.19B, and in S7 $1.39B (the package).
- Ghai's timing estimate (inference): a 2035 Ducted, ready 2041, gives up only about $0.60B in S2 and $0.52B in S5, because new types ramp slowly. Embraer gives up its whole +1.39 in S7.
- At my weights the wait costs about $0.35B. It saves $2.7B of package bill in S1 and S6 (each 6.00 times its weight).
- A Ducted is a one-way door: a 2035 cancel writes off $3.33B of the $4B.
- The installed-base lens could rationalise the package as 'the price of admission' [CX-0557]. I name that and resist it: it buys nothing in the column the record supports.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CHOICE
- Embraer on hold: my record is silent, so I follow the doctrine default. It also needs a CFM engine, and has none.
- Lobby on hold: it does nothing without an Open Fan.
- GEnx: inferred from my defend-the-787-on-product record [CX-0615, CX-0599].

2035 TRIGGERS
- The Ducted, or the package with Embraer, goes ahead if an airframer launches with CFM in its code, or if Embraer launches and agrees CFM volumes. It must still beat GEnx alone by more than $1B, with Ali's durability gate and the Safran sentence.
- 2035 is the last round in which an Open Fan launch can be ready by 2045-2050. It launches then only on an airframer path, or as the declared RISE allowance with no wait penalty in any plausible column.
- Open question for the GM, from Ghai: does a 2030 GEnx count as a running project for strain in 2035?
  - Even if it does, a 2035 Ducted + Embraer triggers the strain on its own, and ordering the GEnx later alongside a Ducted alone would carry it for certain. So ordering now is weakly better.
  - Ordering now also catches a rival Re-engine early.

Treat a Ducted as a one-way commitment: a 2035 cancel writes off about $3.33B of the $4B, and passes our test only if it is at least zero in every plausible column.

Fund RISE as technology, with no product launch this round. Bring the Open Fan back in the 2035 round, the last round in which a launch can be ready by 2045-2050. Launch it then only if the record shows no new narrowbody can enter service before 2045, with the RISE allowance declared then (at most $15B). Otherwise say plainly that the Open Fan waits.

State the Safran gate for each CFM item and why Safran would agree. The Ducted is a defence that keeps the NGSA and the fps on CFM (the grid's S3/S6 show the slot at risk). Embraer is serving every airframer. Price and capacity terms are joint.

Declare every premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column, within $2.0B this round and $4.0B over the game. Keep the payout of at least 70% of free cash flow whole: a Ducted plus the strain is about $1.0B a year, inside the headroom.

- No CFM price talk without Safran.
- Prefer: 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.'
- On Embraer, say nothing on US-Brazil trade politics: our record is silent and nothing political enters our payoff.

GEnx: Ghai should note how its value changes if a rival 787 or A350 Re-engine launches, since the GEnx gain ends at that entry. Keep it a stand-alone order this round so it adds no strain to a later launch.

frame.question: What game are we playing in 2030, and how do we win? Nothing is launched. The game is the installed base: keep every new narrowbody that launches (NGSA, fps, Embraer's new jet) on a CFM engine, keep the 787 on GEnx, and get paid in dollars for any risk we take [CX-0467, CX-0422, CX-0630]. We are not going for share [CX-0493]. So the question is this: before any airframer has moved, is there a launch that adds value and pays for its risk? Or do we bank the one item that pays in every column (GEnx), keep RISE whole as technology, and save our engine money for an airframer that has committed? We don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564], so we read the columns where we are not selected as hard as the ones where we are.
