cfo.would_change_mind_if: Confirmed data, not early signals. (1) An airframer launches NGSA or fps with CFM in its code on the record (S2, S4 or S5). Then the Ducted passes volumes first, pays in that column (+1.86 / +3.80 against hold, +1.08 / +3.02 against GEnx alone in S2 / S5) and I would pass it, with the package if Embraer adds. (2) A rival narrowbody engine is launched, committed or selected on the record, and the grid shows a Ducted beating its default in the column where the rival takes the slot. Today it does not (S3 -1.07, S6 -4.00). (3) Embraer launches its jet and agrees volumes for a CFM engine (S7 on the record), where Embraer is worth +7.39 and the package +1.39 against GEnx alone. Even then, the wait costs that whole +1.39 on my estimate, so I would want the volumes this round. (4) Weights drawn from the record move about 0.33 from S1 to S5, enough to put the package more than $1B ahead of GEnx alone. (5) The GM shows that a 2030 GEnx counts as a running project in 2035, which raises the cost of waiting: a 2035 Ducted would net about -0.74 in S2. At my weights the wait still wins. (6) For the Open Fan: only a record showing no new narrowbody can enter service before 2045, with the RISE allowance declared in full.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the money tests in dollars. GEnx upgrade alone passes every one: +0.78 against hold in all seven columns, no R&D on the board, no strain, no Safran gate, premium zero. I'd sign it as upgrade_genx9.

The Ducted doesn't pass, not yet. In S1, the only column the public record supports, it costs its whole $4.00B; the package costs $6.00B against GEnx alone. At my weights (S1 .40, S2 .13, S3 .07, S4 .10, S5 .08, S6 .07, S7 .15) the package trails GEnx alone by $2.28B and the Ducted alone by $2.83B. It wins only in S2, S5 and S7, and each assumes a selection nobody has made. We need to work the volumes with the airframer first. The hard-rule-3 trigger doesn't rescue it: -1.07 in S3, -4.00 in S6. Embraer fails the same volumes test.

But the good news is the wait is cheap. A 2035 Ducted, ready 2041, gives up roughly $0.6B in S2 and $0.5B in S5, because new types ramp slowly. Embraer in S7 is the real cost, about $1.4B. Against that, waiting saves $4-6B in S1 and S6, and a 2035 cancel would write off $3.33B of the $4B.

Open Fan: $8.78B behind GEnx alone in S1, $31.04B in S5. Hold it; RISE R&D stays protected.

Capex: even the package is $1.0B a year, under 2% of revenue. Rating and 70% payout stay whole.

Book expected PV low, about -$12B, no S1 upside until confirmed. What the case leaves out: S6, -52.15.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off: ready years of every order (binding date test)
tests.threshold: No order's value may depend on a ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted: launch + 6. Open Fan: launch + 10 and not before 2045. Partner Embraer: counts at launch + 7. GEnx: launch + 3, and not before the first re-engined 787 or A350 enters service (2042 if none does). The rule is my test standard applied to the board's development times (inference).
tests.numbers: Every order launches in 2030. Ducted ready 2036 (2030+6). Open Fan ready 2045 (2030+10 = 2040, raised to the 2045 floor). Partner Embraer counts from 2037 (2030+7). GEnx counts from 2042 (2030+3 = 2033, but no 787 or A350 Re-engine appears in any column S1-S7, so 2042). Every grid value in round1.md uses these years. None of Culp's rows 1-6 depends on an earlier year. The test basis, said plainly: these are board dates, not test results. My record has no ducted product programme and no 'turn on and turn off' run on one. The nearest test evidence is RISE: over 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216], and dust testing on next-generation HPT blades from October 2025 [CX-0222].

tests.name: Test, not analysis: dates in the public statement and other moves (binding date test)
tests.threshold: Every date said in public must be one a test can back. No Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, no ready date before launch + development years, and no fly-demo or flight-test date.
tests.numbers: Culp's proposed line gives no date: 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer', RISE technology on track, LEAP durability facts. Pass. These dates would fail at my veto check: (a) an Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, including the 2024 phrase 'available by the middle of the next decade' [CX-0608], which the game's 2045 overtakes by about ten years; (b) a Ducted ready before 2036 on a 2030 launch, or before 2041 on a 2035 launch; (c) a CFM engine on Embraer's jet at its 2034 entry, when the partnership counts only from 2037; (d) any RISE flight-test date, since my 'middle of this decade' demo became 'this decade' [CX-0151, CX-0211]. I will check the final text at step 4.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice; report of the gap)
tests.threshold: Give each engine's ready year against each first new-narrowbody entry into service. An Open Fan ready after the first new NB enters service takes the board's 35 pp loss (20 pp with Lobby). A Ducted ready after entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year.
tests.numbers: DUCTED 2036: 1 year before NGSA 2037 (S2/S3/S5) and before the 7-year fps 2037; 4 years before the 10-year fps 2040 (S4/S5/S6); 2 years after Embraer's jet 2034 (S7), where the Ducted alone earns nothing (-4.00, its bill). Pass. One year of margin to 2037 is thin given my record: the RISE demo slipped about five years and the 1B kit about one. A slip past 2037 delays the +10 pp, but the share is not lost and CFM is never dropped (LEAP derivative). PARTNER EMBRAER counts 2037: 3 years after the jet's 2034 entry, so the jet flies P&W from 2034 to 2036. It still adds +7.39 in S7 against Ducted + GEnx. OPEN FAN 2045: 8 years after NGSA and the 7-year fps (2037), 5 years after the 10-year fps (2040), 11 years after Embraer (2034). Fail. Wait penalty against hold: -28.53 (S2), -14.55 (S4), -30.26 (S5). H2 confirmed: no Open Fan launched this round can be ready before a new narrowbody can enter service. A 2035 launch is ready in 2045 exactly, with no slack; a 2045 launch is ready in 2055, too late for the objective.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A Ducted gets 'less than half' the gain and is never called the next generation (hard rule 3 is doctrine; the physics is mine).
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check. Confirmed: a ducted engine 'has less than half the fuel burn improvements that can come from an open fan' [CX-0183], and 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics' [CX-0180]. RISE's design point is 'more than 20%' [CX-0001], against Culp's 'at least 20%' [CX-0217]. Culp's red line therefore holds for RISE. For any Ducted it is rebutted only by naming it a defensive derivative, with RISE staying the next engine. Caution: 'more than 20%' is a design goal. The fly test that proves it is not in my record, so I confirm the physics, not a tested number. Culp's proposed line does not call a Ducted the next generation: pass.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule.
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data, and no order claims any. LEAP status, reported against my own promise: I said LEAP-1A production engines would reach mature time on wing by end-2024 and that 1B 'will follow in 2025' [CX-0008]. 1A: HPT hardware certified 6 December 2024 [CX-0225]; in all 1A deliveries and shop visits by July 2025 [CX-0209]; new 1A engines at CFM56 levels by November 2025 [CX-0996]. Targets are 8,000 cycles harsh and 17,000 neutral [CX-0655], against fleet leaders of 9,882 benign and about 4,800 harsh in 2023 [CX-0006]. 1B: in certification for 1H 2026 [CX-0210], about a year late. The outcome is not in my record. Retrofits go in at shop visits, 'years, not months' [CX-0649]. NO safety or durability FLAG on a Ducted or on the GEnx upgrade: no test shows a failure on either. A CONDITION, not a flag: a Ducted would be a new hot-and-harsh engine, so durability must be gated by test the way RISE's is (an open-fan durability chief [CX-0223], early dust testing [CX-0222]), never traded for the 2036 date [CX-0208].

That is -0.99 at equal weights and -2.05 at Culp's weights (S1 .40, S2 .15, S3 .05, S4 .10, S5 .10, S6 .05, S7 .15). What Embraer + GEnx add on top of a Ducted, net of the strain: -1.22 / +0.11 / +1.44 / 0.00 / +1.05 / -1.22 / +6.17. The grid pays the strain in S2, S3, S5 and S7, not in S1 or S6. Fail in the expected S1. Context: in the brief, CFM's NB engine volume climbs from 2,131 (2030) to 2,553 (2034) while a Ducted would be in development, alongside the GE9X ramp [CX-0933]. 80% of past shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. The company's 2023-24 ramp promises missed by a quarter to a half, and 2024 reversed [CX-0590, CX-0176, CX-0954]. Is $2B the right size? No evidence of mine sizes it. Following doctrine: read it as a floor, not a ceiling.

tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This is no argument against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: genx: upgrade_genx9 is a derivative: +0.78 in every column against hold, counting from 2042. 'We only needed to change a handful of parts' [CX-0005]. The GE90 and GEnx cycles behind the hot section are the moat [CX-0169]. Do Nothing on the narrowbody keeps LEAP, with RISE technology fed into upgrades now [CX-0162]. I prefer upgrade_genx9 to invest_genx on wording only; the board treats them as identical.

tests.threshold: A problem or order that touches safety or durability needs a cross-functional team, not one person.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Test and field data, never analysis. (1) On a Ducted: a core or demonstrator run that turns on and turns off the hot-and-harsh failures LEAP had (9,882 benign and about 4,800 harsh cycles against the CFM56's 17,000 and 7,000-8,000). That would back 2036 as a tested date, not only a board date. (2) On the Open Fan: completed RISE ground and flight test with Airbus showing 'more than 20%', plus durability in dust on the open-fan blade and compact core. Without it I back no RISE date beyond the board's 2045 floor for a 2035 launch. (3) On supply: measured supplier output, the 9 suppliers at 15 sites, holding the LEAP climb to 2,553 engines in 2034 alongside the GE9X ramp. Then I would read the $2B strain as sufficient rather than a floor. (4) On the record: an airframer launch whose code includes CFM, or a rival NB engine launched or selected. The weighting is Culp's call, but either would move my supply test into S2, S5 or S7, where the stack pays its strain. (5) A durability finding on the LEAP-1B kit, whose outcome after its 1H 2026 certification is not in my record. That would go to a cross-functional team, and I would want it closed before any new launch.
ops.memo:
Every order on the table rests on the board's ready years: Ducted 2036, Open Fan 2045, Embraer counting from 2037, GEnx from 2042. None rests on an earlier year. No binding veto.

2036 is a board date, not a test result. No test in my record has turned on and turned off anything on a ducted engine. Against NGSA 2037 it has one year of margin; against the 10-year fps, four. My own demonstration dates slipped: the RISE fly demo went from "the middle of this decade" to "this decade". So I promise no date in public.

The Open Fan launched now is ready 2045, eight years after a 2037 NGSA. That is the wait penalty: hold. The physics is ours; the calendar is the airframer's.

Physics: a ducted engine has less than half the open-fan gain. A defensive derivative, never the next generation. RISE is designed for more than 20%; the flight test that proves it is not yet in my record.

Durability: LEAP-1A certified December 2024, new engines at CFM56 levels. I said 1B would follow in 2025; it moved to 2026, outcome not in my record. No safety or durability flag on the Ducted or GEnx.

Supply: GEnx alone is one project, no strain. The stack adds $2B of strain while LEAP climbs to 2,553 engines in 2034; 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers. It does not pay in S1. Following doctrine on the strain's size.

Orders: GEnx upgrade, hold the rest. Launch timing: following Culp.

other_moves.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
other_moves.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme, with no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. We give no entry date and no flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice, and Safran is a full partner in RISE.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability and delivery first
other_moves.detail: LEAP durability hardware keeps going into new engines and, at shop visits, into the fleet. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]. We report facts only, with no new promise dates [CX-0436].

other_moves.move: Engine talks with every airframer, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: CFM stays open to Airbus, Boeing and Embraer: a LEAP derivative, and a new CFM engine once an airframer commits. We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586]. No price, no launch-era terms and no concession. Any CFM narrowbody terms are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

other_moves.move: Supplier readiness, lean before capital
other_moves.detail: Ali works the 9 suppliers behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613] to hold the LEAP climb to 2,553 engines in 2034 alongside the GE9X. He measures supplier output so that we know whether the stack can be carried before any 2035 launch [CX-0633, CX-0540]. There is no capital commitment and no board effect.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. Our customers fly LEAP and GEnx today, and our job is to deliver those engines and keep them on wing. LEAP durability upgrades are going into new engines and, through the shops, into the fleet. On the 787 we're upgrading the GEnx, because our airline customers make their money on time on wing, and so do we.

Here's what we don't know: when the next narrowbody will be launched, and by whom. That's really not for us to say; it's the airframers' call. CFM, with our partners at Safran, will be ready to support every airframer that moves, with a LEAP derivative or with a new engine. CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
Nothing is launched and no rival engine is on the record. The game is the installed base: keep each new narrowbody (NGSA, fps, Embraer's jet) on a CFM engine, keep the 787 on GEnx, and get paid for any risk we take [CX-0422, CX-0630]. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- GEnx: upgrade_genx9.
- Hold the Ducted, the Open Fan, Partner Embraer and Lobby.
- RISE stays all in as technology.
- Premium $0. No RISE allowance used.

THE BOARD ITEM: GEnx, against its default (hold everything), S1-S7
- Submitted row: +0.78 / -10.99 / -37.39 / -19.59 / -29.89 / -52.15 / -3.27.
- Default row: 0.00 / -11.77 / -38.16 / -20.37 / -30.67 / -52.93 / -4.05.
- Item value: +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78.
- It is one project: no strain and no R&D on the board. It is GE alone, so no Safran gate.
- It is the best plan in S1, S3, S4 and S6.
- It is the best weighted plan at my weights (-11.25), at Ghai's (-12.23) and at equal weights (-21.79).
- Every other field is at its default, so nothing else goes to the Board.

THE TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. Before any new narrowbody is on the record, a launch buys nothing in S1 and costs its whole bill:
  - Ducted: $4.00B against hold, $4.78B against GEnx alone.
  - Package (Ducted + Embraer + GEnx): $6.00B against GEnx alone.
  - Open Fan: $8.78B against GEnx alone.
  - At my weights the package trails GEnx alone by $2.05B and the Ducted alone trails it by $2.62B. At equal weights the gaps are $0.99B and $1.90B. None clears the Board's $1B margin in any record-based weighting.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column S1, from the record, not from hoped-for selections.
- No birthright [CX-0564]. I read the columns where we are not selected as hard as the ones where we are.
  - In S3 (-37.39) and S6 (-52.15) nothing on this grid buys the slot back. The Ducted is -1.07 and -4.00 there against hold.
  - So the hard-rule-3 trigger is met on the grid, but it permits a launch; it does not pay for one. I do not invoke it.
- H2. Any Open Fan launched now is ready in 2045, 8 years after a 2037 NGSA and 5 years after a 2040 fps. It carries the wait penalty: -28.53 (S2), -14.55 (S4), -30.26 (S5). Hold.
- H3. A Ducted is defence only. Not launched.
- H5. RISE is not cancelled and stays funded as technology.
- H7. No CFM narrowbody order this round, so the gate is not engaged. The joint RISE technology work continues inside joint practice.
- H8. The statement names no one and blames no one.
- H9. Premium $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game.
- My 20% and durability lines.
  - No Ducted is launched, and the statement does not call anything 'the next generation'. RISE stays the next engine, at 'more than 20%' as a design goal that has not yet been flight-proven [CX-0001, CX-0217].
  - Any future Ducted would be a defensive derivative with less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183]. Its durability would be gated by test and never traded for its date [CX-0208].
- Tie-break. Not needed: GEnx alone leads every alternative by more than ε at every record-based weighting.

COLLEAGUES' TESTS
- Ghai. His binding vetoes fall on the Ducted, Embraer, the Open Fan, Lobby without an Open Fan, and Ducted + GEnx. All are held, so I make no override. His GEnx tests all pass.
- Ali. No binding veto. No safety or durability flag. The statement carries no date. His supply advice against the stack in S1 agrees with the decision.

THE COST OF HOLDING, said plainly
My deference to airframers can make us late [CX-0452].
- In S5, holding gives up $3.02B against a Ducted alone and $4.07B against the package. In S2 it gives up $1.08B and $1.19B, and in S7 $1.39B (the package).
- Ghai's timing estimate (inference): a 2035 Ducted, ready 2041, gives up only about $0.60B in S2 and $0.52B in S5, because new types ramp slowly. Embraer gives up its whole +1.39 in S7.
- At my weights the wait costs about $0.35B. It saves $2.7B of package bill in S1 and S6 (each 6.00 times its weight).
- A Ducted is a one-way door: a 2035 cancel writes off $3.33B of the $4B.
- The installed-base lens could rationalise the package as 'the price of admission' [CX-0557]. I name that and resist it: it buys nothing in the column the record supports.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE THE CHOICE
- Embraer on hold: my record is silent, so I follow the doctrine default. It also needs a CFM engine, and has none.
- Lobby on hold: it does nothing without an Open Fan.
- GEnx: inferred from my defend-the-787-on-product record [CX-0615, CX-0599].

2035 TRIGGERS
- The Ducted, or the package with Embraer, goes ahead if an airframer launches with CFM in its code, or if Embraer launches and agrees CFM volumes. It must still beat GEnx alone by more than $1B, with Ali's durability gate and the Safran sentence.
- 2035 is the last round in which an Open Fan launch can be ready by 2045-2050. It launches then only on an airframer path, or as the declared RISE allowance with no wait penalty in any plausible column.
- Open question for the GM, from Ghai: does a 2030 GEnx count as a running project for strain in 2035?
  - Even if it does, a 2035 Ducted + Embraer triggers the strain on its own, and ordering the GEnx later alongside a Ducted alone would carry it for certain. So ordering now is weakly better.
  - Ordering now also catches a rival Re-engine early.

The NB share objective (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is met in the status quo, with a worst year of 70.5% in 2050. The GEnx order does not touch NB share. The brief gives objective status only for the status quo, so slot-loss columns such as S6 may put it at risk, and no lever on this grid buys those slots back.

The Open Fan objective (launched and ready by 2050) is not met. That is a deliberate choice: we take no premium and do not breach H2. 2035 is the last round in which a launch can be ready by 2045-2050, and I revisit it then, only on an airframer path or as the declared RISE allowance.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: I'll start with the bad news. For years the GTF fleet was not where our customers needed it to be. We own that, and we have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. So we control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch. It will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life, and time on wing, not just fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. It comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. For the fleet flying today, the GTF Hot Section kit is available at shop visit on standard terms, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. When we've seen the demand and we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE (round 1, 2030).

1. Start from Eddy's proposal: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Row A). Mitchill recommends the same orders, and so does my framing lean.

2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto.
- Mitchill, ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine), binding on the unconditional `launch` (Rows C and E). Its edge over `launch_if_selected` is -2.00 / 0 / +0.29 / 0 / 0 / +0.90 / -2.00 / -2.00. That is -0.94 expected on my weights, -1.00 on his, and -0.82 even with a 2035 cancel. Struck.
- Mitchill, ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven), binding on `jv_with_rr: commit` (Rows D, E and F). Its only case is a Rolls-Royce commitment nobody has made. It adds -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, -0.10 expected. Struck.
- Eddy's two grounds pass on Row A. GTF2 is ready in 2036, against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, and fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040. The brief shows no live parts or fleet problem. He records no binding veto. His standing condition, no compressed testing and no EIS before launch + 6, is written into the statement and the internal moves.
- What is left: Row A and Row B (Do Nothing).

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035]. The trigger launches GTF2 only if it can be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS, so by construction no P&W engine goes on an airframe before it is ready. That leaves a year of margin on a 2037 EIS and four years on 2040. Durability is the gate, not the date [PX-0073]. On my weights:
- Row A: expected -1.59, worst -19.28 (S3/S6).
- Row B: expected -7.45, the same worst.
- Row A minus `hold`: 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0. It never trails `hold`: +5.86 expected on my weights, +5.03 on Mitchill's.
- The ranking A > D > C = E > B > F holds on both weight sets.

4. My tests.
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: `launch_if_selected` commits in the same round a selection appears. It is the visible-demand order.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071] (said RTX-wide, so applying it here is inference): `hold` gives up $24-26B in S2 and S5. A 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, after every EIS a 2030 airframe can have. So 2030 is the only round that can answer a 2030 selection, and Row A answers it.
- Responsible bet: the doctrine-favoured order is also the best expected PV and the order that serves the objective, so the premium is $0B.
- Dividend: Mitchill confirms that the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched. The spend is $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, and it competes with buybacks, not the dividend.
- Value, not share: standard terms only.

5. Doctrine relief, declared. Every P&W selection on this grid is shared-source (S2 is code 6, S4 code 7, S5 codes 7 and 6). The sole-source red line [P-0746] is therefore relieved, as dashboard_game.md §5 allows. On NGSA this is franchise defence: we held about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. The relief costs $0B.

6. Tie-breaks.
- The fleet beats a new engine: the conditional order keeps engineers, castings and forgings on fleet lift until a customer selects us.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer: none is on the record, and we answer on product and standard terms.

7. What I give up and why. Mitchill names an unbooked option. A 2030 airframe on code 3 or 5 might switch to a P&W code in 2035, and only a live 2030 GTF2 (ready 2036) could serve it. It would be worth about $23.9B in S3 and $23.3B in S6, and it breaks even against the -1.00 edge only at a switch probability of about 0.21. Nothing on the record supports that. I invest on visible demand, not ahead of it, so I accept forgoing the option and declare it here rather than book it.

8. My biases, named. My single likeliest column is S1, because I have assumed the next single-aisle comes mid-next decade [PX-0093]. That is my incrementalism. My operating dates have slipped before [PX-0017][PX-0098]. Both are reasons to let the conditional order, not my judgement of timing, answer a 2030 selection, and to state no EIS date of my own.

9. Where my record is thin. My record has no evidence on a Joint Venture (Low), so `hold` there follows company doctrine and Mitchill's and Eddy's tests, not my own words. Launch thresholds are Medium-confidence inference.

10. Board. The only Board item is `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`. Its item value against `hold` is never negative, Eddy's checks pass, Mitchill raises no veto against it, `overrides` is empty and the premium is $0B. `jv_with_rr: hold` is the default and is not a Board item.

From Calio: his expected scenario column, `predictions` over S1 to S8, and `premium_b`, which the Board expects to be 0 for `launch_if_selected` because that order never trails `hold`. From Mitchill: his column probabilities and the expected edge over `hold` and over `launch_if_selected`. Also his envelope check ($2B over six years, about $0.33B a year inside about $6B), confirmation that the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched, and the outcome of his four veto checks. For any unconditional `launch`, he should give the cancel round and write-off (2035, $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B). From Eddy: the ready year for GTF2 (2036 if triggered in 2030) set against each live airframe's EIS (NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040), his durability and pacing-parts result, and the outcome of his two veto checks. The Board also expects an empty `overrides`. Finally, a public statement that promises no EIS earlier than launch + 6, no durability not yet proven, nothing about an airframer's dates, and no selection or Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record. If a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so; a missing piece alone is not grounds for a veto.
would_approve: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`. Its item value against `hold` is 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0 across S1 to S8, so it is never below `hold` under any weights and clears the return hurdle with no premium. Its downside is bounded (it never loses against `hold`), and a selection that triggers it is its own condition, not booked upside. It is ready by 2036, ahead of the earliest 2037 EIS, and costs about $0.33B a year inside the envelope. The only condition is that neither Mitchill nor Eddy has an unresolved veto and Eddy's durability and parts check passes.

`gtf2_solo: launch` (unconditional), but only on one of two grounds. (a) A P&W selection on the public record: that cannot exist this round, since orders are sealed and no programme has been launched. (b) Franchise defence where the weighted edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least +$0.5B. The edge is -2.00 in S1, S7 and S8, 0 in S2, S4 and S5, +0.29 in S3 and +0.90 in S6. Clearing +$0.5B needs at least 86% weight on S6 if the rest sits in the losing columns (break-even is 69%), or at least 56% even with no weight in the losing columns. S3 can never clear it on its own (2.5 / 2.29 > 1).

`jv_with_rr: commit` in a later round. It needs Rolls-Royce's commitment on the public record or a live airframe whose code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). Its weighted item value must be at least 0, and the Joint Venture engine (formation + 6) must be ready by that airframe's EIS.
`hold` on either field. It is not a Board item and is never vetoed, though on `gtf2_solo` the Board recommends `launch_if_selected` instead.
would_veto: `gtf2_solo: launch` (unconditional) this round, on the Committed airframe ground. No selection is on the public record. The franchise-defence edge over `launch_if_selected` falls short of +$0.5B under any plausible weighting: -2.00 in S1, S7 and S8, and at most +0.90 in S6. In S8 (Embraer launches) the launch only cuts the outcome from +4.15 to +2.15. Acceptable alternatives: `launch_if_selected`, `hold`.

`jv_with_rr: commit` this round, on two grounds. Joint Venture conditions: no Rolls-Royce commitment is on the record and no live airframe has a Rolls-Royce code. Return hurdle: the item value is -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, so it is below zero under any weight on S7. A premium cannot cover it, because with no live airframe and no EIS the commitment does not serve the 2050 objective. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.
Any Board item that carries an unresolved veto from Mitchill (four grounds) or Eddy (two grounds), a red-line flag that is neither struck nor rebutted, or any entry in `overrides` (governance).
Any `launch_if_selected` or `launch` that Eddy fails on durability or parts, unless his veto check shows the problem resolved (Durability first).

Any case that rests on an unrecorded selection, an unrecorded Rolls-Royce commitment or unrecorded partner money (Proof before commitment). Any premium above $0.5B, any premium that is undeclared or does not serve the objective, or any premium used to excuse an uncommitted launch, which no premium can do. A public statement that books such upside on its own draws a recommendation, not a veto.

recommendations.text: Miss a cycle: order `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` this round. Without it, an NGSA or fps launched in 2030 that selects P&W leaves P&W at -19.28 (S2, S5) or -4.56 (S4) rather than +4.95, +6.96 or +3.32. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is not ready until 2041, after a 2037 or 2040 EIS, so this is the only round that can serve a 2030 airframe. A round in which every order is `hold` never reaches the Board.

Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Give the item-value vector for each Board item, the CEO's `predictions`, and Mitchill's expected edge. For a $2B bill, a triggered GTF2 returns +24.23, +7.88 or +26.24 against `hold`, well above the 10% grid WACC. Present the case with all the data, so the Board can frame it as a question of long-term shareowner value.

Do not launch GTF2 unconditionally to hedge against an NGSA or fps on a code without P&W. On the grid, an unselected GTF2 recovers only +0.29 in S3 and +0.90 in S6, and loses $2B in S1, S7 and S8. The way to win the selection is durability and standard terms, not a speculative launch or a discount; a rival's discount never moves the answer.

Joint Venture: hold this round. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041, so check that date against the airframe's EIS before committing. Any terms should share risk and investment and keep P&W's gear and core technology out.

Durability first: Eddy's memo should show that the 2036 ready date leaves time on wing proven before a 2037 EIS, which is only one year of margin, and that GTF2 work does not draw pacing parts away from the GTF fleet and the shops.

Disclosure: make the conditional offer public. P&W will launch GTF2 in any round in which an airframer selects P&W; it is ready six years after launch, with durability proven before entry into service. Promise no EIS earlier than launch + 6, no durability not yet proven, nothing on an airframer's dates or rates, and no selection or Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record.

Capital: confirm that the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched and that GTF2 (about $0.33B a year, roughly 5.6% of the $6B envelope) fits without stretch. Write the exit plan into the package. If a triggered GTF2 loses its selection before it is ready, review a cancel in 2035 (write-off $1.67B). A GTF2 that a live airframe still asks for is protected from a premature cancel.

frame.question: Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Round 1, decision year 2030. Nothing is launched and nothing is on the record. The question is narrow. If Airbus or Boeing launches this round and selects P&W, how do we make sure we are committed and ready by its EIS, without carrying an engine nobody has asked for and without a Joint Venture that has no trigger? On the grid that means one thing. Is `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` with `jv_with_rr: hold` the right package? Or does anything justify an unconditional `launch` as an NGSA franchise hedge, or a `jv_with_rr: commit`? The timing is what makes this round matter. A GTF2 triggered now is ready in 2036. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is not ready until 2041, which is after a 2037 EIS (NGSA, or fps 7-year) and after a 2040 EIS (fps 10-year or via Embraer). So 2030 is the only round in which we can answer a 2030 selection. If you miss a cycle in these businesses you get shut out for decades [PX-0071, P-1347]. That line was said RTX-wide, so applying it to GTF2 is inference. My answer to it is to commit on visible demand, not ahead of it [PX-0109, PX-0009].
frame.situation:
Public record, 2030: no programme launched. No engine selection on fps or NGSA. No Joint Venture commitment from Rolls-Royce. Everyone is on today's products. Embraer is a sixth player and can launch its own narrowbody, which flies P&W engines unless CFM's Embraer partnership is live. Supply and demand is on, so our NB volumes follow the aircraft actually delivered: 24.2% NB engine share, 682 NB engines in 2030. The A320neo slot is split CFM 60% / P&W 40%. We keep it only until NGSA enters service.

Our position: ΔPV -0.00 $B against the status quo (EV $110B, WACC 10%).

Objective status:
- Restore credibility (a GTF2 or Joint Venture engine in service on fps or NGSA by 2050): NOT MET.
- Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV ≥ 0): NOT MET, at -0.00.

What the grid says. The airframers' selection is worth far more than any order we can give. NGSA on P&W (S2) against NGSA without P&W (S3) is +4.95 against -19.28: about $24B, and it is the airframer's call. Row by row, against `hold`:
- `launch_if_selected` adds 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0 across S1-S8. It never trails `hold`.
- `launch` minus `launch_if_selected` is -2.00 / 0 / +0.29 / 0 / 0 / +0.90 / -2.00 / -2.00.
- `jv_with_rr: commit` adds -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, on either GTF2 row.

Worst columns: -19.28 for `hold` and `launch_if_selected` (S3/S6), -18.99 for `launch` (S3). No order of ours closes the S3/S6 gap. Only winning the selection on product does.

Board guidance (risk appetite 3.5). It would approve `launch_if_selected` with no premium. It would veto an unconditional `launch` this round: no selection on the record, and the franchise edge falls short of +$0.5B. It would also veto `jv_with_rr: commit` this round: no trigger, and -2.00 in S7. It expects empty `overrides`.
levers_in_play: `gtf2_solo`: `hold` (Do Nothing, continue GTF1) | `launch` (unconditional; $2B; ready 6 years after launch, 2036) | `launch_if_selected` (launches this round only if a live airframe not yet in service selects a code with P&W, 2, 6 or 7, this round, and GTF2 would be ready by its EIS; otherwise nothing is spent)

`jv_with_rr`: `hold` | `commit` (public at once and standing; forms only when Rolls-Royce also commits; P&W share $2B; ready 6 years after formation, sooner if a folded solo programme is further along; a live GTF2 folds in and its spend counts toward our $2B)
Other moves (no grid effect): public conditional offer on GTF2; GTF Hot Section / durability kit announcement; standard terms only, no launch-style pricing
Board items this round: any order that differs from `hold` (`launch_if_selected`, `launch`, `commit`)
options_to_test: Row A (my lean): `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. S1-S8 = -0.00 / +4.95 / -19.28 / +3.32 / +6.96 / -19.28 / -0.00 / +4.15. Never below `hold`. Serves credibility in S2, S4 and S5.
Row B (Do Nothing baseline): `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. S1-S8 = -0.00 / -19.28 / -19.28 / -4.56 / -19.28 / -19.28 / -0.00 / +4.15. Misses the only round that can serve a 2030 airframe.

Row C (NGSA franchise hedge): `gtf2_solo: launch`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. S1-S8 = -2.00 / +4.95 / -18.99 / +3.32 / +6.96 / -18.38 / -2.00 / +2.15. Edge over Row A is -2.00 in S1, S7 and S8, +0.29 in S3, +0.90 in S6. Cancel round 2035, write-off $1.67B, which saves only $0.33B against running on. Test it only on Mitchill's expected edge. The Board's bar is +$0.5B.

red_lines: Safety and durability first [PX-0035, PX-0073]. No P&W engine goes on an airframe before it is ready. GTF2 triggered in 2030 is ready in 2036, against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040. Eddy's readiness and durability check binds on me, and on the Board.

No new engine without a committed airframer [P-0746]. On this board that means `launch_if_selected`. No unconditional `launch` this round: no selection is on the record. The franchise hedge passes only if Mitchill's expected edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least zero. The Board's bar is at least +$0.5B, and it says it would veto. No hedge for fps alone. Never launch for share alone.

A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted and declared as doctrine relief. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we held about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058, P-1292]. This is inference from the sole-source rule.

Joint Venture: share risk and investment, never our core technology or the gear [P-1233]. Commit only once Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record, or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). Neither holds today. A commitment is public at once.
No widebody engine: we are narrowbody focused [PX-0027]. There is no move here anyway.
Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081, P-0686, P-0669]. No plan that needs a dividend cut or reverses the debt path. Mitchill confirms.
Value, not share [PX-0055, PX-0100]. No launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the public statement.

Disclosure discipline [PX-0062]. Nothing on an airframer's dates or rates. No EIS earlier than launch + 6. No durability claim not yet proven. No selection or Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record. No booked upside [PX-0311].

Governance: empty `overrides`. A binding veto from Mitchill (four grounds) or Eddy (two grounds) means I revise once, within it. The Board vetoes any item that carries an unresolved veto or red-line flag, or a premium above $0.5B.
Premium cap: doctrine plus objective premium never exceeds $1B. A Board item that trails `hold` passes only on a declared premium of $0.5B or less that serves the objective. Row A needs none.
frame.asks_cfo:
Neil, I trust your cash numbers over my own operating dates. Please give me the following.

(1) Your column probabilities for S1-S8. Then, for each row A-F: the worst column and the expected PV.

(2) The `launch` minus `launch_if_selected` vector, which I read as -2.00 / 0 / +0.29 / 0 / 0 / +0.90 / -2.00 / -2.00, and its expected edge Σ p × diff under your weights. Tell me whether it clears zero (your ground 2) and the Board's +$0.5B. My arithmetic: break-even needs about 69% of the weight on S6 against the losing columns. The Board's bar needs about 86%, or 56% even with no weight in the losing columns.

(3) The grid assumes nobody moves after this round. Price, or at least name, the option an unconditional 2030 GTF2 would buy if NGSA picked code 3 or 5 now and then switched to a P&W code in 2035. GTF2 would be ready in 2036, ahead of a 2037 EIS. Record it as unproven; do not book it (your ground 4).

(4) The Joint Venture's cost if Rolls-Royce commits and nobody selects it: -2.00 in S7 on any row. Confirm that a live GTF2 folds in, so the launch+JV row costs no more than the launch row.

(5) The cancel plan. A 2030 GTF2 can be cancelled only in 2035, with a $1.67B write-off ($2B × 5/6). Confirm the write-off, and confirm that a triggered GTF2 which loses its selection before 2036 is reviewed then.

(6) Envelope and capital order. GTF2 is $2B over six years, about $0.33B a year inside the roughly $6B self-funded envelope. 2030E net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA on the analyst models. Confirm the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched, and that this competes with buybacks, not the dividend.

(7) The outcome of your four veto checks on Row A: dividend/debt, carrying an unselected engine, aggressive terms, booked upside. I read `launch_if_selected` as unable to carry an unselected engine by construction; tell me if you disagree.
frame.asks_ops:
Shane, you propose the engine orders and your two vetoes bind. Please give me the following.

(1) Your proposal for `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr` this round, with the reasoning.

(2) Readiness. GTF2 triggered in 2030 is ready in 2036, against each live airframe's EIS: NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, fps 10-year 2040, fps via Embraer 2040. Confirm that a 2035 trigger (ready 2041) can serve none of these. For the Joint Venture: formation + 6, so a 2035 formation is ready in 2041. Give me the fold-in dates: a live GTF2 launched in 2030 (ready 2036), or Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB solo if it launches in 2030 (ready 2037).

(3) Durability. A 2037 EIS leaves one year of margin. Show how time on wing is proven before entry into service, not efficiency alone. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF [PX-0073]. Tell me whether the GTF Advantage durability content and the Hot Section kit are mature enough to carry into GTF2's design.

(4) Pacing parts and capacity. Confirm GTF2 development does not draw castings, forgings, engineers or shop capacity away from the GTF fleet and AOG recovery; the fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080, PX-0123]. (5) The engineering load of a triggered GTF2 alongside the in-service fleet. There is no strain charge on this board, so this is your judgement.

(6) The outcome of your two veto checks (durability before EIS; parts and capacity) on Row A, and on Row C if you consider it.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Row A: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`, no premium ($0B).

Why. It never trails `hold`: +24.23 / +7.88 / +26.24 in S2, S4 and S5, 0 elsewhere. It commits the moment demand is visible, which is our rule [PX-0109, PX-0009]. It answers the miss-a-cycle cost in the only round that can serve a 2030 airframe. And it is the order that serves the credibility objective: GTF2 would be in service on NGSA 2037 or fps 2040, well before 2050. Here the doctrine-favoured order and the objective-favoured order are the same.

Why not the unconditional `launch`. On my illustrative weights (S1 0.30, S2 0.15, S3 0.12, S4 0.08, S5 0.08, S6 0.07, S7 0.05, S8 0.15) its edge over Row A is about -0.90. Expected PV is about -1.48 for Row A, -2.38 for `launch` and -7.84 for `hold`. I will replace these weights with Neil's. A hedge would also need about 69% weight on S6 just to break even. It fails ground 2, which no premium can buy, and the Board would veto it.

Why `jv_with_rr: hold`. There is no trigger on the record and it costs -2.00 in S7. We revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits or an airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7, with the gear protected.

Where I am biased. My single likeliest column is S1 (rivals hold): I have assumed the next single-aisle for mid-next decade [PX-0093]. My operating dates have slipped before [PX-0017, PX-0098]. That is exactly why I want the conditional order, not my judgement of timing, to answer a 2030 selection.

Exit plan, written in now. A triggered GTF2 that loses its selection before it is ready is reviewed for cancel in 2035 (write-off $1.67B). It is protected while a live airframe still asks for it.

Other moves, public, no grid effect:
- Announce the GTF Hot Section durability kit for the in-service fleet, charged on standard terms.
- Restate standard terms: no launch-style pricing. We are not in the early entry phase [PX-0055].

Proposed disclosure, in my voice:
"The GTF fleet has not been where our customers need it, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared, on standard terms. It will be ready six years from launch, with durability proven before entry into service. We will speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. When we've seen the demand and we feel good about it, we invest."

tests.name: Column probabilities and expected PV by row
tests.threshold: One probability per grid column, summing to 1, used for every expected value. Report expected PV and worst column per row, and the expected edge over hold.
tests.numbers: My weights: S1 0.35, S2 0.12, S3 0.13, S4 0.07, S5 0.06, S6 0.07, S7 0.05, S8 0.15 (sum 1.00). P(a launch that selects P&W, S2+S4+S5) = 0.25. P(a launch without P&W, S3+S6) = 0.20. P(no airframe launch, S1+S7+S8) = 0.55. Why: nothing is on the record, the team plans for NGSA in the mid-2030s, I plan below airframers' ramps, and the GTF's reputation weighs on our selection odds. Expected PV and worst column: Row A (launch_if_selected / hold) -1.99, worst -19.28 (S3, S6). Row B (Do Nothing) -7.02, worst -19.28 (S2, S3, S5, S6). Row C (launch / hold) -2.99, worst -18.99 (S3). Row D (launch_if_selected / commit) -2.09, worst -19.28 (S3, S6). Row E (launch / commit) -2.99, worst -18.99 (S3). Row F (hold / commit) -7.12, worst -19.28. Expected edge over hold: A +5.03, C +4.03, D +4.93, E +4.03, F -0.10. On Calio's illustrative weights: A -1.48, B -7.84, C -2.38. The ranking A > D > C = E > B > F holds under both weight sets.

tests.name: Cash by year and the low end
tests.threshold: For each row, the expected and worst column. R&D phased at $2B over 6 years (about $0.33B a year), charged in full. A Joint Venture formed while GTF2 is live adds no new R&D.
tests.numbers: Row A: $0.33B a year in 2030-35 only in S2, S4 and S5 (p 0.25), so about $0.08B a year expected and $0 in S1, S3, S6, S7 and S8. Low end -19.28 (S3/S6), the same as Do Nothing, and no order of ours changes it. Row C: $0.33B a year in 2030-35 in every column, $2B in all. Row D: as Row A, plus $2B over 2030-35 in S7 if Rolls-Royce commits (Joint Venture formed 2030, ready 2036). Row E: $2B at most, because GTF2 folds into the Joint Venture share and the two never stack (S7 -2.00 on both C and E). The gap between S2 and S3 under launch_if_selected (+4.95 against -19.28) is $24.23B. It is the airframer's call, not ours.

tests.name: Envelope fit
tests.threshold: New R&D committed this round fits the self-funded R&D and capex envelope of about $6B a year (inference: threshold).
tests.numbers: The most new R&D any row commits is $2B over six years, or $0.33B a year: 5.6% of about $6B. Rows A and D spend it only on a selection. Row E does not stack GTF2 and the Joint Venture (fold-in). No stretch is needed.

tests.name: Dividend and debt path (veto ground 1)
tests.threshold: No plan that needs a dividend cut or halts deleveraging to pre-ASR debt. The board does not model this, so the test is not applicable unless the envelope test fails (inference).
tests.numbers: The envelope passes, so ground 1 is not reached. Context from the analyst models: 2030E RTX net debt is 0.76x EBITDA (MS, $16.6B) to 0.94x (GS, $21.0B). Dividends are $5.0-5.6B and buybacks $4-5B in 2030E. About $10-16B is left after shareholder returns over 2026-30E. GTF2 at $0.33B a year comes out of the residual after the dividend and debt paydown, so it competes with buybacks, not the dividend. The dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched.

tests.name: Unselected engine (ground 2): gtf2_solo launch_if_selected (Rows A, D)
tests.threshold: Spends only on a selection on the record that round, and only if GTF2 is ready by that airframe's EIS.
tests.numbers: Against hold, by column S1-S8: 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is never below hold. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2036, against EIS dates of 2037 (NGSA, fps 7-year) and 2040 (fps 10-year or via Embraer). I agree it cannot carry an unselected engine by construction. One caveat: a 2030 selection can be changed in 2035. That is the 2035 review, not a carry in round 1. The trigger on codes 6 and 7 (shared source) is declared doctrine relief and costs $0B.

tests.name: Unselected engine (ground 2): unconditional gtf2_solo launch (Rows C, E)
tests.threshold: Expected edge over launch_if_selected must be at least 0, with p* = cost / (cost + gain). Board bar is +$0.5B. Cancel round written in.
tests.numbers: Launch minus launch_if_selected, by column: -2.00 / 0 / +0.29 / 0 / 0 / +0.90 / -2.00 / -2.00. Expected edge on my weights: -1.00 (Calio's weights -0.90). With a 2035 cancel in S1, S7 and S8 (loss -1.67): -0.82. Odds of a launch without P&W against no launch: 0.27 on my weights, against p* = 2 / (2 + 0.50) = 0.80. On S6 alone, break-even needs S6 / (S6 + losing columns) of 0.69. Mine is 0.07 / 0.62 = 0.11. The Board's +0.5 needs 0.86, or 0.56 with no weight in the losing columns. S3 alone breaks even only at 0.87 and can never clear +0.5. Stress case (S3 0.30, S6 0.20, losing columns 0.20): edge -0.13, still below zero. Cancel round 2035, write-off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, saving $0.33B against running on.

tests.name: Cancel arithmetic
tests.threshold: Write-off = R&D x years elapsed / 6. Cancel a live GTF2 at the first round no live airframe can still select it in time (inference).
tests.numbers: A 2030 GTF2 can be cancelled only in 2035: write-off $1.67B, saving $0.33B. It is ready in 2036, before the 2045 round. A triggered GTF2 is reviewed in 2035. The 2035 orders are sealed at the same time as the airframer's last code change (its EIS is 2037 or 2040). So the review rests on the 2030 record, and while that airframe can still select GTF2 it is protected. Cancel only if the airframe is cancelled or publicly off P&W. For an unconditional launch the cancel round is 2035, written in. Nothing is live today.

tests.name: Terms (ground 3)
tests.threshold: No discounted engines or spares in any other move; list price is the floor. A ground-3 veto is binding.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: On the unconditional launch, three things would move me. One is a P&W selection on the public record; launch_if_selected already answers that this round. Another is hard evidence that S6 carries at least 69% of the weight against the no-launch columns (86% for the Board's bar). On launch_if_selected: a failed durability or parts check from Eddy, which I would defer to, or a brief that adds spend breaking the about $6B envelope.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. Every row has a minus-19 column: an NGSA or fps that launches without us. No order of ours closes that gap; only the selection does, and that is the airframer's call. The question is what we spend to be ready.

On my weights (S1 0.35, S2 0.12, S3 0.13, S4 0.07, S5 0.06, S6 0.07, S7 0.05, S8 0.15), `launch_if_selected` with `jv_with_rr: hold` is -1.99 expected against -7.02 for Do Nothing: +5.03, and it never trails `hold`. It spends nothing unless a P&W code is on the record, then $0.33B a year for six years, about 5.6% of the $6B envelope. The dividend and the debt path don't move; this competes with buybacks.

The unconditional `launch` buys +0.29 in S3 and +0.90 in S6 and costs $2.00B in S1, S7 and S8. Expected edge -1.00. Break-even needs 69% of that weight on S6; I have 11%. A 2035 cancel writes off $1.67B and saves only $0.33B. That is carrying an unselected engine: ground 2, binding.

`jv_with_rr: commit` helps in no column and costs $2.00B in S7. Its case rests on a Rolls-Royce commitment nobody has made: ground 4, binding.

The 2035 switch option, a 2030 airframe moving to a P&W code after seeing a live GTF2, is real but unproven. It breaks even at about a one-in-five chance of a switch. I'm not booking it.

My booked number for our package is zero. We'll cross that bridge when an airframer gets us to it.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ENGINE ORDERS (round 1, decision year 2030): gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr: hold. This is a Board item (launch_if_selected).

WHY gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected. It ties the launch to a customer. Until an airframer picks a code with P&W in it (2, 6 or 7), engineering, castings and forgings stay on the fleet. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2036, which is before every EIS a 2030 airframe can have (2037 or 2040). It is the only round that can serve a 2030 selection. Grid ('GTF2 Solo if selected' minus 'GTF2: hold') = 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0 for S1-S8, so it never trails hold. I accept a shared code (6 or 7): the A320neo is shared today and we hold over 50% of its deliveries [PX-0127]. Calling that doctrine relief is Calio's job.

WHY NOT an unconditional launch. My rule: an unconditional launch only into a code with P&W already on the public record. None exists in 2030. It passes both of my veto grounds, so it is not my veto. The -2.00 in S1, S7 and S8 is Mitchill's ground and the Board's.

WHY jv_with_rr: hold. Neither trigger is on the record: Rolls-Royce has not committed, and there is no live airframe on code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Commit only adds -2.00 in S7. When a trigger appears, my technical conditions are: the JV engine is ready by the airframe's EIS, and P&W keeps its gear and core [P-1233]. The call is Calio's.

ANSWERS TO CALIO
(1) As above.

(2) Readiness.
- 2030 trigger, ready 2036: NGSA 2037 (1 year of margin), fps 7-year 2037 (1 year), fps 10-year 2040 (4 years), fps via Embraer 2040 (4 years).
- Confirmed: a 2035 trigger is ready in 2041 and serves none of these. It is 4 years late for 2037 and 1 year late for 2040.
- Joint Venture: formed 2030, ready 2036; formed 2035, ready 2041. A 2035 formation with a 2030 GTF2 folded in is ready 2036. With a 2030 UltraFan NB solo folded in (7 years), it is ready 2037.
- Embraer's narrowbody (EIS 2034 if launched in 2030) flies today's GTF, not GTF2.

(3) Durability.
- How time on wing is proven: endurance testing in severe environments (the hot and sandy fleets are where the GTF fell short [PX-0122]), at the Advantage's multiple (more than double, and 3x the base programme [P-0779][P-1095]).
- New features are instrumented (the seat's doctrine [P-1214]). All life-limited parts are at full life at EIS [PX-0128]. We trade fuel burn for durability [PX-0095].
- Gate (inference): endurance testing and life-limited part lives are proven by the 2036 ready year. 2036-37 is margin, not test time, and we don't compress testing to hold 2037.
- The margin is thin. My own certification slipped a year (mid-2024 to 2025), and the company's prior for a derivative is a 1.5-2 year slip.
- What to carry in: the Advantage (certified 2025, up to 2x time on wing, full-life LLPs [P-0785]) and the Hot Section kit (90-95% of the Advantage's gains, in shop visits from 2026 [PX-0088][PX-0106]) are the right baseline for GTF2.
- Whether they have matured in service by 2030 is not in my evidence; the profile says it takes about 1M fleet hours to surface issues [P-0847]. I want the 2030 fleet removal data before the hot-section design is frozen.
- The new risk is in the composite fan, the CMCs and the new gear [P-0790]. Those get instrumented and tested on their own. If a feature isn't proven in time, it waits for a later block.

(4) Pacing parts.
- The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, and the board does not model parts.
- Row A draws nothing until it triggers. If it triggers, development hardware comes from the same castings and forging lines. Airbus engines and fleet lift keep first call in the daily allocation, reviewed weekly [PX-0123][PX-0131].
- S8: yes, Embraer can fly today's GTF with no new engine (+4.15 on hold and on Row A). Its line rises to 8 a month 6 years after EIS, about 192 engines a year around 2040 (my arithmetic). Forging capacity takes 2-2.5 years to add [P-0079], so plan it early.

(5) Engineering load. My judgement: manageable as one programme. The Advantage's engineering began shifting to other priorities in 2025 [PX-0351], and a 2030 trigger does not overlap the kit's first years (from 2026). The crowded window is 2034-40, if S2 or S5 and S8 come together.

(6) Veto checks.
- Row A: durability before EIS passes (2036 is no later than 2037 or 2040). Parts and capacity passes (no live problem, and the order is conditional).
- Row C: both checks pass; no veto from me. I don't propose it.

CANCEL. I have no record on cancelling, so this defers to Calio and Mitchill. Fact: a 2030 GTF2 can be cancelled only in 2035, with a $1.67B write-off. In 2035 I will report whether it can still be ready by the EIS of any live airframe whose code includes P&W.

Where my record is thin: the views on the Joint Venture, cancelling and engineering load are the seat's doctrine and my inference, not my words.

The trigger itself requires 'ready by its EIS', so a triggered GTF2 cannot go on an airframe before it is ready. A 2035 trigger is ready in 2041 and misses all four (-4/-4/-1/-1). Grid S2/S4/S5: 'GTF2 Solo if selected' +4.95/+3.32/+6.96 against 'GTF2: hold' -19.28/-4.56/-19.28. Embraer's narrowbody (S8, EIS 2034) flies today's GTF: +4.15 on both rows.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Things that would change my mind:
- A later brief shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem (an AOG spike or a supplier escape). Then fleet lift comes first: any unconditional launch fails ground 2, and I would want containment with a dated recovery before any new commitment.
- An airframe's EIS falls before GTF2's ready year (for example, a selection in a round where launch + 6 exceeds the EIS). Then I veto on ground 1.
- Severe-environment fleet data shows the GTF Advantage or Hot Section kit short of its time on wing. I would then want more test time than a 2037 EIS allows, and would warn Calio that only a 2040 EIS gives real margin.
- A P&W code (2, 6 or 7) appears on the public record. Then an unconditional launch in that round passes my test.
- Rolls-Royce commits on the record, or a live airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Then I would state the JV technical conditions and leave commit to Calio.
ops.memo:
The bad number first: one year. A GTF2 triggered in 2030 is ready in 2036. An NGSA or 7-year fps launched in 2030 enters service in 2037. That is the whole margin, and my own GTF Advantage certification slipped a year. So I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. I'll tell you how we hold it: severe-environment endurance testing, time on wing proven and not just fuel burn, and all life-limited parts at full life right at entry into service. We don't compress testing to make a date. A 10-year fps, or fps via Embraer, in 2040 gives us four years.

My proposal: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Only a 2030 order can answer a 2030 selection: a 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, too late. It ties engineering to a customer. Until someone selects us, castings, forgings and engineers stay on fleet lift. The fleet beats a new engine.

Parts: the brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, and the board doesn't model parts. Both my veto checks pass. No unconditional launch, because no P&W code is on the record. The Joint Venture waits for Rolls-Royce on the record, and it keeps our gear.

Where my record is thin: one investor day, June 2023, before the recall. Nothing in my own words on Joint Ventures or cancels; that is the seat's doctrine, not my record.

This is the next GTF, not a clean sheet. We earn the dependable engine reputation every day.

It is ready six years from launch, on standard terms, and does not enter service until durability is proven. No EIS date is stated, nothing is said about an airframer's dates, and no selection is claimed. No grid effect.

At that point check the ready date: formation + 6, or 2036 with a 2030 GTF2 folded in. Terms share risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233].

decision.public_statement: I'll start with the bad news. For years the GTF fleet was not where our customers needed it to be. We own that, and we have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. So we control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round in which an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch. It will not enter service until its durability is proven: endurance testing in severe environments, life-limited parts at full life, and time on wing, not just fuel burn. We will not compress testing to make a date. It comes on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. For the fleet flying today, the GTF Hot Section kit is available at shop visit on standard terms, and we will report its time on wing once the fleet has proven it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. When we've seen the demand and we feel good about it, we invest. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE (round 1, 2030).

1. Start from Eddy's proposal: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Row A). Mitchill recommends the same orders, and so does my framing lean.

2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto.
- Mitchill, ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine), binding on the unconditional `launch` (Rows C and E). Its edge over `launch_if_selected` is -2.00 / 0 / +0.29 / 0 / 0 / +0.90 / -2.00 / -2.00. That is -0.94 expected on my weights, -1.00 on his, and -0.82 even with a 2035 cancel. Struck.
- Mitchill, ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven), binding on `jv_with_rr: commit` (Rows D, E and F). Its only case is a Rolls-Royce commitment nobody has made. It adds -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, -0.10 expected. Struck.
- Eddy's two grounds pass on Row A. GTF2 is ready in 2036, against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037, and fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040. The brief shows no live parts or fleet problem. He records no binding veto. His standing condition, no compressed testing and no EIS before launch + 6, is written into the statement and the internal moves.
- What is left: Row A and Row B (Do Nothing).

3. Constraint first, then optimise [PX-0035]. The trigger launches GTF2 only if it can be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS, so by construction no P&W engine goes on an airframe before it is ready. That leaves a year of margin on a 2037 EIS and four years on 2040. Durability is the gate, not the date [PX-0073]. On my weights:
- Row A: expected -1.59, worst -19.28 (S3/S6).
- Row B: expected -7.45, the same worst.
- Row A minus `hold`: 0 / +24.23 / 0 / +7.88 / +26.24 / 0 / 0 / 0. It never trails `hold`: +5.86 expected on my weights, +5.03 on Mitchill's.
- The ranking A > D > C = E > B > F holds on both weight sets.

4. My tests.
- Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]: `launch_if_selected` commits in the same round a selection appears. It is the visible-demand order.
- Miss a cycle [PX-0071] (said RTX-wide, so applying it here is inference): `hold` gives up $24-26B in S2 and S5. A 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, after every EIS a 2030 airframe can have. So 2030 is the only round that can answer a 2030 selection, and Row A answers it.
- Responsible bet: the doctrine-favoured order is also the best expected PV and the order that serves the objective, so the premium is $0B.
- Dividend: Mitchill confirms that the dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched. The spend is $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, and it competes with buybacks, not the dividend.
- Value, not share: standard terms only.

5. Doctrine relief, declared. Every P&W selection on this grid is shared-source (S2 is code 6, S4 code 7, S5 codes 7 and 6). The sole-source red line [P-0746] is therefore relieved, as dashboard_game.md §5 allows. On NGSA this is franchise defence: we held about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. The relief costs $0B.

6. Tie-breaks.
- The fleet beats a new engine: the conditional order keeps engineers, castings and forgings on fleet lift until a customer selects us.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer: none is on the record, and we answer on product and standard terms.

7. What I give up and why. Mitchill names an unbooked option. A 2030 airframe on code 3 or 5 might switch to a P&W code in 2035, and only a live 2030 GTF2 (ready 2036) could serve it. It would be worth about $23.9B in S3 and $23.3B in S6, and it breaks even against the -1.00 edge only at a switch probability of about 0.21. Nothing on the record supports that. I invest on visible demand, not ahead of it, so I accept forgoing the option and declare it here rather than book it.

8. My biases, named. My single likeliest column is S1, because I have assumed the next single-aisle comes mid-next decade [PX-0093]. That is my incrementalism. My operating dates have slipped before [PX-0017][PX-0098]. Both are reasons to let the conditional order, not my judgement of timing, answer a 2030 selection, and to state no EIS date of my own.

9. Where my record is thin. My record has no evidence on a Joint Venture (Low), so `hold` there follows company doctrine and Mitchill's and Eddy's tests, not my own words. Launch thresholds are Medium-confidence inference.

10. Board. The only Board item is `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`. Its item value against `hold` is never negative, Eddy's checks pass, Mitchill raises no veto against it, `overrides` is empty and the premium is $0B. `jv_with_rr: hold` is the default and is not a Board item.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily. Under the team rule I trust Mitchill's cash numbers over my own operating dates.
- His column weights and mine give the same ranking. His figures: A -1.99, B -7.02, C -2.99.
- His two binding vetoes are on allowed grounds, and I accept both: ground 2 on the unconditional `launch` and ground 4 on `commit`. Neither order is in my package, so no revision is needed.
- His envelope check ($0.33B a year, 5.6% of about $6B), his dividend and pre-ASR debt confirmation, and his cancel arithmetic (2035, $1.67B) go into the Board package as given.
- I take his advice on wording. The Hot Section kit is announced with no time-on-wing number, and 'durability proven before entry into service' is phrased as a commitment, not a claim.
- I name his 2035 switch option and do not book it.
- Tension, recorded: his line is 'we'll cross that bridge'. Mine is 'miss a cycle'. The conditional order serves both: it crosses the bridge the moment an airframer brings us to it, and that is the only round it can be crossed.
memo_weighing.ops:
Eddy's proposal is my starting point, and I adopt it unchanged. His readiness check binds on me. It is rules arithmetic, verifiable against the brief: ready 2036 against an EIS of 2037 or 2040, and a 2035 trigger, ready 2041, serves none of them. I weigh it fully.

His seat rests on one event, the June 2023 investor day, before the recall, so his record is Low. He says so himself: his views on the Joint Venture, cancels and engineering load are the seat's doctrine and his inference. I weigh those as advice, not evidence.

I adopt the following:
- His durability gate: severe-environment endurance, full-life life-limited parts at EIS, no compressed testing, and new features deferred to a later block if unproven.
- His request for 2030 fleet removal data before the GTF2 hot section is frozen.
- His note that Embraer would fly today's GTF in S8, so forging capacity should be planned early.

His warning that one year of margin is thin, given his own one-year certification slip, is exactly why the public statement gives no EIS date. He has no binding veto on Row A. On Row C his position is advice, not a veto, and I don't need it because Mitchill's ground 2 already strikes that row.

recommendations.text: Disclosure, next round. The 2030 statement passes: it states launch + 6, gives no EIS date, says nothing about any airframer's dates, books no selection, announces no Joint Venture, and phrases durability as a commitment. Two changes for 2035. First, qualify the 'in any round' offer with 'where GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service', so it cannot be read as a date we cannot hold; that misreading is how pressure to compress testing starts (Eddy's advice). Second, `launch_if_selected` acts only in the round it is ordered. If the public offer stands, the order has to be sealed again in every round where it is legal.

Durability before entry into service. A 2037 EIS leaves only one year of margin. Bring the 2030 GTF Advantage and Hot Section fleet removal data to the Governance and Public Policy Committee before the GTF2 hot-section design freezes. Do not compress the endurance test programme to hold 2037; an unproven feature waits for a later block. Announce the Hot Section kit with no time-on-wing figure until the fleet has proven it, and keep the fleet first on castings and forgings.

2035, if the order triggered (S2, S4 or S5). Keep GTF2 whole. While a live airframe not yet in service has a code that includes P&W and GTF2 can be ready by its EIS, a cancel passes only if the cancel row beats `hold` in every plausible column. Review a cancel only if that airframe is cancelled or publicly moves off P&W; the write-off is $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, saving $0.33B. Bring Eddy's 2035 readiness check against each live EIS, Mitchill's envelope check, and the programme's whole-life NPV against `hold`.

2035, if no airframe launched (S1, S7 or S8). Order `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` again (Miss a cycle). A 2035 GTF2 is ready in 2041. That can still serve an airframe launched in 2035 (NGSA or fps 7-year EIS 2042, fps 10-year 2045), and it keeps the 2050 credibility objective reachable. A round in which every order is `hold` never reaches the Board.

2035, if an airframe launched without P&W (S3 or S6). Do not book Mitchill's switch option, and do not chase it with an unconditional launch. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, after a 2037 or 2040 EIS, so it cannot serve a 2030 airframe that switches codes. Any unconditional `launch` still needs a selection on the record, or a weighted edge over `launch_if_selected` of at least +$0.5B. We win selections on durability and standard terms, not with a discount.

Shared-source relief. The Board accepts the declared relief on codes 6 and 7, including Boeing fps on code 7 (S4, item value +7.88, above the hurdle), as dashboard_game.md §5 allows. It is relief for a conditional order only. It is not the NGSA franchise exception, and it never justifies an unconditional launch for the fps alone. Restate this in each round's rationale.

Joint Venture and capital. If Rolls-Royce commits in 2030 (S7), its commitment is on the record in 2035 and `jv_with_rr: commit` becomes testable. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041, unless a live GTF2 folds in. Its weighted item value on the 2035 grid must be at least 0, and P&W's gear and core technology stay out. Each round, also report the dividend, the pre-ASR debt path and the envelope fit. If the Embraer forging-capacity plan for S8 needs capital, bring it through the Finance Committee.

rolls_royce.public_statement: So. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. Our route into the narrowbody is a partnership, not a solo programme: Rolls-Royce stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. We take a narrowbody engine forward only for an airframe that has chosen it. Entry into service will be no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation, with in-service support through partner shops in place before entry into service. We don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This moves `ultrafan_nb_solo` away from my framing proposal (`launch_if_selected`). I took the decision openly, as the Board asked, on the memos' new numbers.

1. TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
- I started from my proposal: 'UltraFan NB if selected', everything else hold.
- Binding vetoes. No one vetoes either the proposal or hold. McCabe co-signs either one. Watson invokes no Civil veto and says he concurs with Do Nothing.
- Best grid plan inside the red lines, on expected PV: 'UltraFan NB if selected', which is +1.25 on my weights and +2.63 on the Board's.
- My order is 'UltraFan NB: hold', the plan favoured by the mission and the Board, kept within the $3B cap. Declared premium: $1.25B on my weights ($2.63B on the Board's illustrative weights, also inside $3B).
- Tie-break: mine.

2. HOW THE EXCO WEIGHED THE $8B BREACH AGAINST THE SELECTED-CASE VALUE
For the conditional order:
- It costs nothing unless selected, and is worth +11.89 (S2), +7.96 (S4) and +20.80 (S5).
- The three selected columns carry 10% of my weight (P 0.10, nothing on the record).
- It is the only way to serve an airframe launched in 2030.

Against it, from the memos:
- Control's bound. A trigger puts $8.0B against a $4B limit with no way back. A 2035 fold still counts $5.7B, and a 2035 cancel writes off $5.71B. Control's wording is that the bound "sets the terms" of the narrowbody entry, and I read it that way: it constrains how we enter, not just one goal among several.
- McCabe's envelope test fails. A triggered Solo is about £0.84bn a year, 91% of 2030E company-funded R&D (£927m). It roughly doubles R&D, so it cannot sit in a flat envelope.
- Watson's capacity figures. A trigger means about 1,200-2,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050, against 197 Trent. That is 6-10 times our OE rate, and we have no narrowbody MRO scale. The Trent ramp and time on wing must keep first call. That is exactly the risk to the cash cow Control describes.
- Zero margin. An NGSA EIS of 2037 against UltraFan ready in 2037 leaves no float. My own dates have slipped: the Trent 1000 blade promised for end-2023 was certified in June 2025 [RX-0077, RX-0129]. Actually, I've seen this movie before. "Until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing" [RX-0124].
- Strain. A triggered Solo bars any widebody programme for the rest of the game unless we take $5B of strain.

recommendations.text: Safety first, before anything else. The public statement gives no EIS earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB, or + 6 for the Joint Venture and UltraFan WB, and nothing on any airframer's dates. If `launch_if_selected` is submitted, Watson states its zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year EIS of 2037 and the support plan he would have in place before EIS.

Control's mission sets the terms of the narrowbody entry: our own narrowbody money within $4B. The board's narrowbody route is therefore the Joint Venture with P&W, the risk-sharing form our doctrine prefers. A triggered UltraFan NB Solo is $8B with no way back inside the bound: a fold in 2035 still counts $5.7B, and a cancel counts its spend to date.

On `launch_if_selected` the ExCo should decide openly and record the decision in `rationale`. Its case: it costs nothing unless selected and is worth +11.89 (S2), +7.96 (S4) and +20.80 (S5). Round 1 is the only window to serve an airframe launched in 2030, since a 2035 Solo is ready in 2042 and a Joint Venture formed in 2035 in 2041, both after a 2037 or 2040 EIS. Its cost: if triggered, $8B against the $4B bound, and an NB programme on the record that bars any widebody programme for the rest of the game without the $5B strain. The board leans to Do Nothing. We will approve the conditional form if the CEO, with McCabe's co-signature, judges the selected case worth it, but we will not accept the unconditional form.

No widebody programme this round. No Re-engine is on the record, WB share is 58% in 2050 in every column (the Widebody franchise test is not triggered), the upgrade is −0.98 and UltraFan WB −4.00 on the grid, and either would make any later Joint Venture breach 'never both' and carry the $5B strain. Keep the one-programme slot for the narrowbody entry. Revisit the Trent 1000 upgrade only once the narrowbody door has closed or a rival-engined Re-engine is on the record, and UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record.

Use the public statement to open the partnership. The Joint Venture with P&W has precedent (IAE, the 2012 next-generation venture): say Rolls-Royce prefers a partner for narrowbody and stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with P&W. Make it a few binding words, said only when we are sure, with no dates. The board will look to approve a `jv_with_pw: commit` in 2035 once P&W's commitment is on the record and a live airframe can use it by its EIS.

Show the worst column of every item and its capex a year against a broadly flat R&D envelope. A Solo at about $1.14B a year (about £0.84bn) would roughly match all company-funded R&D in the MS model (£590m in 2026E, £927m in 2030E). The Joint Venture halves it. The capital order stays: balance sheet, then the dividend, then investment.

Next round, cancel what no airframe can use. If both airframers launch in 2030 on codes without RR, any UltraFan NB that never triggered costs nothing. But any narrowbody programme left with no live airframe should be cancelled before its spend grows, inside the $4B bound.

It spends nothing unless an airframer selects Rolls-Royce this round, and it is worth +7.96 to +20.80 if one does. But if it fires, we commit $8B against Control's $4B narrowbody bound, with no way back inside it. The alternative is Do Nothing on all four fields: narrowbody money stays at $0 and we wait for a Joint Venture route in 2035, which gives up any airframe launched in 2030. The widebody programmes (Trent 1000 upgrade, UltraFan WB) are a separate question: is there any reason to spend on widebody blind this round?

The cost, said plainly:

On widebody:

- The upgrade is -0.98 on this board, widebody share is already 58%, and the upgrade would close the Joint Venture door under the mission.

No Joint Venture commit until P&W's commitment is on the record.
