"So. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for the narrowbody in the round an airframer selects it, and not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. Our preference is partnership. We stand ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. Widebody is our core. We won't do anything not profitable."

cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet; that order does not change. On the numbers, `launch_if_selected` is 0 in seven columns and +11.89, +7.96 and +20.80 where an airframer selects us. Expected gain is +1.25 on my weights (P 0.10) and +2.63 on the Board's; once it fires, +12.5 to +13.1. The selected case clears the +$2B bar and, on a crude check, a high-teens hurdle, with S4 thinnest at about 19-20%. Its unselected loss is zero. Do not confuse it with the unconditional Solo: -8.00 in five columns, -4.68 expected on my weights. I will not sign that.

If it fires, it is about £0.84bn a year for seven years: 11% of 2030E free cash flow. No equity, no new debt, net cash intact, buyback untouched. The balance sheet passes. The envelope does not: that is 91% of 2030E company-funded R&D, so it is redeployed, not added. And it is $8B against Control's $4B bound, with no way back; a 2035 cancel still writes off $5.7B. That is the CEO's call, made openly. I price holding at $1.25-2.63B expected, inside the cap. I co-sign either.

No Joint Venture commit until P&W is on the record: -0.40 expected, -4.00 in S7. No widebody spend blind: the upgrade is -0.91, UltraFan WB -3.69, and either beside the narrowbody item loses more than its own bill.

My record on engine-launch economics is thin; these are board numbers. That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

A 2030 Solo folded into a 2035 Joint Venture would keep 2037, because it is further along, but it counts $5.7B under the mission.

tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037 for a 2030 trigger), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB (2036), or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (2036 if formed in 2030). Nothing on airframers' dates.
tests.numbers: CEO's draft says 'Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch': that is launch + 7, so 2037 at the earliest for a 2030 trigger. 'We stand ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney' carries no date. No airframer date appears. I suggest adding 'with in-service support through partner shops in place before entry into service', with no date. I recheck the final text at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS, because RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (inference).
tests.numbers: This passes only if the following plan goes into the rationale with the trigger. (1) MRO through partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model: partner named by mid-programme and checked at the 2035 round. (2) Repair technology, a spares pool and field service, funded inside the $8B across the 7 development years (2030-37 for NGSA; to 2040 for fps 10-year). (3) An EIS support team with the airframer before entry into service, so we can respond and intervene early. (4) Narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers, not the Trent lines. Our V2500 support 'into the 2030s' gives us existing A320-operator relationships (inference). If the plan is not on record, the order goes to hold and the Civil veto applies at step 4. For a 2035 Joint Venture, P&W's narrowbody network could carry support (inference).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: $5B strain whenever a narrowbody and a widebody programme are both on record, whatever their dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference).
tests.numbers: Recommended plan ('UltraFan NB if selected', all else hold): $0 strain in all ten columns. Rejected plans: (1) 'if selected + T1000 upgrade': $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5, where the upgrade item is -5.98, with 2030-33 development overlapping UltraFan NB 2030-37 for 3 years. Red-line breach. (2) 'if selected + UltraFan WB': $5B in S2, S4 and S5, item -9.00, overlap 2030-36 (6 years). Red-line breach. (3) 'commit to JV + T1000 upgrade': $5B in S7 (-9.98). Once a Solo triggers, any later widebody programme carries $5B for good: strain is charged even after one programme is ready, and only a cancel before ready removes it. Cost if Airbus or Boeing re-engines: on this grid UltraFan WB is -0.90 and the upgrade -0.29 even in S8 and S9, so the bar costs no PV now. It gives up only the 63-68% share upside; a later grid may differ (inference).

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports one. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers: Brief's year table (hold): 197 widebody engines a year from 2026 to 2060, and 0 narrowbody. If UltraFan NB triggers, the 2050 narrowbody engine share is 32.3% (S2), 31.6% (S4) or 51.2% (S5). The brief has no year table for the triggered plan, so I estimate (inference): 2050 demand of 1,933 aircraft at two engines each is 3,866 engines, giving about 1,250, 1,220 and 1,980 narrowbody engines a year. That is 6 to 10 times our Trent OE rate. My own midterm ramp was widebody: OE from 190 to 300-350 a year, major refurbishments 700-750, total shop visits 1,100-1,200. I use my shop-visit figure, not the 1,400-1,500 Helen gave. MS shows Trent deliveries rising from 259 (2025A) to 391 (2030E). Advice: put narrowbody supply and overhaul through high-performing suppliers and partner shops; Trent time on wing and the Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ramps keep first call.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
tests.numbers: Hold: 58.0% in every year to 2060 (brief year table), and 58.0% in 2050 in all ten columns. 'If selected': 58.0% in 2050 in all ten columns; with no widebody programme it does not move in 2040 or 2045 either. Worst case under the rules: a GEnx upgrade (CFM +5 pp widebody) leaves 53%. The upgrade gives 63% and UltraFan WB 68% (S8, S9 only); neither is needed. Note: the board's widebody engine share does not move with the 787/A350 split, and Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 25.2% in S8.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: A cancelled or idle UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values are never adjusted (inference).
tests.numbers: If no airframer selects us, nothing is spent, and UltraFan technology (the geared architecture, 25% more efficient than the first Trent) keeps feeding Trent time on wing. If it triggers, the narrowbody programme feeds the fleet too. No grid adjustment.

vetoes.plan: UltraFan NB if selected (all other fields hold)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. I hold the Civil veto for step 4, on its grounds only. Under the team rule it binds if (a) the final statement or a public other move gives an EIS or ready date before 2037 for a 2030 trigger (launch + 7); (b) the statement, an other move or the rationale counts on the engine being in service before 2037; or (c) the rationale has no partner-shop support plan before EIS. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns.

vetoes.plan: UltraFan NB if selected: zero margin against a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-year EIS
vetoes.ground: Note, not a veto ground. It is a full 7-year programme and nothing is compressed, but it leaves no float for a test slip. If testing slips, maturity wins over the date and we tell the airframer early, as we did with NMA.

vetoes.plan: UltraFan NB if selected + T1000 upgrade; UltraFan NB if selected + UltraFan WB (option G)
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not a Civil veto. It breaks two rules: no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development, and no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected. $5B strain in S2, S4 and S5; overlap of 3 years (upgrade) and 6 years (UltraFan WB). The CEO strikes it.

vetoes.plan: UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade (option C)
vetoes.ground: Advice. The upgrade is my time-on-wing tool, but on this grid it is -0.98 (-0.29 in S8 and S9) and counts no earlier than 2042 with no Re-engine. Once it is on record, any later narrowbody programme carries $5B of strain. Defer it.

vetoes.plan: Triggered UltraFan NB (S2, S4, S5); 2035 Solo or Joint Venture for a 2030 airframe
vetoes.ground: Advice. A triggered engine means about 1,200-2,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050 with no narrowbody MRO scale, so the Trent ramp keeps first call on engineers and shops. A 2035 Solo (ready 2042) or Joint Venture (ready 2041) fails Ready by EIS for a 2030 airframe; that is advice, and McCabe prices it. The $8B against Control's $4B bound is the CEO's and CFO's call, not my ground.

vetoes.plan: Unconditional UltraFan NB Solo, first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB (options D, E, F)
vetoes.ground: No Civil ground. Readiness passes: Solo 2037, Joint Venture 2036 if formed in 2030, UltraFan WB 2036. They are rejected on the Board's and CFO's grounds. Any unconditional narrowbody launch or commit would still need the partner-shop support plan before EIS.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would move UltraFan NB to hold in four cases. (1) The ExCo record has no partner-shop support plan before EIS; the Civil veto would then bind. (2) The final statement or a public move gives an EIS before 2037 for a 2030 trigger, or before formation + 6 for a Joint Venture; the veto would bind. (3) There is evidence that the 7-year test schedule cannot be protected, for example if the UltraFan 30 demonstrator's 2028 ground test has not run. Zero margin to 2037 would then be compressed maturity in practice (inference). (4) Tufan and Helen decide Control's $4B bound governs. Do Nothing on all four passes every test of mine, and I would concur. I would move toward the Joint Venture in 2035 once P&W's commitment is on the record: ready at formation + 6, and P&W's gearbox and narrowbody support network answer our gearbox-sizing and MRO constraints (inference). I would revisit the Trent 1000 upgrade only once the narrowbody door has closed or a rival-engined Re-engine is on the record. A named airframe selection is what turns the conditional order into a programme.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: one Rolls-Royce, one programme at a time.

Maturity. A 2030 trigger runs the full seven years: UltraFan NB ready 2037. Zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year EIS of 2037, three years against an fps 10-year or via-Embraer EIS of 2040. Zero margin is a pass, not compressed maturity: nothing comes out of the test programme. No float: if testing slips, maturity wins over the date and we tell the airframer early. A 2035 Solo (2042) or Joint Venture (2041) serves no 2030 airframe.

Support. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so the trigger carries a plan: partner shops on the Singapore model, named by mid-programme; repair technology, spares and field support funded inside the $8B; an EIS support team with the airframer before entry into service. Put it in the rationale, or the order goes to hold.

Load. Nothing widebody beside it: strain $0 in every column. Once triggered, UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade carry $5B of strain for good. On this grid that costs nothing; both are negative even against a Re-engine.

Capacity. A triggered engine means about 1,200 to 2,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050, against 197 Trent. Trent time on wing and the XWB and 7000 ramps keep first call on engineers and shops.

Widebody: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, every column; 53% at worst.

The $8B breach of Control's $4B bound is your call and Helen's, not my ground. I recommend launch_if_selected, the rest hold. No veto.

other_moves.move: Open the door to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney
other_moves.detail: The public statement says Rolls-Royce prefers a partner for the narrowbody and stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the UltraFan technology we bring. No dates. It is not a `jv_with_pw: commit` order; we commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record (the Board's rule, and the team rule of partner first).

other_moves.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work goes on inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing. No programme launch, no new bill, no dates.

other_moves.move: Prepare narrowbody support groundwork (Watson)
other_moves.detail: A no-capex study of partner-shop MRO on the Singapore Joint Venture model and of P&W's narrowbody network, plus narrowbody castings and forgings placed with high-performing suppliers rather than on the Trent lines. If a Joint Venture is formed in 2035 the support plan is ready to name, so it is in place before any EIS.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

decision.public_statement: So. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. Our route into the narrowbody is a partnership, not a solo programme: Rolls-Royce stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology we bring. We take a narrowbody engine forward only for an airframe that has chosen it. Entry into service will be no earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation, with in-service support through partner shops in place before entry into service. We don't commit that easily. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on all four fields: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold`, `jv_with_pw: hold`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This moves `ultrafan_nb_solo` away from my framing proposal (`launch_if_selected`). I took the decision openly, as the Board asked, on the memos' new numbers.

1. TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
- I started from my proposal: 'UltraFan NB if selected', everything else hold.
- Binding vetoes. No one vetoes either the proposal or hold. McCabe co-signs either one. Watson invokes no Civil veto and says he concurs with Do Nothing.
- Best grid plan inside the red lines, on expected PV: 'UltraFan NB if selected', which is +1.25 on my weights and +2.63 on the Board's.
- My order is 'UltraFan NB: hold', the plan favoured by the mission and the Board, kept within the $3B cap. Declared premium: $1.25B on my weights ($2.63B on the Board's illustrative weights, also inside $3B).
- Tie-break: mine.

2. HOW THE EXCO WEIGHED THE $8B BREACH AGAINST THE SELECTED-CASE VALUE
For the conditional order:
- It costs nothing unless selected, and is worth +11.89 (S2), +7.96 (S4) and +20.80 (S5).
- The three selected columns carry 10% of my weight (P 0.10, nothing on the record).
- It is the only way to serve an airframe launched in 2030.

Against it, from the memos:
- Control's bound. A trigger puts $8.0B against a $4B limit with no way back. A 2035 fold still counts $5.7B, and a 2035 cancel writes off $5.71B. Control's wording is that the bound "sets the terms" of the narrowbody entry, and I read it that way: it constrains how we enter, not just one goal among several.
- McCabe's envelope test fails. A triggered Solo is about £0.84bn a year, 91% of 2030E company-funded R&D (£927m). It roughly doubles R&D, so it cannot sit in a flat envelope.
- Watson's capacity figures. A trigger means about 1,200-2,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050, against 197 Trent. That is 6-10 times our OE rate, and we have no narrowbody MRO scale. The Trent ramp and time on wing must keep first call. That is exactly the risk to the cash cow Control describes.
- Zero margin. An NGSA EIS of 2037 against UltraFan ready in 2037 leaves no float. My own dates have slipped: the Trent 1000 blade promised for end-2023 was certified in June 2025 [RX-0077, RX-0129]. Actually, I've seen this movie before. "Until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing" [RX-0124].
- Strain. A triggered Solo bars any widebody programme for the rest of the game unless we take $5B of strain.

Conclusion: the bound governs. We enter the narrowbody inside $4B through partnership: "We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that" [RX-0118]. Narrowbody is optional: "we don't need to do it" [RX-0075]. Widebody is the franchise [R-1574].

3. GRID ROWS (ΔPV $B, S1-S10)
Submitted plan, 'UltraFan NB: hold':
- 0 in every column. Worst column 0.
- It holds every field, so there are no Board items and no item row to set against hold.

Alternatives against hold, for the record:
- 'UltraFan NB if selected': 0, +11.89, 0, +7.96, +20.80, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. Expected +1.25 (mine) or +2.63 (Board's). Worst 0.
- 'UltraFan NB Solo': worst -8.00, expected -4.68 (mine). The Board vetoes it and McCabe withholds her signature.
- 'hold + commit to JV': -4.00 in S7, expected -0.40. P&W is not on the record, so it fails partner first and would be a Board veto.
- 'hold + T1000 upgrade': -0.98 in eight columns and -0.29 in S8-S9; expected -0.91.
- 'hold + UltraFan WB': -4.00 in eight columns and -0.90 in S8-S9; expected -3.69.

4. WEIGHTS (mine, McCabe's are the same)
- S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.05, S9 0.05, S10 0.05.
- Expected PV of the submitted plan: 0.00.

5. CONTROL'S MISSION METRICS FOR THE SUBMITTED PLAN
- All ten columns are the same: own narrowbody money $0.0B, strain $0B, widebody share in 2050 58.0%, narrowbody share in 2050 0.0%.
- Airbus's widebody airframe share is 41.2%, except 25.2% in S8.
- Both mission metrics are met in every column.

6. OBJECTIVE
- Widebody dominance is met: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column. My inference is 53% at worst if CFM funds a GEnx upgrade, still above 50%.
- Narrowbody entry is not met this round in any column. What we give up is entry through a 2030 airframe in S2, S4 and S5.
- The route stays open (inference from the public rules):
  - A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2041 and serves an airframe launched in 2035 or later.
  - If P&W runs a GTF2 Solo from 2030 and folds it into a 2035 Joint Venture, the engine is ready earlier (about 2036). It could then serve a 2030 airframe that recodes to 4 or 7, at our $4B share.

7. WIDEBODY
- No Re-engine is on the record.
- The upgrade is -0.98 and UltraFan WB -4.00.
- Either one would make any later Joint Venture carry $5B of strain and break 'never both'.
- Both hold, so there is no widebody premium. This departs from the team's round-1 upgrade default, which came from the old engine and does not carry over to this board.

8. VETO AND RED-LINE CHECKS
- CFO balance sheet: passes. No equity raise, no new leverage, buyback untouched.
- Civil: passes. The statement discloses no EIS earlier than Joint Venture formation + 6, nothing on any airframer's dates, and support through partner shops before EIS.
- Watson's support plan is recorded for any future narrowbody engine:
  - partner-shop MRO on the Singapore model, or P&W's network for a Joint Venture;
  - spares and field service funded inside the programme bill;
  - an EIS support team with the airframer;
  - castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
- Red-line flags: McCabe and Watson both flagged option G (a widebody item beside the conditional narrowbody). It is struck, and none is in the plan.
- No company red line is breached. Overrides are empty.

9. DOCTRINE VERSUS RECORD
- My record has no narrowbody launch decision (Medium confidence). The +$2B bar, the P weights and the $3B cap are doctrine and inference, not my words.
- The Joint Venture fold readiness is inferred from the public rules.

10. NEXT ROUND (2035)
- If P&W's commitment is on the record and a live airframe can use the Joint Venture by its EIS, I commit, with McCabe's co-signature, at $4B (about £0.49bn a year).
- If the narrowbody door has closed, I re-test the Trent 1000 upgrade as a durability case.

memo_weighing.cfo: Weighed fully. Her numbers carry the decision. I accept her hurdle pass on `launch_if_selected`: +1.25 on our weights and +2.63 on the Board's, worst 0, an IRR of about 19-28% on a crude check, with S4 the thinnest. Her advice line decided it. A triggered Solo at about £0.84bn a year is 91% of 2030E company-funded R&D, so it cannot sit in a flat envelope, and it carries $8B against Control's $4B bound with no way back ($5.7B on a fold or a cancel). She named "the CEO weights Control's $4B bound above the selected-case value" as a case in which she co-signs hold at a declared premium of $1.25-2.63B, inside the cap. That is the case I chose. Her binding vetoes (unconditional Solo, a first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, the upgrade beside the narrowbody item or alone without a premium) are all respected: no such order is submitted. Her balance-sheet tests pass trivially. I take her £0.49bn a year Joint Venture figure as the 2035 reference.
memo_weighing.ops: Weighed fully on maturity, support and load. He passes `launch_if_selected` on Ready by EIS with zero margin and says nothing is compressed. But he adds that there is no float, and that if testing slips maturity wins over the date. Given my own slipped dates [RX-0077, RX-0129], I take that as the reason I am not sure we would deliver to a 2037 EIS [RX-0124]. His capacity estimate decided it with McCabe's: 1,200-2,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050 against 197 Trent, with no narrowbody MRO scale. So does his point that a trigger bars widebody programmes for good unless we take $5B of strain. He concurs with Do Nothing on all four and invokes no Civil veto. His support plan is recorded for the Joint Venture route. I adopted his suggested support line in the public statement, which gives no EIS earlier than formation + 6 and nothing on any airframer's dates. His red-line flags on option G are struck, and they are not in the plan.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold (weight 0.40). Nothing is launched in 2030 and the narrowbody decision moves to 2035, when a Joint Venture formed with P&W (ready at formation + 6) can serve an airframe launched then.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the best plan is 'UltraFan NB: hold' (+0.00), the plan submitted. 'UltraFan NB if selected' ties in S1 at +0.00 and is the best plan on expected PV across all columns (+1.25 on my weights, +2.63 on the Board's), because of S2, S4 and S5.
decision.premium_reason:
Holding instead of 'UltraFan NB if selected' gives up +1.25 expected on my weights (+2.63 on the Board's illustrative weights; +11.89 in S2, +7.96 in S4, +20.80 in S5). It buys four things:
- Control's $4B narrowbody bound is kept in every column. A trigger would be $8.0B with no way back.
- Company-funded R&D stays inside a flat envelope. A trigger would add about 91% of 2030E R&D.
- The one-programme slot is kept and strain is $0.
- The narrowbody entry goes through the partner-first Joint Venture route the Board and doctrine prefer.
The premium is inside the $3B cap on both weight sets. It is a narrowbody premium, not a widebody one, so the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap does not apply.
decision.objective_note:
Widebody dominance:
- Met: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column.
- Worst case under the rules (inference): 53% if CFM funds a GEnx upgrade.

Enter the narrowbody market:
- Not met this round in any column (0% in 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection).
- Given up: entry through a 2030 airframe in S2, S4 and S5.
- Kept open for 2035 through a Joint Venture with P&W at our $4B share. It is ready at formation + 6, or earlier if P&W folds in a GTF2 Solo that is further along (inference from the public rules).

Protect the widebody cash cow:
- Own narrowbody money is $0.0B in every column.
- Narrowbody plus widebody strain is $0 in every column.
- Both mission metrics are met.

Premium paid for the objective's terms: $1.25B expected (my weights).
decision.predictions:
Column weights (mine, the same as McCabe's): S1 0.40, S2 0.05, S3 0.15, S4 0.03, S5 0.02, S6 0.10, S7 0.10, S8 0.05, S9 0.05, S10 0.05. My reading of each player:
- Airframers: more likely to wait than launch in 2030. If one moves, Airbus with NGSA is likelier than Boeing with fps. A selection naming RR alone is unlikely with nothing from us on the record.
- P&W: unlikely to commit to the Joint Venture first (0.10). More likely to keep GTF1 or a GTF2 option.
- Embraer: may launch its own narrowbody (S10) on P&W or CFM engines. That does not touch our engines.
- CFM: may fund a GEnx upgrade. That takes our widebody share to about 53%, still above 50%.
- Re-engines: a 787 or A350 Re-engine is unlikely this round (0.05 each column).

For 2035 I expect our public Joint Venture line to make a P&W commitment more likely. That would let us commit then, within the $4B bound.

board_response.recommendation: Safety first: no EIS earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB) or + 6 (Joint Venture, UltraFan WB), nothing on airframers' dates, and Watson states the zero margin and support plan if `launch_if_selected` is submitted.
board_response.response: Taken up. The public statement gives no EIS earlier than six years from the Joint Venture's formation, names no airframer date, and commits to partner-shop support before entry into service. `launch_if_selected` is not submitted. For the record, Watson's zero margin (UltraFan ready 2037 against a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-year EIS, no float) and his support plan are in the rationale, and the plan carries forward to any Joint Venture.

board_response.recommendation: Control's mission sets the terms: own narrowbody money within $4B, so the narrowbody route is the Joint Venture with P&W. A triggered Solo is $8B with no way back.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. That is the basis of the decision. Own narrowbody money is $0.0B and strain $0 in all ten columns. The narrowbody route is the Joint Venture at our $4B share, committed once P&W is on the record.

board_response.recommendation: Decide `launch_if_selected` openly and record it in the rationale; the Board leans to Do Nothing and would approve the conditional form but not the unconditional one.
board_response.response: Decided openly: hold. The rationale sets the selected-case value (+11.89 S2, +7.96 S4, +20.80 S5; +1.25 expected on my weights, +2.63 on yours) against the $8B breach with no way back. It adds McCabe's envelope fail (91% of 2030E R&D), Watson's capacity load (1,200-2,000 narrowbody engines a year against 197 Trent) and his zero margin to 2037. The $1.25B premium is declared, inside the $3B cap. The unconditional Solo is not submitted.

board_response.recommendation: No widebody programme this round; keep the one-programme slot for the narrowbody entry; revisit the upgrade only once the narrowbody door closes or a rival-engined Re-engine is on the record, and UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record.
board_response.response: Taken up. `ultrafan_wb: hold` and `t1000_upgrade: hold`. No widebody shortfall, so no widebody premium. I adopt your revisit conditions for 2035 and after.

board_response.recommendation: Use the public statement to open the partnership: Rolls-Royce prefers a partner and stands ready to commit to a Joint Venture with P&W, in a few binding words with no dates.

- Joint Venture: about £0.49bn a year. Worst -4.00 in S7 on a first commit.

board_response.recommendation: Next round, cancel what no airframe can use; any narrowbody programme left with no live airframe should be cancelled before its spend grows, inside the $4B bound.

In 2035 I apply the same test to any standing Joint Venture commitment no airframe can use (`jv_with_pw: withdraw`) and to any programme without a live airframe: "that activity is gone" [R-1573].

cfo.red_line: None. The orders hold all four fields, so there is no UltraFan launch without an airframe, no cancel, no narrowbody and widebody programmes overlapping, and no Trent 1000 upgrade beside an UltraFan. The declared premium of $1.25B is inside the $3B cap.

The binding vetoes in my test memo all stand unexercised: no unconditional Solo, no Joint Venture commit before P&W is on the record, no UltraFan WB, and no Trent 1000 upgrade, alone or beside the narrowbody item. embraer.public_statement: Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We focused on delivering the results in our plan to 2030 with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. We keep doing that, with a very healthy cash generation to support a potential next move. On a new product, I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies because it is important that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. We need a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. Any large investment will be made with partners, and we talk to many partners and to all the engine makers. Today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. This does not depend only on us. It depends on the technology available in the market and on the partners, and the investment has to prove its return. On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions, and I can only speak for Embraer. On trade, Embraer is about engineering, and we focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic. We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost.
embraer.rationale:
Decision: Hold (Do Nothing, no new narrowbody). Hold is the default and not a Board item. It is the best grid plan in all five columns: +0.00 $B, 100.0%.

Columns. The expected column is S1, Rivals hold, as I named it in my frame: the public record shows no rival launch, and S1 to S4 lie within $0.01B of one another for a Launch, so the reading does not depend on that choice. The risk column is S5 (Boeing fps 10-yr plus Airbus NGSA), the worst column the bulletin has not ruled out.

The ExCo took my four questions on the brief's numbers.

(1) Strong product, strong value proposition? The product is adequate, not compelling. By the rules it is slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX and worse than a new-generation type. After the 10% US cut it wins 10.8% of new customers while neither fps nor NGSA is in service, 6.3% with one and 3.6% with both. At $50M and a 12% margin it earns $6.0M an aircraft. The line rises from 16 in 2034 to 96 a year from 2039, so full rate is worth about $0.58B a year of operating profit. The window at a 2034 entry into service is open in every column; the earliest rival entry into service is 2037. The value proposition fails on value: the line caps the margin pool at a level that cannot carry our share of the bill.

(2) Robust funding, no risk to financial health? It fails. Team Korea carries 30% ($3.0B), the risk-sharing suppliers 10% and Brazilian state research money 5%, so H1 passes. Our 55% is still $5.50B, booked at entry into service in 2034. Net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of the $11B enterprise value), and the debt penalty rises by $0.59B in 2034, $0.26B in present value, already netted in the grid and not subtracted twice. Santana's funding test fails leg 2 (S1: -1.02 $B, -9.3 yp, against at or above zero) and leg 3 (S5: -1.24 $B, -11.3 yp, against the 5-point limit). Under the team rule that veto binds, with no override. His advice lines confirm it, though they do not decide it: about 7.5x leverage against the inherited "below 2x", investment grade at risk, and a cash call of $1.375B a year in 2030-33, 3.4 times the capex run rate and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor each year.

(3) Technology available? Yes, on the brief. The board fits P&W, the E2's maker, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem, so both of Meijer's legs pass. His flags are advice: a clean sheet in four years where the E2 took about five, and a supply base carrying about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039.

(4) Will the investment prove its return against Do Nothing? No. Launch is 9.3 yp below Hold in S1 and S2, 9.4 yp below in S3 and S4, and 11.3 yp below in S5. That is 4.6 to 5.6 times the 2-yp tie band ($0.22B) and beyond the 5-yp premium cap ($0.55B). One eye on the fish and the other eye on the cat, right? I mean, the investment has to prove its return [EX-0079].

By the team rule: the Launch fails the CFO's funding test, so it is out, and no override exists. Meijer raises no soft veto on 2030, so there is nothing to override; the override margin, a plan more than 5 yp better than Hold, could not apply to a plan that sits below Hold. The gap is far outside the tie band, so the 2030 tie-break does not come into play: this is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.

Hard rules: H1 passes. H2 would be breached by a Launch (the grid is below zero in the expected column and the funding test fails). H3 is open at 2034. H4 does not apply. H5: premium zero. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing orders it this round, its order would stand and any launch of ours would be refused, so a launch cannot pre-empt it. That risk is no reason to launch at -9.3 yp, and the Board would veto a launch argued on it.

One-way door: a 2030 launch enters service in 2034, before the 2035 round, and the rules allow a cancel only before entry into service, so no round could cancel it. Even in 2034 the write-off would be the whole $5.50B.

Objective: "in service by 2040" stays unmet this round. Closing it now would cost at least $1.02B (9.3 yp), beyond the $0.55B cap and against a binding veto, so I pay no premium and log $0.00B. "ΔPV at or above zero with the debt penalty included" is kept.

2035: it is the last round that can meet 2040 (entry into service 2039). On Santana's rebuild, confirmed by my own (work/r1_decide_calc.py), a 2035 launch on S1 terms at our 55% is -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp). It reaches zero only near a 35% own share, partners near 65%, about $2.0B more than the brief shows. So at today's terms the 2035 option is also below Hold. The window may also narrow or shut on this round's rival orders (S3 and S4 narrow, S5 shut), but at these terms losing it costs nothing on the grid; it costs only the objective.

Record and doctrine: my record drove the posture: funding first [EX-0046, EX-0034], financial health [EX-0140], return before capacity [EX-0079], the plan to 2030 [EX-0080, EX-0081] and rivals not setting the date [EX-0093]. Doctrine (profile H2 and H5, teams.md) supplied the numeric thresholds: ΔPV at or above zero, the 5-yp risk limit, and the 2-yp band and 5-yp cap. Bias check: the "Not yet" label does not apply, because every test is resolved. The Launch failed on the numbers; we are not studying without deciding. "Return first" is on display, within the cap.

memo_weighing.cfo: Taken in full; it decides the round. Santana's binding funding veto stands, and I seek no override, since the rule allows none. Leg 1 passes: partners carry 45% ($4.5B), Team Korea 30% of it. Leg 2 fails: S1 -1.02 $B (-9.3 yp), and S2 to S4 read the same. Leg 3 fails: S5 -1.24 $B (-11.3 yp) against -5 yp. His reconciliation is right. My frame's -0.96 came from the brief's rounded rows ($0.6B for $0.576B a year); the exact $6.0M a jet gives -1.023, and I adopt the brief's -1.02. I accept that the debt penalty is counted once ($0.59B rise in 2034, $0.26B in present value). I weighed the advice lines as confirming the result, not deciding it: about 7.5x leverage, investment grade at risk, a $1.375B yearly cash call (3.4 times capex, 69% of the cash floor) and four years of suspended cash conversion. The leverage line rests on his EV/EBITDA inference, which is why I keep it as advice. His 2035 bar becomes our bar for the next package: -0.61 $B at 55%, break-even near a 35% own share, and net debt still about 38-39% of enterprise value at that share. No credit for money a brief does not show.
memo_weighing.ops: Taken in full as advice; it raises no veto. Both legs pass for 2030. (a) The window is open in every column at 2034, with the earliest rival entry into service in 2037. (b) P&W is fitted, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. The line, not demand, sets deliveries in S1 to S4, so the US cut costs nothing there. The share binds only in S5 from 2040, at about 25 aircraft a year short of the line, which is the grid's $0.22B. His flags go into the 2035 package, not into this order: an edge that is slight, not compelling; a clean sheet in four years against the E2's roughly five; about 216 commercial jets a year on the same supply base by 2039; and a brief margin of 12% against the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025. The board prices no shortfall there, so the real-world risk is to the downside (inference). One correction: he attributes my -0.96 to counting 16 deliveries in 2034, but my frame calculation had 0 in 2034. The gap was rounding, as Santana says; it does not matter here. I adopt his 2035 window count: S1 open, S2 open by one year (fps in 2040), S3 and S4 narrow (his soft veto), S5 shut (H3).

Premium logged at $0.00B (0 yp).
embraer.objective_note: The brief's objective has two parts. "New narrowbody in service by 2040" is not met this round. It stays open only through a 2035 launch (entry into service 2039), the last round that can meet it. On this brief's terms, that launch rebuilds at -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp) at our 55% share. It would need partners near 65% of the bill, an open window on this round's bulletin, and the funding and window tests passed. "ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included" is met (+0.00 $B). We keep the balance sheet safe and do not buy the first part with a loss of 9.3 to 11.3 yp, which is beyond the 5-yp cap.

For 2035, I expect the brief's Launch row to stay below zero at a 55% share: around -0.6 $B on S1 terms, worse if a rival type is due. So Do Nothing is likely right again unless a brief shows partners carrying near 65% of the bill.

A Launch argued on the 2040 objective alone, as a pre-emptive move against Boeing's fps via Embraer, or because rivals held: vetoed on the same grid grounds. None of these reasons offsets a failed test, and the grid already prices the rivals' moves.

recommendations.text: Hold in 2030, and put the grid in the rationale: the Launch is 9.3 to 11.3 yield points below Do Nothing in every column, so it fails the CEO's own condition of a funding strategy that does not put the company's financial health at risk. This is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.
Keep technology readiness funded and keep Team Korea talks going through the harvest: deliver the plan to 2030 and build the cash for a potential next move, so that a 2035 decision is a real one.

Santana should show, for 2035, what would close the gap on the brief's own terms. The Board's rough rebuild from the brief's rows (about -0.96 $B against the brief's -1.02 $B) puts the Launch near zero only if Embraer's share of the $10.0B bill falls from 55% to about 35-37%, meaning partners carry about 18-20 points more. The brief does not show that money, so it gets no credit until a brief does. Also show the net-debt rise to about $6.2B (56% of enterprise value) against the inherited 2x comfort and the cash floor of about $2B.

Flag 2035 as the last round in which a Launch (in service 2039) meets the 2040 objective. Meijer should count the 2035 window from this round's bulletin. An fps 7-yr or an NGSA launched now would be in service in 2037, a narrow window and Meijer's soft veto. Both launched now, as in S5 (NGSA in 2037, fps 10-yr due in 2040), would shut it. The Board will not approve a Launch for the objective alone.

Public statement on economics, not politics. Name no segment and no entry-into-service date before a launch, and make no comment on Boeing's or Airbus's choices. On US tariffs, argue jobs and a return to zero tariffs; the 10% share cut is already in the brief.

Golden share and Boeing. No game order moves control, and a Team Korea development partnership needs no state consent. Any other move that would hand over control of a business or military technology, such as a Boeing arrangement like the 2018 deal, needs the state's consent first. If Boeing orders fps via Embraer, our new narrowbody is barred for good. That risk is not a reason to launch at -9.3 yield points. Log any premium in the decision; none is expected for a Hold.

frame.question: Do we launch the new 150-180 seat narrowbody with Team Korea this round (2030 launch, entry into service 2034), or do we Hold, deliver the plan to 2030 and keep a real decision open for 2035? I mean, I take it through my four questions on this brief's numbers, right? (1) Is it a strong product with a strong value proposition? (2) Is the funding robust, so it does not put the financial health of the company at risk? (3) Is the technology available? (4) Will the investment prove its return against Do Nothing? Any launch is a Board item. Hold is the default.
frame.situation: Round 1, decision year 2030. Public record: no programme has been launched. Everyone is on today's products (737 MAX, 787, A320neo, A350; LEAP, GTF, GEnx, Trent). Neither fps nor NGSA is launched. Boeing's production plan (fps at new sites) and Airbus's (A320 base plan) apply only once each one launches. Narrowbody delivery shares were 39.4% Boeing and 60.6% Airbus every year from 2026 to 2029, and Embraer delivered no narrowbodies. We have no launched programme, so there is nothing to continue or cancel. Our position: ΔPV +0.00 $B, yield 100.0%, enterprise value $11B, net debt $0.7B, WACC 11.0%. Objective (brief §2): in service by 2040 is not met; ΔPV ≥ 0 with the debt penalty included is met. The jet's economics in the brief: a $10.0B bill. Team Korea carries 30%, risk-sharing suppliers 10% and Brazilian state research money 5%. Our 55% is $5.50B, booked at entry into service. Price is $50M at a 12% margin, so about $6M per aircraft. The line runs 16 in 2034, 32 in 2035, and rises to 96 a year from 2039, worth $0.6B of operating profit a year at full rate. US trade climate: Brazil is at odds with Washington. The brief cuts our share of new customers by 10%, from 12% to 10.8% while neither new-generation type is in service (6.3% with one, 3.6% with both). BNDES credit, the golden share and any US response to a Brazil-Korea airliner are not priced. Grid, Launch against Do Nothing, debt penalty included: S1 Rivals hold -1.02 (90.7%); S2 Boeing fps 10-yr -1.02 (90.7%); S3 Boeing fps 7-yr -1.03 (90.7%); S4 Airbus NGSA -1.03 (90.7%); S5 Boeing fps 10-yr plus Airbus NGSA -1.24 (88.7%). Do Nothing is +0.00 (100.0%) in every column. EXPECTED COLUMN: S1 (Rivals hold). The public record shows no rival launch. Boeing's and Airbus's choices are theirs and I do not speculate on them. S1 to S4 are within $0.01B of one another, so the expected leg reads the same in any of them, and S1 is the column most favourable to our launch: if the launch fails there, it fails everywhere. RISK COLUMN: S5, the worst column the bulletin has not ruled out. Window for a 2030 launch: open in every column. No rival new-generation type can be in service by 2034; the earliest is 2037 (fps 7-yr or NGSA launched now).
levers_in_play: enb, our one order this round: `hold` (the default, Do Nothing: no new narrowbody; we keep the E2 and the business jets; not a Board item) or `launch` (the new narrowbody with Team Korea, entry into service 2034; a Board item). `cancel` is not on this round's list because nothing has been launched.

A 2030 launch is a one-way door. Entry into service in 2034 comes before the 2035 round, and the rules allow a cancel only before entry into service. No later round could cancel it (my reading of rules.md; Santana to confirm).

Boeing's fps via Embraer (H6): not live. If Boeing orders it this round while we order launch, Boeing's order stands and ours is refused. Once it is launched, our narrowbody is barred for good. So a launch cannot pre-empt it this round, and that risk is no reason to launch.

The partner split (Team Korea 30%, suppliers 10%, Brazilian research 5%, Embraer 55%) is the game master's term. No order changes it this round. More partner money counts only once a later brief shows it.

Other moves the board does not price: keep technology-readiness studies funded; keep the Team Korea and KAI talks going (the July 2026 civil MoU), naming no segment and no date; deliver the E2 and business-jet plan to 2030 and build cash 'to support a potential next move'; a public statement on engineering, US content and jobs, and a return to zero tariffs.
options_to_test: Row 1, Hold (Do Nothing, no new narrowbody): +0.00 $B (100.0%) in S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5. The best plan in every column; not a Board item; no premium. It keeps the 2035 option (entry into service 2039, which still meets the 2040 objective). The window at 2039 by column of this round: S1 open; S2 open (fps 10-yr due 2040, not yet in service); S3 and S4 narrow (fps 7-yr or NGSA in service from 2037: Meijer's soft veto); S5 shut (NGSA in service from 2037 and fps due in 2040, within 2 years: H3, no launch).

Row 2, Launch the new narrowbody with Korea (2030 launch, entry into service 2034): -1.02 $B (90.7%, -9.3 yp) in S1 and S2; -1.03 $B (90.7%, -9.4 yp) in S3 and S4; -1.24 $B (88.7%, -11.3 yp) in S5. Below Hold in every column, by 4.6 to 5.6 times the 2-yield-point tie band ($0.22B) and beyond the 5-yield-point premium cap ($0.55B), so neither the tie-break nor a logged premium can reach it. A Board item, and on the Board's would-veto list in every column.

Not an order this round, a test for the 2035 option: Hold now, Launch in 2035. The brief has no row for it yet. My rough rebuild from the brief's own rows, in work/r1_frame_calc.py, gives about -0.96 $B at our 55% (the brief says -1.02). The case nears zero only if Embraer's share falls to about 37%, meaning partners carry roughly 18 points more than the brief shows. No credit for money the brief does not show. I want Santana's and Meijer's reading of what would have to change, on the brief's terms.
red_lines: H1, no launch without the partner: our launch exists only with Team Korea, and the partner's money must be defined at approval [EX-0046, EX-0034, EB-0035]. Team Korea's 30% is in the brief's economics.

H2, no launch that puts the company's financial health at risk: the grid, debt penalty included, must show the launch at or above zero in the expected column, and Santana's funding test must pass. That veto binds with no override [EX-0140, EB-0015].
H3, no launch into a shut window: never when fps and NGSA are each in service, or due within 2 years, at our entry into service. Open for a 2034 entry into service in every column this round.
H4, cancel only before entry into service and only when writing off beats continuing by more than 2 yield points; never in reply to a rival bulletin. Not in play this round.
H5, money rule: 2 yield points ($0.22B) is the tie band; at most 5 yield points ($0.55B) may be given up for a soft doctrine choice or the 2040 objective; every premium is logged.
H6, no launch while Boeing's fps via Embraer is live; if both are ordered in the same round, Boeing's order stands and ours is refused.

My own red lines: no launch before the technology is ready [EX-0141]; no product for a small market that leaves the big one behind [EX-0085]; no aircraft sold below cost (said in statements, not priced); no politics in public [EX-0100]; no comment on Boeing's or Airbus's decisions [EX-0093]; no entry-into-service date and no segment named before a launch.

Set it against the cash floor of about $2B and the inherited comfort below 2x leverage, and say whether investment grade survives. frame.initial_lean: Hold. My lean comes from the grid itself; the tie-break is not needed. The launch is 9.3 to 11.3 yield points below Do Nothing in every column, -1.02 $B in my expected column S1 and -1.24 $B in the risk column S5. It fails my own condition of a funding strategy that does not put the financial health of the company at risk, and the investment does not prove its return. The product is adequate. The window at 2034 is open, P&W engines are fitted and the brief reports no supply problem. But the line caps us at 96 aircraft a year at about $6M of margin each, and that does not carry our $5.50B share plus the debt from $0.7B to about $6.2B. The launch would also be a one-way door, with no round to cancel it before 2034. The 2040 objective stays unmet this round. Closing it would cost at least 9.3 yield points, beyond the 5-point cap, so I pay no premium and log a premium of zero. I do not launch to pre-empt Boeing's fps via Embraer: by rule Boeing's order would stand anyway. I do not launch because rivals hold either: their decisions are theirs. So we deliver the plan to 2030 and build the cash to support a potential next move. We keep technology readiness funded and the Team Korea talks going, and we decide again in 2035 on that round's bulletin, which is the last round that meets 2040. What would change my mind: a brief showing ΔPV at or above zero in the expected column, with partners carrying more of the bill. One eye on the fish and the other on the cat, right?

tests.name: Funding test, leg 1: partner money (binding veto leg)
tests.threshold: The brief's economics show Team Korea carrying a share of the bill, with any supplier and Brazilian state money. Fail if there is no partner share.
tests.numbers: Brief §1. The bill is $10.0B. Team Korea 30% = $3.0B, risk-sharing suppliers 10% = $1.0B, Brazilian state research money 5% = $0.5B, so partners carry 45% = $4.5B, inside the grid's economics. Embraer's 55% = $5.50B, booked at entry into service in 2034. CEO ask (1) confirmed. H1 passes.

tests.name: Funding test, leg 2: pays its cost of capital (binding veto leg)
tests.threshold: In the expected column (S1, Rivals hold, as Gomes Neto named it), ΔPV for Launch against Do Nothing, debt penalty included, is at or above zero. The brief discounts at our 11.0% WACC.
tests.numbers: Row 'Launch the new narrowbody with Korea', column S1: -1.02 $B (90.7%), -9.27 yp against a threshold of >= 0. Short by $1.02B. CEO ask (3): the reading does not change in any other column. S2 is -1.02 (-9.27 yp), S3 and S4 are -1.03 (-9.36 yp). The worst column other than the risk column (advice) is S3/S4 at -1.03. My rebuild from the brief's year table at $50M x 12% = $6.0M a jet: PV of operating profit $1.62B, minus PV of our bill $2.39B, minus PV of the penalty rise $0.26B, gives -1.02. It matches the brief. The CEO's -0.96 used the rounded rows ($0.6B for $0.576B a year).

tests.name: Funding test, leg 3: the bad case (binding veto leg)
tests.threshold: In the risk column (S5, Boeing fps 10-yr plus Airbus NGSA, the worst column the bulletin has not ruled out), Launch loses no more than 5 yield points (-$0.55B) against Do Nothing.
tests.numbers: S5: -1.24 $B (88.7%), -11.27 yp against a -5 yp limit. Fails by 6.3 yp ($0.69B). S5 is $0.22B (2.0 yp) worse than S1. CEO ask (4) answered.

tests.name: Leverage line (advice)
tests.threshold: Net debt below 2x EBITDA. At 13.3x EV/EBITDA that is about 15% of the brief's enterprise value: (net debt + our share) / EV <= 15% at entry into service.
tests.numbers: ($0.7B + $5.50B) / $11B = 56.4% of EV against a 15% line, about 7.5x the implied EBITDA of $0.83B ($11B / 13.3) against 2x. The line would pass only if our own share were <= $0.95B (9.5% of the bill). CEO ask (2): net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B. CEO ask (5): far above the inherited 2x comfort.

tests.name: Rating (advice)
tests.threshold: Keep investment grade at all three agencies. A plan that fails the leverage line puts the rating at risk (inference).
tests.numbers: Leverage at entry into service would be 56% of EV (about 7.5x). Garcia regained investment grade only as leverage fell to 1.4x and below. My reading on CEO ask (5): investment grade does not survive a fully debt-funded $5.50B share (inference, inherited from Garcia).

tests.name: Debt penalty, counted once (rule)
tests.threshold: The grid's ΔPV already nets the debt penalty: never subtract it again. Within the 2 yp tie band ($0.22B) the team tie-break decides; name the plan that adds less debt.
tests.numbers: Penalty D x 0.3 x (D/EV)^2 goes from $0.0009B at D = $0.7B to $0.591B at D = $6.2B. The rise is $0.590B in 2034, or $0.256B in PV at 2026. It is already inside the -1.02 (my rebuild reconciles only with it included), so it is not subtracted twice (CEO ask 2). The gap of 9.3 to 11.3 yp is far outside the 2 yp band, so the tie-break does not come into play. The plan that adds less debt is Do Nothing ($0).

tests.name: Cash path and envelope (advice)
tests.threshold: Our share / 4 development years is the yearly cash call. Above 1x the capex run rate (close to $400M a year) is the 'large investment' that needs partners. Set it against the cash floor of about $2B.
tests.numbers: $5.50B / 4 = $1.375B a year in 2030-33. That is 3.4x the $0.4B capex run rate, 6.9x the $0.2B free-cash-flow guide, and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor each year (2.75x the floor over four years). The brief gives net debt, not cash. The floor holds only if the whole share is borrowed, and borrowing it is what takes net debt to $6.2B, so either the floor or the 2x line gives way. Partners are in, yet our own call is still 3.4x the run rate. CEO ask (5).

tests.name: Cash conversion (advice)
tests.threshold: Free cash flow of at least 50% of EBITDA is the planning minimum. A launch suspends it in its development years.
tests.numbers: The $1.375B yearly call is 1.7x the implied EBITDA of $0.83B. Conversion is suspended for 2030-33, all four development years.

tests.name: One-off or trend (advice)
tests.threshold: Label each risk as one-off or trend, with its size. A rival new-generation type in service is a trend, never a one-off.
tests.numbers: Nothing in the gap is a one-off to look through. The -1.02 in S1 is structural, a trend: the line is capped at 96 a year x $6.0M = $0.58B a year against a $5.50B bill and a $0.59B penalty rise. S5's extra -$0.22B (2.0 yp) is a trend: both rival types are in service from 2040 and our share of new customers falls toward 3.6%. The US tariff cut (12% to 10.8%) is a trend but does not bind in S1, where deliveries equal line capacity in the brief's table.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel (rule)
tests.threshold: Write-off = our share x years elapsed / 4. Cancel only before entry into service, and only when writing off beats continuing by more than 2 yp (H4).
tests.numbers: Nothing has been launched, so the order list has no Cancel. CEO ask (6) confirmed: a 2030 launch enters service in 2034, before the 2035 round, and the rules allow a cancel only until entry into service, so no cancel round exists. Even in 2034 the write-off would be $5.50B x 4/4 = $5.50B, the whole share. It is a one-way door.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (rule)
tests.threshold: Any value given up for the 2040 objective is reported in $B and yp, inside the 5 yp cap ($0.55B) of H5. The objective never overrides a failed leg.
tests.numbers: Meeting the 2040 objective with a 2030 launch would cost $1.02B (9.3 yp) in S1 and $1.24B (11.3 yp) in S5. Both are beyond the $0.55B cap, and legs 2 and 3 have already failed. On Do Nothing the logged premium is $0.00B (0 yp).

tests.name: Hard-rule watch (H1, H2, H4, H5, H6)
tests.threshold: Flag any breach as a red line for the CEO to strike.
tests.numbers: H1 passes (Team Korea 30% in the brief). A Launch breaches H2: the grid is below zero in the expected column and the funding test fails. H4 does not apply. H5: the gap is outside both the tie band and the cap. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing ordered it this round, Boeing's order would stand and ours would be refused, so it is no reason to launch. Do Nothing breaches nothing.

tests.name: 2035 option: what closes the gap on the brief's terms (advice; no brief row yet)
tests.threshold: Launch at or above zero with the debt penalty included, using only money and terms the brief shows.
tests.numbers: CEO ask (7). My rebuild (S1 terms, net debt $0.7B, entry into service 2039, the same ramp and 20-year window) gives -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp, PV at 2026) at our 55%. A later start shrinks the loss by the five-year discount (x0.59) but does not change its sign. Break-even is an own share of about 35% (partners about 65%, roughly $2.0B more than the $4.5B shown, about 20 points). The CEO's 37% came from the rounded rows. I see no other route in the brief. Tariffs: the line binds in S1, not demand, so lifting the 10% cut adds nothing there. Price, margin and line rate are the game master's terms and no order moves them. The penalty moves only with our share. Even at a 35% share, net debt at entry into service is about 38% of EV, still past the 2x line (advice). No credit until a brief shows the money.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea (2030 launch, entry into service 2034)
vetoes.ground: Funding test fails on legs 2 and 3. Leg 2: in S1, the CEO's expected column, Launch against Do Nothing is -1.02 $B (90.7%, -9.3 yp), below zero with the debt penalty included. It is also below zero in S2 (-1.02) and S3/S4 (-1.03). Leg 3: in S5, the risk column, it loses 11.3 yp (-1.24 $B, 88.7%) against Do Nothing, past the 5 yp limit. Leg 1 passes (Team Korea 30%, partners 45% in the brief). Under the team rule this veto binds, with no override.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea (2030 launch, entry into service 2034)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding (inherited from Garcia). Net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of EV, about 7.5x against the 'below 2x' comfort, and investment grade is at risk. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2030-33, 3.4x the capex run rate and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor each year. Cash conversion is suspended for four years. There is no cancel round before entry into service in 2034.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: A brief whose grid shows 'Launch the new narrowbody with Korea' at or above zero, debt penalty included, in the expected column Gomes Neto names, and no worse than -5 yp (-$0.55B) against Do Nothing in the risk column. On my rebuild from this brief's terms, that needs our share of the $10.0B bill near 35% (partners near 65%, about $2.0B more than the $4.5B shown), and the money must appear in the brief's economics, not in a promise. To pass the advice lines as well (2x leverage, investment grade), our own share would have to fall to about $0.95B. The 2035 bulletin also has to show the fps and NGSA entry-into-service years, which set the window for a 2039 entry into service.
cfo.memo:
Felipe here. Funding test on the brief's numbers: Gomes Neto's expected column S1, risk column S5. The tests and thresholds are inherited from Garcia, unchanged; the 5-point limit is the team rule.

Leg 1, partners: pass. Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), suppliers 10%, Brazilian research 5%, all inside the brief's economics. Our 55% is $5.50B, booked at entry into service in 2034.

Leg 2, cost of capital: fail. Launch against Do Nothing in S1 is -1.02 $B, -9.3 yield points, with the debt penalty already netted (up $0.59B in 2034, $0.26B in present value; I do not subtract it twice). S2 to S4 read the same, -1.02 to -1.03.

Leg 3, bad case: fail. S5 is -1.24 $B, -11.3 points, against a 5-point limit.

So I veto the 2030 launch, and the team rule makes it binding. Advice, inherited from Garcia: net debt goes to $6.2B, 56% of enterprise value, about 7.5x against "below 2x". In my reading investment grade does not survive that. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2030-33, 3.4x our capex run rate. And there is no cancel: entry into service comes before the 2035 round.

For 2035: my rebuild, at $6M a jet, reconciles to the brief's -1.02. The gap closes only near a 35% share for us, partners near 65%. Tariffs do not help, right? The line binds, not demand. No credit until a brief shows that money.

Recommendation: Do Nothing, premium zero. A conservative approach; we wait for visibility.

tests.name: Market window against fps and NGSA (veto leg a)
tests.threshold: Pass if no fps or NGSA is launched, or the window covers our ramp; flag (advice) if shorter than the ramp; fail (soft veto) if a new-generation type is due in service at or before our EIS. Record on the E2 applied to the narrowbody by inference, plus company record.
tests.numbers: Public record: nothing launched. EIS 2034 (2030 + 4). Earliest rival EIS from a launch this round: 2037 (fps 7-yr or NGSA), then 2040 (fps 10-yr). Window = first rival EIS minus ours: S1 open-ended, S2 6 years (2040), S3 3 years (fps 2037), S4 3 years (NGSA 2037), S5 3 years to NGSA 2037 and 6 to fps 2040. Nothing is in service or due at or before 2034 in any column. H3 not triggered (2037 is more than 2 years after 2034). Advice flag: in S3 to S5 the 3-year window is shorter than our ramp to 96 a year (2034-2039). How much of the value depends on the rivals: $0.01B (S3, S4, -1.03 against S1 -1.02) and $0.22B (S5, -1.24), about 2 yp. Little, because the line binds (next tests). (Window rule: record [EX-0544, EX-0546] by inference; company record [EB-0500, EB-0501].)

tests.name: Share path through the ramp, by column (line against demand)
tests.threshold: Read our share at EIS and at full rate in the brief; say whether the line or customer demand sets deliveries (inference, using the rules' demand curve).
tests.numbers: Share of new customers after the US cut: S1 10.8% throughout; S2 10.8% to 2039, 6.3% from 2040; S3 and S4 10.8% to 2036, 6.3% from 2037; S5 10.8% to 2036, 6.3% 2037-2039, 3.6% from 2040. Line: 16 (2034), 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 from 2039. Wanted against line (share x the rules' total demand, an upper bound): 10.8% gives 151-213 a year (2038-2040) against 96; 6.3% gives 95 (2037, line 64), 88 (2038, line 80), 106 (2039), 113-124 (2040-2053) against 96; 3.6% gives 65-75 a year from 2040 against 96. So the line binds in S1 to S4 every year; the share binds only in S5 from 2040, about 25 aircraft a year short of the line (my upper bound about $0.28B PV; the grid's gap is $0.22B, overflow filling some slots). CEO's reading confirmed. Brief, S1: deliveries 0 in 2034 (firm backlog takes the year), 32 in 2035 (1.9% of market deliveries), 96 from 2039 (5.0%), 4.8-5.2% through the 2040s. My rebuild of S1 from the brief's rows: operating profit PV $1.62B, bill PV $2.39B, debt-penalty rise $0.59B in 2034 (PV $0.26B): ΔPV -1.02, matching the grid (the CEO's -0.96 appears to count 16 deliveries in 2034, which the brief shows as 0). Work: work/r1_meijer_test_calc.py.

tests.name: Product edge over the A320neo and 737 MAX
tests.threshold: State the edge in the brief's numbers and whether it is compelling (company record: no head-to-head entry without a compelling advantage over current offers). Inference that the E2 case does not carry over.
tests.numbers: Rules: 'slightly better for airlines than the 737 MAX and A320neo and worse than a new-generation airplane'. In numbers: 12% of new customers with neither fps nor NGSA in service, 7% with one, 4% with both (10.8%, 6.3%, 3.6% after the US cut). Price $50M at 12% margin: $6M an aircraft, $0.576B a year at 96. Slight, not compelling. My E2 case (25-30% lower trip cost at near-equal seat cost, complementing the big jets) does not carry over to a 150-180 seater that fights them head-on, and the first E-Jet 'struggled to get to the right cost level' against them. I name my E2 anchoring here. Advice only: product edge is not a veto leg; the CEO called it adequate and I agree.

tests.name: Customers and campaigns
tests.threshold: Back a launch only where Embraer's share is positive at EIS and at full rate in the expected case and Hold's E2 business is not reduced (inference from record).
tests.numbers: Expected column S1: share of market deliveries 0.0% in 2034 (16 slots, 0 delivered), 1.9% in 2035, 5.0% at full rate in 2039, 4.8-5.2% in the 2040s. Positive from 2035. Brief: E-Jets and business jets are the same in every plan, so Hold's E2 business is not reduced. Buyers (inference): E-Jet operators moving up, multi-OEM buyers, low-cost carriers; customers want about twice what the line builds in S1 to S4. Campaign optimism noted: only the brief's share is in my numbers.

tests.name: Price discipline
tests.threshold: Report the price effect from the brief and whether it reaches Embraer's own margin, as a number (inference).
tests.numbers: Rules: from 1 year before EIS (2033), Boeing's and Airbus's single-aisle prices fall by up to 2.0%, rising in a straight line over 7 years (2.6% on Boeing in years it has no new narrowbody in service). It falls on their margins, not ours: our $50M and 12% are fixed in the brief. Advice (inference against company record): the brief's 12% margin is about 4.6 times the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025; the board prices no shortfall.

tests.name: Supply chain and ramp (veto leg b)
tests.threshold: Take the brief's ramp as given, never a faster one. Fail (soft veto) if the brief reports a supply-chain problem that would hold the line; flag a lesser risk (advice). Mostly company record.
tests.numbers: Brief reports no supply-chain problem. Ramp taken as given: 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 (2034-2039). Flag, advice only (company record plus inference): the E-Jet line targets about 100 in 2027 and 120 commercial jets a year by 2030, 'if the investments justify the return', and 'the bottlenecks moves from one critical supplier to another'. Adding 96 a year by 2039 means about 216 commercial jets a year, 1.8 times the 2030 target, on largely the same supplier base. Our hit has been 'a lot less than on the competitors' partly because core work stays in-house (record).

tests.name: Engines and system supply (veto leg b)
tests.threshold: Pass if the brief shows an engine on offer by EIS with no live delivery or durability problem; fail (soft veto) if no engine is on offer or a live engine problem would hold the line. Record plus company record.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody flies P&W engines (the E2's maker), or CFM's if CFM's Embraer partnership is live. Brief and bulletin report no engine problem; no engine programme is launched and the board does not tie our fit to a GTF2. Company record: E2 engine deliveries 'under control' in May 2026. Advice: Korea brings no airliner engine (research, unverified); engines were 'part of the supply chain challenges' in our guidance (record); the turboprop's cancellation was reported as engine immaturity (research, unverified). Flag (company record plus inference): the E2, a re-wing and re-engine of an existing family, took about five years from launch (June 2013) to first delivery (April 2018), with a clean EIS. The board gives a clean-sheet 150-180 seater, a step Embraer has never taken, four years. Embraer integrates and certifies; the partner cannot fill that gap (research, unverified). The board prices no slip.

tests.numbers: Brief: US climate cuts our share of new customers by 10% (12% to 10.8%, 7% to 6.3%, 4% to 3.6%). Effect on deliveries: none in S1 to S4, where the line binds (10.8% wants 151-213 a year, 6.3% wants 88-124, against a 96 line). In S5 from 2040: 4.0% against 3.6% is about 8 aircraft a year at about 1,950 demand, roughly $0.05B a year of profit. So the jet can still sell its line into the big markets; the US cut does not set our volume. Not priced: BNDES credit, the golden share, a US response to a Brazil-Korea airliner. Over 40% US content cuts both ways (company record).

S3 (fps 7-yr, 2037): narrow, my soft veto leg (a). S4 (NGSA, 2037): narrow, my soft veto leg (a). S5 (NGSA 2037, fps 10-yr 2040): shut, H3, no launch. vetoes.plan: Launch in 2030 (EIS 2034): no soft veto from me, advice only

Advice, not binding: the window in S3 to S5 (3 years) is shorter than our ramp to 96 (2034-2039); the line, not demand, sets deliveries in S1 to S4; the supply base would carry about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039; the board's four-year clean-sheet schedule is shorter than the E2's five.
