If it shows NGSA (2037) and fps 10-yr (2040): shut window, hard rule H3, no launch at all. Advice now; I will test it on the 2035 brief.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Toward a launch: a brief that shows ΔPV at or above zero in the expected column with the debt penalty included, for example partners carrying more of the bill or a larger line, since customers want about 150-210 a year in S1 against a 96 line. I give no credit to either until a brief shows it. Toward a veto: a bulletin showing fps or NGSA due in service at or before our EIS, or a brief reporting an engine or supply-chain problem that would hold the line. For 2035: fps 7-yr or NGSA launched this round (EIS 2037) puts a 2035 launch under my soft veto; NGSA plus fps 10-yr shuts it under H3.
ops.memo:
That's a triple layer question, so three parts.

First, the window. At our 2034 entry into service no new-generation type is in service in any column; the earliest is 2037. Three years of clear air in S3 to S5, six in S2, open-ended in S1. Leg (a) passes.

Second, the line. P&W is fitted and the brief reports no engine or supply problem, so leg (b) passes. Two flags, not vetoes: a clean-sheet 150-180 seater in four years, when the E2 took about five to first delivery; and a second line climbing to 96 a year on the same suppliers as an E-Jet line going to 120, where the bottlenecks move from one critical supplier to another.

Third, the customers. They are there. At 10.8% of new customers they want 150 to 210 aircraft a year; our line builds 96. So the line, not demand, sets our deliveries in S1 to S4, and the US cut costs us nothing there. Only S5, at 3.6% from 2040, takes us to about 70 a year: that is the $0.22B.

The window is not what stops this. It is 96 aircraft at $6M against a $5.50B bill: minus $1.02B in S1. The funding verdict is Felipe's, but no test of mine turns that positive, right?

My recommendation: hold. No veto from me on 2030. For 2035, watch this bulletin: fps 7-yr or NGSA launched now means a narrow window and my soft veto; both means shut.

other_moves.move: Deliver the plan to 2030 and build cash for a potential next move
other_moves.detail: Keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan. Productivity comes before new capacity, and commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it. The cash this builds is there to support a potential next move [EX-0080, EX-0081, EX-0053, EX-0079]. The board does not price this move.

other_moves.move: Keep technology readiness funded for a new product cycle
other_moves.detail: Studies continue for a new cycle of products, naming no segment and no date. We keep talking to all the engine makers and select none, since engine selection comes before any business case [EX-0112, EX-0141, EX-0133, EX-0044]. We stay prepared to make that decision when the time comes.

other_moves.move: Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
other_moves.detail: The talks continue under the July 2026 civil MoU (research, unverified), and I follow them personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034]. On this brief's terms, a launch reaches zero only with our own share near 35%: partners near 65%, about $2.0B more than the $4.5B the brief shows. Nothing counts until a brief shows that money. No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control, and no military technology moves, so the state's consent should not be needed (golden share; inference).

other_moves.move: Prepare the 2035 readiness package (CFO funding and ops window and supply)
other_moves.detail: Santana brings the 2035 Launch row: the partner share that would close the gap, the net-debt path against the inherited 2x comfort and the ~$2B cash floor, and the risk column against the 5-point limit. Meijer counts the 2035 window (entry into service 2039) from this round's bulletin. He also maps supplier headroom for a second line beside the E2 ramp: about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039, 1.8 times the 2030 target, with bottlenecks that move between suppliers [EX-0088, EX-0159]. He sets certification of a clean sheet in four years against the E2's roughly five.

other_moves.move: Trade: argue for zero tariffs on aerospace, on data
other_moves.detail: More than 40% of our aircraft is US content [EX-0124]. Tariffs mean fewer aircraft sold in the US, fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs [EX-0101]. We ask both governments to talk and take no side, and we discuss no politics [EX-0100, EX-0098, EX-0106].

decision.public_statement: Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We focused on delivering the results in our plan to 2030 with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. We keep doing that, with a very healthy cash generation to support a potential next move. On a new product, I will give the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies because it is important that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. We need a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. Any large investment will be made with partners, and we talk to many partners and to all the engine makers. Today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. This does not depend only on us. It depends on the technology available in the market and on the partners, and the investment has to prove its return. On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions, and I can only speak for Embraer. On trade, Embraer is about engineering, and we focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic. We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost.
decision.rationale:
Decision: Hold (Do Nothing, no new narrowbody). Hold is the default and not a Board item. It is the best grid plan in all five columns: +0.00 $B, 100.0%.

Columns. The expected column is S1, Rivals hold, as I named it in my frame: the public record shows no rival launch, and S1 to S4 lie within $0.01B of one another for a Launch, so the reading does not depend on that choice. The risk column is S5 (Boeing fps 10-yr plus Airbus NGSA), the worst column the bulletin has not ruled out.

The ExCo took my four questions on the brief's numbers.

(1) Strong product, strong value proposition? The product is adequate, not compelling. By the rules it is slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX and worse than a new-generation type. After the 10% US cut it wins 10.8% of new customers while neither fps nor NGSA is in service, 6.3% with one and 3.6% with both. At $50M and a 12% margin it earns $6.0M an aircraft. The line rises from 16 in 2034 to 96 a year from 2039, so full rate is worth about $0.58B a year of operating profit. The window at a 2034 entry into service is open in every column; the earliest rival entry into service is 2037. The value proposition fails on value: the line caps the margin pool at a level that cannot carry our share of the bill.

(2) Robust funding, no risk to financial health? It fails. Team Korea carries 30% ($3.0B), the risk-sharing suppliers 10% and Brazilian state research money 5%, so H1 passes. Our 55% is still $5.50B, booked at entry into service in 2034. Net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of the $11B enterprise value), and the debt penalty rises by $0.59B in 2034, $0.26B in present value, already netted in the grid and not subtracted twice. Santana's funding test fails leg 2 (S1: -1.02 $B, -9.3 yp, against at or above zero) and leg 3 (S5: -1.24 $B, -11.3 yp, against the 5-point limit). Under the team rule that veto binds, with no override. His advice lines confirm it, though they do not decide it: about 7.5x leverage against the inherited "below 2x", investment grade at risk, and a cash call of $1.375B a year in 2030-33, 3.4 times the capex run rate and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor each year.

(3) Technology available? Yes, on the brief. The board fits P&W, the E2's maker, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem, so both of Meijer's legs pass. His flags are advice: a clean sheet in four years where the E2 took about five, and a supply base carrying about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039.

(4) Will the investment prove its return against Do Nothing? No. Launch is 9.3 yp below Hold in S1 and S2, 9.4 yp below in S3 and S4, and 11.3 yp below in S5. That is 4.6 to 5.6 times the 2-yp tie band ($0.22B) and beyond the 5-yp premium cap ($0.55B). One eye on the fish and the other eye on the cat, right? I mean, the investment has to prove its return [EX-0079].

By the team rule: the Launch fails the CFO's funding test, so it is out, and no override exists. Meijer raises no soft veto on 2030, so there is nothing to override; the override margin, a plan more than 5 yp better than Hold, could not apply to a plan that sits below Hold. The gap is far outside the tie band, so the 2030 tie-break does not come into play: this is a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.

Hard rules: H1 passes. H2 would be breached by a Launch (the grid is below zero in the expected column and the funding test fails). H3 is open at 2034. H4 does not apply. H5: premium zero. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing orders it this round, its order would stand and any launch of ours would be refused, so a launch cannot pre-empt it. That risk is no reason to launch at -9.3 yp, and the Board would veto a launch argued on it.

One-way door: a 2030 launch enters service in 2034, before the 2035 round, and the rules allow a cancel only before entry into service, so no round could cancel it. Even in 2034 the write-off would be the whole $5.50B.

Objective: "in service by 2040" stays unmet this round. Closing it now would cost at least $1.02B (9.3 yp), beyond the $0.55B cap and against a binding veto, so I pay no premium and log $0.00B. "ΔPV at or above zero with the debt penalty included" is kept.

2035: it is the last round that can meet 2040 (entry into service 2039). On Santana's rebuild, confirmed by my own (work/r1_decide_calc.py), a 2035 launch on S1 terms at our 55% is -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp). It reaches zero only near a 35% own share, partners near 65%, about $2.0B more than the brief shows. So at today's terms the 2035 option is also below Hold. The window may also narrow or shut on this round's rival orders (S3 and S4 narrow, S5 shut), but at these terms losing it costs nothing on the grid; it costs only the objective.

Record and doctrine: my record drove the posture: funding first [EX-0046, EX-0034], financial health [EX-0140], return before capacity [EX-0079], the plan to 2030 [EX-0080, EX-0081] and rivals not setting the date [EX-0093]. Doctrine (profile H2 and H5, teams.md) supplied the numeric thresholds: ΔPV at or above zero, the 5-yp risk limit, and the 2-yp band and 5-yp cap. Bias check: the "Not yet" label does not apply, because every test is resolved. The Launch failed on the numbers; we are not studying without deciding. "Return first" is on display, within the cap.

memo_weighing.cfo: Taken in full; it decides the round. Santana's binding funding veto stands, and I seek no override, since the rule allows none. Leg 1 passes: partners carry 45% ($4.5B), Team Korea 30% of it. Leg 2 fails: S1 -1.02 $B (-9.3 yp), and S2 to S4 read the same. Leg 3 fails: S5 -1.24 $B (-11.3 yp) against -5 yp. His reconciliation is right. My frame's -0.96 came from the brief's rounded rows ($0.6B for $0.576B a year); the exact $6.0M a jet gives -1.023, and I adopt the brief's -1.02. I accept that the debt penalty is counted once ($0.59B rise in 2034, $0.26B in present value). I weighed the advice lines as confirming the result, not deciding it: about 7.5x leverage, investment grade at risk, a $1.375B yearly cash call (3.4 times capex, 69% of the cash floor) and four years of suspended cash conversion. The leverage line rests on his EV/EBITDA inference, which is why I keep it as advice. His 2035 bar becomes our bar for the next package: -0.61 $B at 55%, break-even near a 35% own share, and net debt still about 38-39% of enterprise value at that share. No credit for money a brief does not show.
memo_weighing.ops: Taken in full as advice; it raises no veto. Both legs pass for 2030. (a) The window is open in every column at 2034, with the earliest rival entry into service in 2037. (b) P&W is fitted, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. The line, not demand, sets deliveries in S1 to S4, so the US cut costs nothing there. The share binds only in S5 from 2040, at about 25 aircraft a year short of the line, which is the grid's $0.22B. His flags go into the 2035 package, not into this order: an edge that is slight, not compelling; a clean sheet in four years against the E2's roughly five; about 216 commercial jets a year on the same supply base by 2039; and a brief margin of 12% against the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025. The board prices no shortfall there, so the real-world risk is to the downside (inference). One correction: he attributes my -0.96 to counting 16 deliveries in 2034, but my frame calculation had 0 in 2034. The gap was rounding, as Santana says; it does not matter here. I adopt his 2035 window count: S1 open, S2 open by one year (fps in 2040), S3 and S4 narrow (his soft veto), S5 shut (H3).

decision.expected_scenario: S1: Rivals hold. The public record shows no fps or NGSA launch, and Boeing's and Airbus's choices are theirs. For a Launch, S1 to S4 are within $0.01B of one another, and S1 is the column most favourable to it. The Launch fails in S1, so it fails everywhere. The risk column is S5 (Boeing fps 10-yr plus Airbus NGSA).
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: Do Nothing (no new narrowbody): +0.00 $B (100.0%) in S1. It is also the best plan in S2 to S5. Launch the new narrowbody with Korea is -1.02 $B (90.7%, -9.3 yp) in S1.
decision.premium_reason: No value is given up. Hold is the best grid plan in every column (+0.00 $B). Meeting the 2040 objective with a 2030 launch would cost $1.02B (9.3 yp) in S1 and $1.24B (11.3 yp) in S5, beyond the $0.55B (5 yp) cap of H5, and Santana's binding veto has already struck it. Premium logged at $0.00B (0 yp).
decision.objective_note: The brief's objective has two parts. "New narrowbody in service by 2040" is not met this round. It stays open only through a 2035 launch (entry into service 2039), the last round that can meet it. On this brief's terms, that launch rebuilds at -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp) at our 55% share. It would need partners near 65% of the bill, an open window on this round's bulletin, and the funding and window tests passed. "ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included" is met (+0.00 $B). We keep the balance sheet safe and do not buy the first part with a loss of 9.3 to 11.3 yp, which is beyond the 5-yp cap.
decision.predictions:
Private. This round, our Hold stands without Board review: ΔPV +0.00 $B, yield 100.0%, in every column. I do not forecast Boeing's or Airbus's orders. The decision holds in all of S1 to S5, and I keep S1 as the planning column.

For 2035, I expect the brief's Launch row to stay below zero at a 55% share: around -0.6 $B on S1 terms, worse if a rival type is due. So Do Nothing is likely right again unless a brief shows partners carrying near 65% of the bill.

If this round's bulletin shows fps 7-yr or NGSA launched (entry into service 2037), the 2035 window is narrow and under Meijer's soft veto. If it shows NGSA plus fps 10-yr, the window is shut under H3. If Boeing orders fps via Embraer, our narrowbody is barred for good, and we hold by rule.

The 2035 brief should show net debt still low and cash built, since the plan to 2030 has been delivered (not priced on the board).

board_response.recommendation: Hold in 2030 and put the grid in the rationale: the Launch is 9.3 to 11.3 yp below Do Nothing in every column, so it fails the CEO's condition of a funding strategy that does not put financial health at risk; a Hold on the grid, not on the tie-break.
board_response.response: Taken up. The order is Hold, and the rationale carries the full grid: Launch is -1.02 $B (S1, S2), -1.03 $B (S3, S4) and -1.24 $B (S5), with the debt penalty included and counted once. S1 is the expected column and S5 the risk column. Santana's binding veto stands on legs 2 and 3. The gap is 4.6 to 5.6 times the 2-yp tie band, so the tie-break does not come into play. Hold is not a Board item; this record is for the Board's information.

board_response.recommendation: Keep technology readiness funded and keep Team Korea talks going through the harvest: deliver the plan to 2030 and build cash for a potential next move, so a 2035 decision is a real one.
board_response.response: Taken up as three other moves. The plan to 2030 and the cash build are public. board_response.recommendation: Santana should show, for 2035, what closes the gap on the brief's own terms (own share near 35-37%, partners about 18-20 points more), with no credit until a brief shows it; also show the net-debt rise to about $6.2B (56% of EV) against the 2x comfort and the ~$2B cash floor.
board_response.response: Taken up. Santana's memo shows it, and my check confirms it. A 2035 launch on S1 terms at our 55% rebuilds at -0.61 $B (-5.5 yp). Break-even is an own share near 35%: partners near 65%, about $2.0B or 20 points more than the $4.5B shown. The 2035 readiness package will carry these lines.

board_response.recommendation: Flag 2035 as the last round in which a Launch (in service 2039) meets the 2040 objective; Meijer to count the 2035 window from this round's bulletin; no Launch for the objective alone.
board_response.response: Taken up. 2035 is flagged as the last round for the 2040 objective. Meijer's count by this round's columns: S1 open; S2 open by one year (fps in 2040); S3 and S4 narrow (rival in service from 2037, his soft veto); S5 shut (H3, no launch). He will recount it from the actual bulletin. I agree that the objective alone never justifies a launch: any premium for it stays inside the 5-yp cap, and it never overrides a failed funding test.

board_response.recommendation: Public statement on economics, not politics: no segment and no entry-into-service date before a launch, no comment on Boeing's or Airbus's choices; on US tariffs, argue jobs and a return to zero tariffs.

ops.note:
Concur. My answer has three parts.

First, there is nothing for my veto to test. The order is enb: hold. My soft veto covers only a launch, on two legs: (a) a narrow window, or (b) a supply-chain or engine problem that would hold the line. No launch is ordered, so neither leg applies. Hold is the default and not a Board item. It is also the best grid plan in every column: +0.00 $B against a Launch at -1.02 (S1, S2), -1.03 (S3, S4) and -1.24 (S5). The CEO reads my memo correctly. The window at a 2034 entry into service is open in every column, and the earliest rival entry into service is 2037. P&W is fitted, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. In S1 to S4 the line sets our deliveries, not demand. The share binds only in S5 from 2040.

Second, two corrections, both mine to make. (1) I stand corrected on the -0.96. I rebuilt both versions (work/r1_meijer_vetocheck_calc.py). On the brief's rounded profit rows (0.2 to 0.6) the result is -0.956; at the exact $6.0M an aircraft it is -1.023. The difference is rounding, not 16 deliveries in 2034, so I withdraw that attribution. (2) The grid shows S3 and S4 at 90.7%, the same as S1 and S2, so the loss against Hold there is 9.3 yp, not 9.4. This makes no difference to the result.

Third, the other moves are consistent with the rule and with my record. Output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it. The engine talks stay open to all makers. The Team Korea talks continue with no segment, no date and no commitment. The public statement names neither the airplane nor a date. I take up the 2035 readiness tasks the CEO gave me:
- recount the 2039 window from this round's actual bulletin;
- map supplier headroom for a second line beside the E-Jet line (about 216 commercial jets a year by 2039, 1.8 times the 2030 target);
- set a four-year clean-sheet certification against the E2's roughly five.

My forward flag stands. If the bulletin shows fps 7-yr or NGSA launched (entry into service 2037), a 2035 launch meets a narrow window and my soft veto. If it shows both NGSA and fps 10-yr, the window is shut (H3). This is record applied by inference, plus company record. Campaign optimism aside, the customers are there. The problem is the bill, not the window.
